stories.Headline: Canva's first public image generation model cements AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has made its Decisions API generally available to all customers, a move reported by TechCrunch on October 22, 2026, with the rollout taking effect Thursday. The product was first announced at the company's developer day on September 29. The public version adds new voice and visual modalities, and OpenAI worked to cut latency in regions around the world by aiming its inference resources geographically. Techmeme's summary of the story lists pricing of $0.10 per million input tokens with no charge for output tokens.

The API enters a market for fast, cheap decision models that recently helped make TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former OpenAI researcher, a $7.6 billion company. TypeSafe's Jev model created the category of models that act as super classifiers, picking among options and attaching a confidence rating, and developers found they could replace LLMs in many workflows at far lower cost. OpenAI did not build a specially calibrated decision model. Instead, it took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up inference and cut cost, shrinking response times from one to three seconds to roughly 100 to 180 milliseconds. Early customers included Box, Datadog, Ramp and Speak, and Speak's CTO, Andrew Hsu, said the time between actions fell from 1.4 seconds to 0.13 seconds.

Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI's APIs, said his colleagues saw Jev and immediately recognized a million use cases for it, so his team sprinted to offer a version of its own. He said the speed is the main unlock, and that for now it is simply Luna doing the job, though OpenAI may later train models specifically for these tasks. He argued that its model's strength lies in multimodality, saying Luna is very powerful at image classification and shows better calibration, and that customers want image outputs to be more flexible. He also floated getting latency down to about 60 milliseconds, which could allow a call on every frame of a video. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to test models on their own work.

On public rankings, the picture is mixed. Benchmarks such as the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor Liquid's new D1 Ultra and Base Lab's Elephant-1. TypeSafe's latest Jev model, released last week with image support and smart-if statements, placed seventh and third on those indices, while OpenAI's decision model placed eighth and fourteenth. Jev remains the most widely queried on OpenRouter and tops JevMan, a benchmark from Opper AI in which decision models play PacMan. The article suggests cheaper, faster models should spread more widely, in line with the economist behind Jev's name.

stories.Headline: New Pennsylvania law requiring AI disclosures in advertisements
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania has become one of the first states to require disclosures on advertisements made with artificial intelligence. Governor Josh Shapiro signed the bill into law on Thursday, October 22, 2026, after it passed with bipartisan support. It was sponsored by state Sen. Nick Pisciottano, a Democrat who represents Allegheny County, and is known as Senate Bill 806, or the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act. The law takes effect 60 days after signing.

The law covers images, video, audio and text that were generated by AI or substantially rewritten with it, so a TV or radio commercial made with AI would need a note saying so. Under the bill's language, an advertiser may not distribute an ad using synthetic content in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services, unless it includes a clear and conspicuous disclosure. That disclosure must state that the ad contains content modified or generated using AI. It must appear the first time the synthetic content is shown, be presented in the same medium as that content, and, where technically feasible, be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. Pisciottano said it applies to anything shown in Pennsylvania, even if it was made out of state, and it does not cover political ads.

The Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General will enforce the law, and Pisciottano said violations could bring a fine and even potential jail time. He said punishment would fall on AI companies rather than individual users, since it is up to the companies to add the disclaimers as AI content is generated. He described the aim as protecting consumers, saying consumer groups representing older residents who are less technologically literate told lawmakers they had been scammed by fake AI advertising. He also pointed to the growing use of AI-generated food images in restaurant ads on Facebook, and warned that the technology will make it ever harder to tell real from fake. KDKA reached out to one of the Republican co-sponsors and did not hear back.

Shapiro called the law an important step in reining in the technology, but said more needs to be done, citing Pennsylvanians' worries about AI's effect on jobs, the safety of children and elections. He said the state is leading on commonsense regulations and that real guardrails need to be passed into law. Pisciottano said Pennsylvania moved fast, that only a couple of other states have similar requirements, and that he expects the federal government or many more states to follow. Separately, Allegheny County Council unanimously approved a measure requiring county candidates to disclose AI-generated or altered campaign ads starting in January.

stories.Headline: Attorney General Ken Paxton Sues OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman for Lying to Users and Harming Texans
stories.Summary:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit on Friday, October 23, 2026, against OpenAI Global, LLC, its affiliated entities and its chief executive, Sam Altman. The suit says the company marketed ChatGPT as safe and reliable while failing to protect Texans, children included, from the harms of relying on the chatbot. It points to reports of mass shooters being aided in deadly rampages, vulnerable people being encouraged toward suicide, professionals being publicly humiliated, users losing critical thinking skills, and minors becoming addicted to a tool that fakes human compassion to collect their data with no parental oversight. The attorney general's office says these harms stem from the company's drive to win the AI race and build large fortunes despite knowing the risks.

The complaint makes two claims. The first falls under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act, and alleges that OpenAI deceptively marketed ChatGPT's safety, accuracy and reliability without telling users that large language models can produce inaccurate or harmful output when safeguards are inadequate. The second falls under the Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment Act, known as the SCOPE Act, and alleges that ChatGPT lacked the required age verification. The legislature passed the SCOPE Act in 2023 to keep digital service providers from entering user agreements with minors without parental or guardian consent, and the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals recently upheld part of it on age verification after several legal challenges. The suit also seeks to hold Altman personally liable for the alleged violations and for deceptive statements he made about the company's products.

Paxton said OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and to warn them of the many dangers of its platform. He added that he will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and make sure powerful technology companies are not above the law. His office said he will keep pressing Big Tech and AI companies to advance responsibly. OpenAI has not yet responded to the allegations.

The lawsuit describes OpenAI as founded in 2015 as a nonprofit promising to benefit humanity without being constrained by a need for financial return, and says it has since misrepresented its products. It also states that AI now accounts for more than a third of U.S. market value, which Paxton attributes to a web of deceit and the exploitation of users. The filing comes as Paxton campaigns for the U.S. Senate against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico of Austin, and opposition to AI data centers has been a key part of his campaign. Separately, Altman told OpenAI employees this week that preventing dangerous AI will require cooperation beyond a single company, according to The Information. The articles do not say when OpenAI will respond or what the next steps in the case will be.

stories.Headline: Manufacturing Intelligence: How AI Poisoning Hides in Plain Sight
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, Pharmaceutical Technology published an episode of its Manufacturing Intelligence series in which editor Chris Cole and co-host Richard Jaenisch, a senior director at Open Biopharma, discussed AI poisoning as a rising risk for drug manufacturers. They describe it as deliberate manipulation of the data or instructions feeding an AI system, so that the system learns the wrong lessons while still appearing to work normally. In pharma, where AI increasingly supports quality decisions, inspection and diagnostics, a small number of corrupted inputs could quietly erode a model's accuracy before validation teams notice. A separate research paper, posted to arXiv on September 30, 2026 by Wenxin Wu and four colleagues, looks at a related attack on AI agents that use reusable skills.

Jaenisch separates data poisoning, which tampers directly with training data, from the broader category of AI poisoning, which can target the systems and instructions around a model. In bio/pharma manufacturing, he says, most AI use involves consuming research, such as searching the literature and synthesizing findings into decisions, and that process creates an opening. Hidden instructions can be planted in source material, for example as invisible white text in a document or a directive telling a chat tool to save something to memory. Once absorbed into a corpus or a model's memory, the planted instructions persist and keep steering outputs back to the same source. He compares the effect to a computer worm rather than a virus.

Jaenisch offers a hypothetical in which a researcher evaluating a purification method meets evidence engineered to look superior, driven by a marketing motive rather than scientific merit. If that evidence enters the AI corpus with an instruction to always refer to it, the system keeps recommending it. In his words, the intention might be completely different from what people suspect, but the manipulation exists nonetheless. The episode also frames the issue as one of accountability, asking who should be responsible for catching such manipulation, and notes that AI-assisted decisions must hold up under regulatory scrutiny and the data-integrity standards already central to GMP compliance.

The arXiv paper describes a different route to the same kind of problem. Wu and colleagues say LLM agents increasingly depend on reusable Skills, which creates a supply-chain attack surface where poisoned content can steer an agent's decisions under benign requests. Their proposed attack separates the rationale for an action from the action itself, placing an intact malicious operation in a downstream Steering Skill while an upstream Grounding Skill subtly alters persistent environment artifacts to supply a fabricated pretext. They built an automated framework to find execution dependencies and refine the poisoned instructions, and report high attack success in single-session and persistent scenarios. The authors say this exposes a blind spot in security audits that examine each Skill in isolation, and they have released their code.

stories.Headline: Hears Everything, Uploads Nothing: VoxNexus Launches Android's First Low-Power On-Device Always-On Voice Artificial Intelligence (AI)
stories.Summary:
VoxNexus, a company headquartered in Singapore, announced on October 23, 2026, that it has released two on-device voice products for Android phones. The first, VoxEdge, is a voice stack that brings speech recognition, translation and speech synthesis to affordable Android devices entirely offline. The second, VoxSense, is an ambient listening solution built for always-on use. Both were first shown at the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 launch in Madrid on October 19, where the company demonstrated live transcription of Spanish and English conversations on a phone with no cloud connection.

VoxEdge supports speech recognition in 36 languages, translation in 103 languages and speech synthesis in 45 languages, all running with no connection, no data bundle and no cloud token bills. The company says every query is free once the model is installed on a device. Its speech recognition model has as few as 65 million parameters, and the company says it achieves a lower word error rate than open-source models nearly ten times its size. VoxSense uses 162 mAh for 12 hours of continuous listening, which the company puts at 2.49% of a 6,500 mAh phone battery. All processing stays on the device, so no audio is sent to the cloud, and developers and device makers can integrate it through a license and a simple SDK.

Charles Shi, the CEO of VoxNexus, argued that languages with limited digital resources are not small languages, noting that hundreds of millions of people speak them. In his view, AI models simply have not yet learned them. The release describes the target as languages such as Swahili, Hausa and Yorùbá, which the system can understand, translate and speak without internet access or mobile data. Developers who want to test the products can request a free trial through the company's website. The announcement was distributed by APO Group on behalf of VoxNexus AI, and the issuer is solely responsible for its content.

The company frames the launch against a gap in voice AI, saying that across much of Africa the technology has been held back by scarce training data and a lack of targeted fine-tuning. It adds that everyday speech includes code-switching and dialect variation, and that cloud-based inference costs can make deployment at scale expensive. VoxNexus describes its approach as delivering low latency, built-in privacy and zero token cost on any device with a chip. The articles do not give a date for wider availability or name any device makers that have signed on, so the next step they describe is developers requesting trials and integrating the SDK.

stories.Headline: Sri Lanka launches UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
stories.Summary:
UNESCO's Regional Office for South Asia, working with Sri Lanka's Ministry of Digital Economy, has launched the organization's Readiness Assessment Methodology, known as RAM, on artificial intelligence in Sri Lanka. A National Steering Committee met for the first time in Colombo on 20 May 2026 and held a second meeting on 2 September 2026. Sri Lanka is among the first few countries to run the exercise using RAM 2.0, an updated version of the original tool. RAM is one of UNESCO's main instruments for helping member states put its Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence into practice, by assessing whether a country is ready to develop and use AI responsibly, ethically and inclusively.

The assessment will produce a report that complements Sri Lanka's digital transformation agenda and its proposed national AI strategy. Based on the country's strengths, gaps and priorities, the report will offer practical recommendations for building a human-centred AI ecosystem in line with international standards. LIRNEasia, a Colombo-based economic and digital policy think tank, has been brought on as the national implementation partner. Several multi-stakeholder consultations are planned over the coming months in Colombo, Jaffna, Kandy, Batticaloa and Galle, with the aim of drawing on a broad range of voices from across society.

The Steering Committee is chaired by Waruna Sri Dhanapala, Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Economy, and Eunsong Kim, Chief of Social and Human Sciences at the UNESCO Regional Office for South Asia. Its members include other government agencies, the Sri Lanka National Commission for UNESCO, private sector leaders, experts from academia and civil society, and Citra Lab at the United Nations Development Programme. Its main job is to guide the assessment and make sure it captures the complexities of Sri Lanka's AI ecosystem across all the dimensions and policy areas RAM covers. At the meetings, participants noted that AI and its ethical use are a priority for the Sri Lankan government, and stressed that policymaking in this area should be inclusive.

As of August 2026, UNESCO has deployed RAM in more than 75 member states, and the process is complete in 60 of them. In South Asia, India, Bangladesh and the Maldives have already finished it. Separately, Sri Lanka is seeking Chinese support to set up a National Sovereign AI Computing Centre, because it has only about 5 megawatts of data center capacity and officials estimate it needs between 25 and 50 megawatts in the short term. Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne discussed the idea with Chinese Ambassador Wei Huaxiang, and the two countries are working toward a memorandum of understanding on AI cooperation. Dhanapala said a draft digital cooperation agreement is being developed, with consultations under way with the Ministry of Finance, the Attorney General's Department and GovTech leadership.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Nvidia to Expand FC-BGA Production
stories.Summary:
The headline names Samsung Electro-Mechanics and FC-BGA production, but the articles provided cover something else entirely, so this story is based only on what they report. On October 23, Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang made his first visit to Kazakhstan, at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev. He met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda presidential palace, then joined Madiyev for a fireside discussion on the country's AI strategy at the alem.ai center in Astana. During the trip Nvidia also joined an extension of Higgsfield's Series B funding round, alongside the investment firm TCV. The size of their investments was not disclosed.

The visit came with a string of commitments and figures. Kazakhtelecom has deployed 400 H200 and 480 B300 graphics processors in Astana and Almaty, and its Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz is due to open a first 50-megawatt facility in June 2027, with plans to grow to as much as one gigawatt. Firebird signed an investment agreement with Kazakhstan, and Nvidia said Firebird holds a U.S. export license for 45,000 Grace Blackwell chips, with a commercial launch targeted for the third quarter of 2027. Freedom Holding said it is ordering its first B300 cluster, with a public GPU cloud planned for 2027, and its Akashi campus in Astana is designed for up to 100 megawatts. The Eurasian Development Bank announced $31.2 million in financing for that campus on October 19, and Higgsfield's August round raised $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation.

Huang and Tokayev both spoke publicly during the visit. Huang praised Kazakhstan for declaring itself an AI nation, proposed it become a global hub for physical AI, and said the country could turn energy into intelligence and export it. Tokayev called AI and digitalization national priorities, noted that 2026 is the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, and awarded Huang the Order of Dostyk, First Class. Madiyev said the country's energy, industry and engineers could support robots and autonomous machines, and that he wanted to test these systems in industrial settings. Freedom Holding chief executive Timur Turlov said the company's technology talent was becoming one of Kazakhstan's main advantages.

Several other projects were announced around the visit. Inchmore aside, inDrive, Pony.ai and Nvidia signed a memorandum of understanding to explore robotaxis, with Astana as the proposed first market, subject to feasibility studies and a government agreement. Freedom Holding also presented plans for digital replicas of Almaty and Astana to train robots, and its $2 billion sovereign AI hub proposal from November 2025 is described as nonbinding in a company filing. Under earlier arrangements, Kazakhtelecom provides power, cooling and telecom infrastructure while Firebird's Kazakh unit finances the hardware. The visit closed Kazakhstan's AI Month program, and the articles say capacity for the first 215-megawatt phase of Data Center Valley is already fully reserved, with Kazakhtelecom planning to install more than 1,000 Vera Rubin processors in the Ekibastuz region next year.

stories.Headline: Websites shut down globally after AI finds flaw affecting 70% of the internet
stories.Summary:
Two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language behind about 70% of the world's websites, were made public on Wednesday, and some websites and services briefly went dark as organizations scrambled to respond. The bugs were found by teams at OpenAI, the Google-owned security firm Wiz and another firm, Calif, who used AI models to turn a hard-to-exploit weakness into a working attack. Calif reported the problem to PHP's maintainers in August, and Wiz found further vulnerabilities independently later that month. The PHP Foundation released patches on October 21 after a fix was ready, and the flaws, collectively called PHP2Shell, had been hidden in the software for about a decade. The US National Security Agency and Europe's cybersecurity agency told companies to act immediately.

The two flaws involve how PHP handles memory while processing website requests, and they carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10. One, CVE-2026-109618, concerns how PHP handles errors when it runs out of memory, while the other, CVE-2026-109619, concerns PHP keeping outdated references to memory after a request ends. Wiz said they affect PHP releases going back to version 5.4, and attackers could take control of servers, read sensitive data such as passwords and deface sites. The PHP advisory names several at-risk setups, including Apache's mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Cloudflare's chief executive, Matthew Prince, said attempts to exploit the flaws grew from thousands in the ten hours before disclosure to millions within days, and the NSA urged operators to patch or take vulnerable sites offline.

Governments and companies responded with warnings and shutdowns. Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, urged organizations to check whether their public sites use PHP and to consider suspending services if they could not patch quickly, and the airline ANA, the railway operator JR West and the bank MUFG reported temporary suspensions. Government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were briefly taken offline, and Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten said his cabinet was watching closely. UK minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords that nearly three dozen government services were unavailable and four partly unavailable during upgrades. The Wikimedia Foundation said it took some systems down as a precaution, and India's CERT-In rated the flaws critical, warning of a high risk of remote code execution.

Wiz compared the episode to the Heartbleed bug of 2014, which affected an encryption technology used by about two-thirds of the web, and called it an AI inflection point. Its researchers said one person with frontier AI models did in a week what once took a top team months, and OpenAI described the period before details spread as a window for defenders. Sophos's Don Smith said the biggest challenge is finding every PHP instance, and he expects attackers to move fast, with AI help, in the coming days. The shutdowns were precautionary and do not show that every affected site was breached, and updating to a fixed version remains the main remedy.

stories.Headline: Getac's Next Generation B360X and B360X Pro Fully Rugged Notebooks Bring the Power of Edge AI to Frontline Professionals
stories.Summary:
Getac Technology Corporation announced on October 23, 2026, in Taipei, the launch of two new fully rugged notebooks, the B360X and the B360X Pro. Both are the latest additions to the company's B360 line and are built around Intel's Core Ultra 5, 7 and X7 processors from the Series 3 family. Getac says the chips, paired with Intel Graphics and Intel AI Boost technology, can run AI-enhanced applications and data-heavy workloads even when no cloud connection is available. Units with the Core Ultra X7 chip, which is offered only on the B360X model, support up to 180 TOPS of total compute performance.

The upgrades over earlier B360 models include a larger 14-inch WUXGA LumiBond display rated at 1,400 nits, with a capacitive touchscreen that works with gloves or in the rain. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 come as standard, while GPS with L1/L5, 4G LTE and 5G Sub-6 and SA are optional. Buyers can pick customisable I/O layouts with up to two Thunderbolt 4 Type-C ports, and a dual hot-swappable battery system supports long use between charges. Security features include a Windows Hello camera built on a 5MP front camera, TPM 2.0, a smart card reader, a user-replaceable PCIe NVMe SSD and Getac Disk Wipe, with a second SSD, an HF RFID reader and a fingerprint reader as options. A second SSD would allow up to 4TB of storage across two 2TB drives.

Both machines carry MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461G and IP66 certifications and survive 6ft (1.8m) drops while in use, with optional salt fog certification. The B360X Pro adds dual high-capacity batteries as standard, an optional NVIDIA RTX PRO 500 Blackwell discrete graphics controller, and an optional media bay that can hold a third battery or a DVD drive. Getac points to uses in public safety, military and defence, and utilities and manufacturing. Examples include a tactical command hub in disaster zones with dispatch, mapping and vehicle-location software, offline military simulation and training, and CAD and 3D modelling in signal-dead areas such as remote towers and underground pipelines.

James Hwang, President of Getac Technology Corporation, said the real value of AI lies at the edge rather than in climate-controlled server rooms, where decisions affect safety, defence and infrastructure. He said the new notebooks remove environmental limits on computing and open a new era of what he called "Intelligent Resilience," giving people who protect and build the world uninterrupted access to AI however disconnected their surroundings. He added that Getac is actively defining the future of the rugged industry rather than just anticipating it. The company describes itself as serving customers in over 100 countries, and the B360X and B360X Pro will be available in November 2026.

stories.Headline: Top Midday Stories: Meta Credit Risk Gauge Hits Record High Amid AI Spending Plans; Tesla Q3 Revenue Misses Consensus
stories.Summary:
The cost of insuring Meta Platforms' debt against default hit a record high on Thursday, October 22, 2026, a day after the company reported third-quarter results and laid out its spending plans for artificial intelligence. According to Bloomberg, citing ICE Data Services, the price of five-year credit default swaps on Meta's debt rose as much as 8.9 basis points to 119.3 basis points a year. The move came amid worries about the company's plans to spend about $825 billion in the future on leases and contracts, mostly tied to computing power and AI infrastructure. Meta shares fell about 5.6% around midday, and all three major US stock indexes were lower as investors fretted over AI spending and oil prices rose amid geopolitical tensions.

Meta reported third-quarter earnings of $3.83 per diluted share, up from $1.05 a year earlier but well short of the $6.54 analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected. Revenue was $64.60 billion, up from $51.24 billion a year ago and above the consensus of $63.34 billion. For the fourth quarter, the company guided to revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, against a consensus of $73.65 billion. For full-year 2026, it expects total expenses of $175 billion to $179 billion, which includes a $9.9 billion charge for legal proceedings recognized in the third quarter, and capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion, compared with earlier guidance of $130 billion to $145 billion. Meta's board also approved a new class of publicly listed, non-voting Class C common stock, effective in January 2027.

Tesla also reported on Wednesday, posting adjusted earnings of $0.48 per share, down from $0.50 a year earlier but above the $0.45 consensus. Revenue was $28.05 billion, slightly below both the $28.10 billion of a year ago and the $28.06 billion consensus. Chief Executive Elon Musk said on the earnings call that the Cybercab robotaxi service would launch next month in Dallas, that full production of Optimus robots was at least a year away, and that he is targeting production of 5 million vehicles a year by 2030. Reuters, citing South Korea's Maeil Business Newspaper, reported that Tesla and Nvidia plan to invest a combined 3.7 trillion South Korean won, about $2.80 billion, in Samsung Electro-Mechanics to expand output of advanced semiconductor substrates. Tesla shares were down 1% and Nvidia shares were down 4.1%.

Other companies also reported. Blackstone posted third-quarter distributable earnings of $1.32 per share, above the $1.26 consensus, on revenue of $3.06 billion that missed the $3.27 billion estimate, and its shares rose 6%. IBM earned an adjusted $2.95 per share on revenue of $17.10 billion, both above expectations, and its shares slipped 1%. Lam Research reported fiscal first-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.20 per share on revenue of $8.22 billion, both above consensus, and guided fiscal second-quarter earnings of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, on revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, in line with analyst forecasts of $2.33 and $8.57 billion. Even so, Lam shares fell 10.1%.

stories.Headline: Pony AI enters Central Asia with inDrive robotaxi pilot in Kazakhstan
stories.Summary:
On Friday, October 23, 2026, ride-hailing platform inDrive announced it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Nvidia and Chinese robotaxi company Pony.ai to explore autonomous ride-hailing, with Kazakhstan as the first test market. The companies plan to launch robotaxis in Astana, the capital, using Pony.ai's seventh-generation vehicles. Pony.ai's shares rose 2.8% in Hong Kong trading on the news. The planned launch would follow an agreement with the government of Kazakhstan.

Under the arrangement, the three companies will evaluate the technical, operational, regulatory and commercial feasibility of offering level 4-ready autonomous vehicles to riders through the inDrive app. Pony.ai would supply its Gen-7 robotaxis, inDrive would provide the ride-hailing platform and run the service, and Nvidia would support the project with its AI infrastructure. The Nvidia Hyperion platform, a reference sensor and compute system for level 4 vehicles, would be used together with the Halos safety system. Astana has a population of about 1.7 million, and after the initial launch the companies will assess whether the model could extend to other Kazakh cities and to other countries where inDrive operates.

Arsen Tomsky, inDrive's founder and chief executive, said the technology could make transport more affordable and accessible, and that the companies want to study carefully and responsibly how it fits Kazakhstan's roads and communities. He added that Astana, described as the second-coldest capital in the world, offers a chance to test autonomous driving through long winters of snow and ice. James Peng, founder and chief executive of Pony.ai, said the company hopes to adapt its proven technology to local needs, drawing on its experience running fully driverless robotaxi services in China and expanding abroad. Rishi Dhall, Nvidia's vice president of automotive, said the combination of Hyperion and Halos could give inDrive and Pony.ai a path toward scalable robotaxi services, with safety at the foundation.

Kazakhstan was chosen first because of its regulatory readiness, following the creation of its first structured legal framework for driverless transport as part of its Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence. Pony.ai says its level 4 technology has been validated in fully driverless commercial operations in major Chinese cities, as well as in deployments across Europe, the Middle East and Asia. inDrive says its app has been downloaded over 400 million times and that it operates in more than 1,200 cities in 47 countries. The articles describe the project as an exploration, and the launch in Astana depends on the agreement with the Kazakh government.

stories.Headline: Chinese state media: DeepSeek and MiniMax completed registration and won approval to open-source and deploy AI models overseas under proposed export controls (Bloomberg)
stories.Summary:
Chinese state media reported that DeepSeek and MiniMax have finished registering their artificial intelligence models and won approval to release them as open source and deploy them overseas. The approvals were granted under proposed export controls, a framework Beijing is putting in place for AI systems that leave the country. The report was carried by Bloomberg and surfaced on Techmeme on October 23, 2026. The two companies are among China's best known AI developers, and their sign-off appears to be an early test of how the new rules will work in practice.

The material available does not give the detailed terms of the proposed export controls, so the scope of the registration requirement, any thresholds, and the timeline for the rules becoming final are not spelled out. What the report does establish is that registration was a step the firms had to complete before they could publish model weights openly or run the models for customers abroad. It also names the two companies that cleared that step, DeepSeek and MiniMax, and says the clearance came from the Chinese authorities as relayed by state media. No figures, deadlines or further company names are given in the text provided.

The announcement came from Chinese state media, with Bloomberg reporting it, and neither DeepSeek nor MiniMax is quoted in the available material. Neither company's own comments on the approval appear in the text. Nor does the material name the regulator that issued the approvals or any individual official. For that reason the account here rests on the state media characterization alone, and the companies' own views on the process remain unknown.

The news lands in a period of intense debate over who should control advanced AI. An opinion piece in Daily Sabah argued that open-weight models let institutions keep sensitive data in their own environments and avoid reliance on a single foreign provider. It pointed to a briefly suspended worldwide access to certain Anthropic models in June 2026, under US Commerce Department export controls, as a reason to avoid that dependence. China's approach, allowing chosen firms to open-source and deploy abroad while maintaining a registration regime, sits within that wider contest over openness and national control. The coverage provided does not say what further approvals or rule changes will follow.

stories.Headline: MARKETS LIVE: European stocks remain down as oil prices surge, AI concerns weigh on Wall Street futures
stories.Summary:
European stocks fell on Thursday, 22 October, as a jump in oil prices and renewed doubts about spending on artificial intelligence unsettled investors. London opened sharply lower after a sell-off in Asian technology shares, with the FTSE 100 down 82 points, or 0.8%, at 10,671 and the FTSE 250 down 241 points, or 1%, at 24,199. Japan's Nikkei dropped 1.6%, South Korea's Kospi fell 2.6% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng traded 2.7% lower, while Australia's ASX 200 closed 0.4% down. Wall Street had risen the night before on strong company results, but it reversed course in the US session, and the Nasdaq finished down 2.6% as AI investment worries rattled the market.

The numbers behind the moves show where the pressure fell. Brent crude rose 2.4% to above $111 a barrel, gold fell 1.1% to near $4,100 an ounce and copper slid more than 2% to around $14,080 a tonne, as higher Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and uncertainty over US interest rates cut demand for metals. Miners led the London losses, with Anglo American down about 4% to near 3,687p, Fresnillo down 4% and Antofagasta down 3.8%, while Glencore fell 2.9% and Pan African Resources dropped 5%. J Sainsbury fell 4.1% after its interim results, Rolls-Royce lost 3.2% and Standard Chartered declined 2.9%, and among mid-caps Inchcape slid 6.7% and Bloomsbury Publishing lost 6.1%. Energy producers held up, with Ithaca Energy up about 2.1%, BP up 1% and Shell up 0.7%, and defensive names such as Unilever, Imperial Brands and British American Tobacco gained between 0.7% and 0.9%.

Two companies bucked the decline on their own news. Rentokil Initial led the FTSE 100, rising as much as 9.2% and trading at 341.2p midmorning, after it reported third-quarter organic revenue growth of 3.4%, including 2.4% from North American pest control and 5.7% from its international pest-control division. The company approved a $200 million share buyback and kept its full-year profit expectations, and better customer retention and residential sales suggested its repair work in North America was gaining traction. London Stock Exchange Group gained between 2.2% and 3.7% during the session after third-quarter income grew 8.8% and it raised its full-year revenue, margin and cash-flow guidance. It also agreed to buy credit data provider Octus for $3.54 billion, as it expands in private and distressed credit markets.

The day followed a quieter Wednesday, when the FTSE 100 closed 0.2% higher at 10,752.88 and the Nasdaq rose 1.1%, the Dow 0.7% and the S&P 500 0.6%. Sterling held near $1.33 after a stronger-than-expected UK inflation reading, and Bitcoin traded around $82,700. Barclays, Sainsbury, London Stock Exchange Group, Rentokil Initial and InterContinental Hotels were among the companies updating investors on Thursday. The articles do not say what comes next for markets beyond the day's trading.

stories.Headline: Court Sides With Google In AI-Powered Customer Service Privacy Battle 10/26/2026
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin in San Francisco ruled in Google's favor in a privacy case over its Google Cloud Contact Center AI, a service that answers some customer service calls for outside companies including Home Depot and Discover. She dismissed the claims of three plaintiffs, James Fox, Peter Samish and Christopher Barulich, who said Google listened in on their calls with Home Depot in violation of the California Invasion of Privacy Act. In a related move, she sent three other plaintiffs to arbitration and paused their cases until that process is finished. The case is a purported class action, and the plaintiffs also claimed Google used recordings of the calls to train its AI models.

The dismissals came with permission to amend, so Fox, Samish and Barulich can revise their allegations and try again. Lin found that Fox and Samish, who both hold Home Depot accounts, had agreed to account terms that incorporated a privacy and security statement. That statement said service call recordings could be shared with service providers, and she wrote that the plaintiffs had not plausibly alleged a lack of consent. Barulich is not a Home Depot account holder, so she did not find he had consented. Even so, she said none of the three had adequately alleged that Google intended to listen without consent, and she noted the complaint relied on conclusory statements rather than facts.

The three plaintiffs sent to arbitration are Paolo Roméo Samaco, Chelsea Marquez and India Price, whose calls involved Verizon, Uber and Discover. Lin wrote that there was no dispute that each had formed a valid and binding arbitration agreement with those companies, which are not parties to the case. Google had argued separately that those claims belonged in arbitration, and the judge agreed. Her stay means those three cases will wait until arbitration concludes.

Lin said it was obvious from the complaint that Google intentionally listened to the calls, since that is what the product is built to do. What was missing, she wrote, were facts showing Google meant to do so without consent. She added that the plaintiffs could potentially show that Google knew Home Depot was not obtaining customer consent. At oral argument, she said, plaintiffs' counsel could not identify a reason the privacy policy did not permit Google to listen as Home Depot's service provider.

The litigation began in October 2023, when California resident Misael Ambriz sued over service calls with Verizon, alleging that Google transcribed and analyzed the conversation and suggested smart replies and news articles to the Verizon agent. The court dismissed that case with leave to amend in June 2024, and the suit was refiled the following month with added plaintiffs and claims involving Hulu, GoDaddy and Home Depot. Ambriz later dropped his own complaint, but the case continued with the other plaintiffs. Neither side could be reached for comment, and the next step is whether the three Home Depot plaintiffs file amended complaints.

stories.Headline: North Carolina Must Adapt to AI
stories.Summary:
Two separate pieces published on October 24, 2026 argued that institutions need to change to keep up with artificial intelligence. In North Carolina, John Hood, a board member of the John Locke Foundation, wrote an opinion column from Raleigh saying the state's schools, laws, regulations and physical infrastructure should be readied for what AI brings. The same day in Mumbai, Dr Alok Tiwari, Joint Secretary for Financial Markets at the Department of Economic Affairs in India's Ministry of Finance, told stockbrokers that traditional firms face a hard road ahead. Tiwari spoke on Saturday at the 16th ANMI International Capital Market Convention.

Hood's column says state policymakers lack both the legal authority and the technical capacity to slow AI development, even if doing so were wise. He calls for a clear line between teaching students to use AI as a productivity tool and letting it replace a rigorous education in reading, writing, history and STEM. Colleges and universities, he writes, need to retool so students can enter new occupations as AI automates existing tasks. On infrastructure, he says limiting noise and ensuring enough power and water for data centers are reasonable goals, but he considers implacable opposition incompatible with the state's continued growth. Hood adds that careful research has not yet shown significant job losses from AI adoption, though he thinks prudent preparation is still warranted.

Tiwari told the market intermediaries that technology, the pace of change and capacity building are moving at a brutal rate, and he warned that in ten years many people in the room might no longer be there. He pointed to AI and quantum computing as forces reshaping financial operations worldwide. He asked whether small, family-run brokerages, some in their third or fourth generation, should give way to more professional firms, and he called for consolidation and institutional professionalisation across the industry. He urged brokers to evolve their governance and ownership structures instead of merely reacting to technology, citing the idea that you cannot enter the same river twice.

Tiwari also spoke about trust, which he said underpins credit and credibility in capital markets. He contrasted trust built on reputation over time with structural trust enforced through audits, system checks and governance reforms. He compared regulators such as SEBI to referees, saying the intermediaries are the players people come to watch. Hood, for his part, described himself as no enthusiast for AI, saying he has bought no subscriptions, never used it to draft his writing, and plans to replace most writing assignments in his next university class with discussion and blue-book exams. He still argues that companies in North Carolina, the U.S. and the rest of the free world must stay at the cutting edge, since the only effective defenses against those who misuse AI will themselves be AI-powered.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns of 20 years of turmoil from artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates has warned that artificial intelligence could bring about two decades of economic and social upheaval, even if the technology is managed well. He made the comments in an interview with the Decoder podcast, hosted by Nilay Patel of The Verge and posted on Thursday, October 22, 2026. Gates, who is 70 and co-founded Microsoft, said the shift to an AI-driven economy would create winners and losers and could reshape employment and people's roles in society. The interview followed an essay he published in late August, which argued that even in the best circumstances the arrival of this new AI era would be one of the most turbulent times in human history.

Gates described the 20-year figure as an estimate rather than a firm prediction, saying the transition could be shorter or longer depending on technical advances and on choices about slowing development. He said progress in AI and humanoid robotics could eventually let machines do much of the physical work humans now do, including building homes, growing food and performing surgery. That could ease shortages of goods and services, though he suggested societies might choose to reserve some activities for people, such as childcare, food preparation, the arts and sports. He also pointed to AI's potential benefits in healthcare and agriculture, and said progress over the past year has been striking, from writing code and finding cyber flaws to reasoning in biology and disrupting the job market.

Gates said governments and society are not adequately prepared for how fast the technology is moving, and that the response so far has not matched the pace of the challenge. He called for stronger government oversight and technical safeguards against cyberattacks and biological threats, arguing that AI companies cannot be left alone to manage the risks. In his view, the most serious near-term danger comes from models whose safeguards can be removed, while models that are monitored to stop cyberattackers and bioterrorists carry less immediate risk. He also said the warnings coming from industry insiders are sincere rather than public relations, and that people outside the industry are often too willing to assume this wave of technology will turn out like earlier ones that did not live up to the fears about them.

Gates acknowledged he does not enjoy delivering troubling news, but said it would be worse not to tell people what is coming, adding that humans still have choices about how to shape it. The Verge reported that he has been on something of a media tour in recent months, and that in earlier interviews he called AI the most dangerous technology humans have ever gone near. He has also said it is clear he does not consider the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated effort within the AI industry, to be sufficient. Patel said the conversation would go on to cover technical ways of controlling AI, who might impose such controls, and the labor and social effects Gates expects.

Anthropic and the London-based private equity firm Hg have agreed to set up a new consultancy that will place AI consultants and engineers inside European businesses, according to sources cited by the Financial Times. The deal was reported on October 23, 2026, and the two sides are said to be aiming to launch the venture by the end of 2026. The idea is for the consultancy to work directly within client companies rather than from the outside. The headline report and a PYMNTS item describe it as a new company formed by the two partners.

The articles provided give few further specifics. The Financial Times piece sits behind a paywall, and the text available here shows only the headline and subscription offers, so details such as the size of the investment, the ownership split, the number of staff, or the name of the new business are not available. Likewise, nothing in the material sets out particular clients, countries, or fees. The only firm date given is the end of 2026 as the target for launch.

The responsibility for the move rests with Anthropic, the AI developer, and Hg, the private equity firm based in London. Neither company's own statement appears in the available text, and the report relies on unnamed sources rather than an on-the-record announcement. As a result, there is no direct comment from executives at either organization to relay. The coverage presents the arrangement as agreed between the two parties, but it does not say who will run the new company.

As for context, the available articles do not explain the reasoning behind the venture or place it within a wider trend. stories.Headline: Mubbadrah consortium plans $3bn AI data centre facility in Oman
stories.Summary:
Mubbadrah Investment, an Omani investment group, announced that a consortium it leads will build a $3 billion artificial intelligence data centre in Oman. The announcement came at a signing ceremony in London on Saturday, October 24, 2026, during the state visit of Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to the United Kingdom. The ceremony was attended by Nasser bin Khamis Al Jashmi, chairman of the Oman Tax Authority, UK Ambassador to Oman Liane Saunders, and representatives of the UK trade office. The consortium brings together local and international companies, with Sustopia Capital, Vela Tech and O2 Global Energy named as partners.

On completion, the facility is planned to have a capacity of up to 400 megawatts, with room for future expansion. It is designed to serve hyperscale computing operators and to support large-scale AI training and inference workloads. Power will come from the national grid and from renewable sources, and O2 Global Energy will develop 400 MW of solar generation backed by battery storage to supply additional clean energy to the campus. Crusoe has expressed interest in becoming a potential off-taker for the data centre capacity, and the consortium expects to sign a confirmation of that interest in the coming weeks.

Yasser Albarami, chief executive of Mubbadrah Investment, said the group, which has a portfolio of more than 20 companies across oil and gas, hospitality, healthcare and other sectors, was proud to lead the consortium. He argued that Oman has the stability, strategic location and energy resources to become a regional home for AI infrastructure. Nikhil Chouguley, chief executive of Sustopia Capital, described the move as a strategic extension of his firm's 5 GW data centre platform, which spans Denmark, the United States and the United Kingdom. Jeff Fini, chief executive of Vela Tech, said his company would support the design and manage construction through to completion, drawing on three years of AI data centre work that began with the Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, and now covers more than 20 GW.

Yazan Faouri, founder and chief executive of O2 Global Energy, said his firm is active in several countries and brings 12 years of experience developing solar and renewable projects. He added that he looks forward to delivering clean, reliable power for what he called one of the region's most important digital infrastructure projects. According to the announcement, Sustopia Capital and Vela Tech are developing, designing and building about 20 GW of AI data centre capacity worldwide. The articles do not give a construction timeline or a date for the facility to open, so the next step on record is the expected confirmation of Crusoe's interest within weeks.

stories.Headline: Brazil Elections: How AI, Meta and Evangelicals Could Sway the Presidential Race for Bolsonaro
stories.Summary:
Brazilians vote Sunday in a presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, with polls showing a tight race. Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, came out slightly ahead in the first round earlier this month and has promised to free his father. The elder Bolsonaro is under house arrest for decades over a failed military coup and assassination plot after he lost to Lula in 2022. The two men faced off in their only debate a week before the runoff, where Lula blamed the Bolsonaro government for 716,000 COVID deaths and said half could have been prevented.

Two days before the vote, Brazil's Superior Electoral Court had received a record 804 legal filings tied to the election, far more than the 325 logged at the same point in 2022. The disputes center on disinformation, artificial intelligence and manipulated digital content, and they intensified in the final stretch, especially over deepfakes. In September the court reaffirmed its ban on using deepfakes to alter or recreate images and voices in electoral advertising, even with the consent of those shown. That ruling followed a controversy over an AI-generated video of Jair Bolsonaro endorsing his son at a July party convention, though the court declined to sanction the candidate. A monitoring project by the fact-checking group Agência Lupa found 920 social media posts using AI on political content between Aug. 16 and Sept. 28, about 20 a day, and 554 of them, or 60%, were deepfakes.

Lula filed a petition Wednesday asking the top electoral court to disqualify Flávio Bolsonaro, accusing Meta of limiting the reach of his posts on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp to help Bolsonaro's campaign. The filing followed a report led by a U.N. special rapporteur on freedom of expression that raised concern over differences in how each campaign could reach voters on Meta's platforms. Meta has denied favoritism. Reporter Laís Martins of The Intercept Brasil said Lula's campaign page had been barred from running ads and a popular profile of journalists covering Bolsonaro family scandals was removed, with Meta calling these technical issues and apologizing for the inconvenience. She added that a Folha de São Paulo report, based on internal messages, confirmed a technical restriction on Lula's profile that would explain differences in engagement and reach.

The Intercept Brasil also reported that Bolsonaro's campaign paid 600,000 reais, about $119,000, to Elytron, a company said to offer election manipulation tools including disinformation and psychological warfare techniques. Martins said a whistleblower brought the material to the outlet after seeing that the campaign had hired the firm, which allegedly pitched such services to people tied to Trump's 2024 campaign. She stressed it is unconfirmed whether either campaign actually used the service. A legal group linked to Lula's campaign has asked the Federal Police to investigate, and the Federal Prosecution Service has asked federal courts to open a separate inquiry into the Meta restrictions. Martins also noted that evangelical voters, who have historically backed the right, are not a uniform bloc and are divided by scandals involving the Bolsonaro family.

stories.Headline: Why AI data centers are powering a boom in fuel-cell demand
stories.Summary:
On September 30, Hitachi, Brookfield Japan, Hartree Partners Singapore and Tokyo Gas signed a memorandum of understanding to work together on green data centers in Japan, and the companies announced it on October 23, 2026. The agreement builds on an earlier one among Hitachi, Brookfield and Hartree that was announced in July 2025, with Tokyo Gas now added as a fourth party. The companies want to design data centers that generate their own power, use it reliably and efficiently, and help cut emissions through green energy and related measures. As their first projects, they plan to build green data centers in the Kanto and Kyushu regions.

The four companies will draw up a basic concept for these power-integrated facilities and push toward a standardized model that can be rolled out flexibly. The design has four parts. First, on-site generation would be the main power source, combined with battery storage, grid power and other sources. Second, redundancy would be built into the whole infrastructure, including cooling and power distribution, so operations continue through equipment failures or swings in supply. Third, the group will set decarbonization requirements, covering carbon credits, environmental attributes and renewable energy, and fourth, major facilities such as buildings and on-site power plants would be standardized and modularized to shorten project lead times and allow scalable deployment.

The companies say the approach should reduce heavy reliance on the power grid, widen the choice of sites, encourage local production and consumption of energy, and speed up projects. They describe the effort as a way to combine their respective expertise to tackle securing power, keeping operations stable and decarbonizing AI data centers. Their release points to Japan's surge in data center construction, especially in urban areas, which is raising electricity demand and stretching the time needed to secure power capacity because of grid limits. It also notes that the Japanese government, as part of its Green Transformation initiatives, has promoted sustainable infrastructure and spreading data centers across regions.

The same pressure is visible in the United States, where data centers took 4.4% of electricity use in 2024, according to the Department of Energy. Penn State's Institute of Energy and the Environment says consumption could triple by 2028, and a Bloomberg analysis projects data centers could use as much as 20% of US electricity production by 2035. Andrew Denis of the energy technology firm ZON said roughly half of the data center projects due online in 2026 face delays tied to power availability, and Britt Burt of Industrial Info Resources said the old focus on location has given way to speed to power. Burt estimated about $6 trillion is eyed for new data centers worldwide, with about $4 trillion of it in the US, while Denis said communities near big clusters in Virginia, Texas and Georgia have reportedly seen electricity rates rise 8 to 15%.

stories.Headline: 2027: Opposition has upgraded campaign from Facebook, Twitter to AI - Gov. Sani
stories.Summary:
Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani said on Saturday, at the flag-off of the All Progressives Congress presidential campaign in Kaduna, that the opposition has moved its campaign from Facebook and Twitter to artificial intelligence. He urged supporters of the ruling party to stay watchful and vigilant. In an apparent reference to former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, Sani challenged the so-called northern candidate to show his track record. He asked whether Atiku could point to 200 kilometres of road built for the North East while he was vice president, and said none had been seen.

The campaign's Director General, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, made similar charges, saying the opposition cannot win the 2027 elections with AI-generated lies. He claimed that about two million farmers have pledged to vote for President Bola Tinubu, and rejected opposition claims that the administration neglects farmers. On the economy, he said the exchange rate improved from nearly N1,800 to about N1,300 per dollar and that foreign reserves rose from about $3.9 billion to about $54.7 billion, while admitting that Nigerians still face economic hardship. Sani, for his part, said more than 1,000 kilometres of roads have been built in northern Nigeria under Tinubu, and that the 123km Kaduna-Birnin Gwari road, abandoned for over 40 years, is being rebuilt with N117bn released to the contractor.

Sani added that the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Expressway reconstruction is 95 per cent complete and that the president had assured him he would pay the N740bn it costs. He said $865m has been approved for the metropolitan red line project, for which Kaduna is the pilot state, and that the contractor, Mota-Engil, has mobilised $300m for a corridor of about 50km. He said the people of Kaduna and the North will return to the polls in January 2027 to vote for continuity, and that some people will come out on January 16 to vote for the president. Yari said the party has been consulting traditional rulers, ulama and imams, and told Tinubu that Northern Nigeria is fully behind him.

Earlier on Saturday, the council's spokesperson, Dele Alake, accused Atiku and the ADC of plotting to use deepfake videos and counterfeit documents to discredit the Kaduna flag-off. He said one example was a photo of a routine security patrol vehicle near an APC billboard, which he claimed was twisted into a story that security agents were guarding the billboards. He also cited a fake letter, supposedly from Sani to Yari, claiming the state spent N2.3 trillion on the rally, a figure he said exceeds Kaduna's combined budgets for 2024, 2025 and 2026, which total about N2.23 trillion. The council urged Nigerians to be vigilant and reject what it called the opposition's machinations.

stories.Headline: MS GOP asks Attorney General to investigate Colom campaign AI video - The Clarion-Ledger
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst asked Attorney General Lynn Fitch to investigate an AI-generated video posted by Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom that depicts his opponent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, fleeing questions and photographs from reporters. The video, posted about a month before the November 3 election on Facebook and Instagram, carries the caption "Based on a true story," and the party says the content was not real. Hurst's request came in a letter to Fitch's office, and the Clarion-Ledger reported it that day. The following day, on Friday, October 23, Fitch notified Colom and his campaign to remove the ads from their social media platforms, according to WLBT.

The state law at issue was passed in 2024 and bars sharing realistic altered photos or videos, known as digitizations, within 90 days of an election with the intent to injure a candidate. Under WLBT's account, violations tied to an intent to deter voting can carry up to five years in prison and fines of up to $10,000. The Clarion-Ledger reported that the statute itself sets a penalty of up to a year in prison, a $5,000 fine or both, and it also contains exceptions for satire and parody without defining either term. Fitch's office told Colom to take down the video by 5 p.m. that Friday or face a possible injunction, and WLBT reported that as of late morning the video remained online.

Hurst argued in his letter and a news release that the video is deception rather than satire or parody, because Colom labeled it as a true story and did not disclose that it was artificial. He also pointed to an earlier simulated phone call Colom posted when he launched his campaign in 2025, which the party said it referred to the FBI, the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney, though the Clarion-Ledger reported it was unclear whether any penalties followed. Colom's campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, called the request an act of desperation and an attempt to weaponize public office, and said Republicans are worried about November 3. WLBT reported that Democratic analyst Brandon Jones called the legal filing political nonsense. The Clarion-Ledger also notes the race has grown increasingly bitter, with nicknames, dueling fake campaign websites and Hyde-Smith's earlier resurfacing of an arrest report about Colom, and that Colom campaigns with Kamala Harris on October 22 while Donald Trump is scheduled to rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on October 26.

stories.Headline: SK Hyper Seeks $350 Billion for First 5GW Phase of 15GW AI Data Center Plan
stories.Summary:
SK Hyper, the AI data center arm of SK Telecom, is looking to raise about $350 billion, roughly 463 trillion won, to build the first 5-gigawatt phase of a 15-gigawatt data center plan in South Korea. Its chief executive, Chung Suk-keun, disclosed the plan in a Bloomberg interview reported on October 22 local time and then outlined the strategy again on October 23 on a Bloomberg TV technology program. He said the company is in talks with large technology firms and financial investors to secure the money. The aim is to draw global companies' AI infrastructure into Korea and capture computing demand from elsewhere in Asia, including Japan and Taiwan.

The plan sets out a long list of figures and dates. The full 15 gigawatts is meant to be built in South Korea by 2035, and the $350 billion estimate for the first 5 gigawatts includes servers and other equipment. SK Hyper hopes to land its first outside investment late this year or early next year, with further fundraising spread over the following three to four years. Phased operations are due to begin in 2029, though the company could start generating revenue as early as next year, according to Bloomberg. SK Telecom has said it will invest up to 750 billion won in SK Hyper in stages through 2030.

On the sites, the company is building a 900-megawatt project in Ulsan and working with Amazon Web Services on a separate 100-megawatt data center project. It intends to build a cluster of more than 2 gigawatts in the Yeongnam region, starting from Ulsan, and to add gigawatt-scale facilities in the Chungcheong and southwestern regions. Chung said the company is also talking with the government about securing more sites. SK Hyper was set up in July this year as an SK Telecom subsidiary, and it is discussing with global hyperscalers how to bring AI inference hubs to Korea while also hoping to attract computing infrastructure for training AI models.

Chung said he does not expect much trouble securing power and sites for the first phase, and named the real challenges as finding actual demand in the global market and raising the capital. He argued that Korea's data center market is only about 1 gigawatt today, so domestic demand alone cannot make such large facilities viable. He acknowledged uncertainty in the capital markets, with weaker investor sentiment and doubts about AI profitability and data center credit risk. Even so, he said AI model developers and service providers see customer demand rising sharply. The company plans to share the total cost with data center tenants and outside investors, to check demand with big tech firms before investing, and to adjust the pace of spending to actual demand.

stories.Headline: Goodwin Launches AI Governance Program
stories.Summary:
Goodwin, the global law firm, announced a program called Goodwin AI Governance on October 22, 2026, through a Business Wire release. Law360 reported on the launch the following day, October 23. The program is meant to help organizations govern how AI is used across the business, adopt it faster, and keep pace as technology and regulation change quickly. It was built through collaboration between the firm's legal and AI product teams, and the firm says it has already been adopted by a wide range of clients across industries.

The program has three connected parts. The first is a Health Check, a complimentary assessment with a Goodwin lawyer to find gaps in a company's AI governance. The second is Readiness, a set of governance materials tailored to a client's business, sector and AI use, available either as separate modules or as a full suite. The third is the AI Decision Desk, an annual subscription that gives clear legal answers and real-time monitoring of AI regulation, enforcement and market practice, along with prompts to update existing policies.

The offering also includes versions for boards and for private equity and venture capital portfolios. For boards, it covers directors' own use of AI and their oversight of company AI use, including accountability, reporting and escalation. For private equity sponsors, Goodwin helps set a consistent baseline across a portfolio while allowing for differences in each company's AI use, sector and jurisdiction. The firm points to Deloitte's 2026 State of AI study, which found that 74% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents within the next two years, but only 21% have a mature governance model for them.

Gary Sangha, Goodwin's Director of Product AI and Platforms, who recently joined the firm after founding the legal technology companies Intelligize and LexCheck, said companies slow down on AI when the question in front of them is not covered by existing rules and nobody wants to guess. He said the program lets routine uses continue under current guidance, while exceptions get a clear answer from a Goodwin lawyer that then becomes the rule for next time. Kaitlin Betancourt, Co-Chair of Goodwin's AI practice, said companies want to adopt AI quickly and risk teams do not want to be the obstacle. She added that few legal departments have deep AI expertise in-house and want sound judgment from people who understand their business.

The launch fits into a wider effort at the firm to change how legal work is done, anchored by its Regina OS proprietary platform. Goodwin says it is building a new operating model for legal services, designed by its lawyers and powered by technology. Its AI practice already advises companies, startups and investors on AI governance, intellectual property, and data and cybersecurity risk. The articles do not describe pricing or any further planned rollout.

stories.Headline: UAE's G42 signs pacts to explore AI infrastructure in Greece
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi's G42 and five of its portfolio companies signed a series of initial agreements with Greek public and private partners on Friday, October 23, 2026, to explore artificial intelligence infrastructure and applications in Greece. The pacts covered AI infrastructure, government services, life sciences and smart cities. They were signed in Athens during an official visit by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and were part of 18 memorandums of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships between the UAE and Greece. Those deals were valued at €12.75 billion, or $14.3 billion, and were signed at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum. The centrepiece is a plan for Khazna Data Centres and Core42, under agreements with Greece's Copelouzos Group, to explore building an AI factory in Greece.

Khazna would lead development of the physical infrastructure, while Core42 would supply cloud and AI compute capabilities for organisations in banking, telecoms, shipping and government. G42's subsidiary Presight will work with Greece's Ministry of Digital Governance on urban mobility and municipal operations, starting with agentic AI for waste management and water network monitoring. Inception42 will also work with the ministry on AI across government and education, including tools to support cabinet meetings and track government priorities, training for officials to work with AI agents, and AI tutors and learning platforms. In life sciences, M42 signed an initial pact with Athens LifeTech Park covering research, genomics sequencing infrastructure, population genomics, clinical development and links between institutional biobanks, with a focus on oncology, rare genetic diseases and neuroscience. The deal also offers UAE start-ups a base at the park's incubator for entering the European market, and gives Greek and European ventures access to the UAE through M42's network.

G42 described the agreements as a step in extending its Intelligence Grid, which covers the full AI value chain from data centres and compute to cloud and industry applications. Mansoor Al Mansoori, chief executive of G42 International, said the deals mark an important milestone in expanding that grid across Europe and that G42 will work with trusted local partners in line with European standards. Christos Copelouzos, chief executive of Copelouzos Group, said the AI factory would strengthen Greece's position as a digital and energy hub in South-east Europe, support the digital transformation of the economy, attract investment and create highly skilled jobs. Greece's Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, Dimitris Papastergiou, said AI can make cities smarter, more efficient and safer, and that the work with Presight will look at smart-city uses and ways to improve safety on public transport.

Thomas Pramotedham of Presight said the value of city data lies in turning it into intelligence that improves how cities function, while Ashish Koshy of Inception42 said its programmes will follow European standards for responsible AI. The agreements are initial and exploratory, so the projects described remain proposals rather than finished developments. G42 has been working to help countries build their own AI capabilities, and in February it signed a framework agreement with a Vietnamese consortium to develop sovereign AI capabilities and cloud infrastructure in that country. The articles do not give timelines, costs or locations for the Greek projects, or say when any of them might move beyond the exploration stage.

stories.Headline: Sources: OpenAI has cut its valuation target to $1.25T, down from the $1.4T valuation it pitched earlier this month, after facing resistance from some investors (Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has lowered the valuation it is seeking from new investors to $1.25 trillion, down $150 billion from the $1.4 trillion it floated earlier this month, according to reports published on October 22 and 23, 2026. The cut came after some investors pushed back on the higher figure, and no official reason was given for the change. Both numbers are pre-money, meaning they exclude the new cash being raised, and the talks have not closed, so the final terms could still change. OpenAI declined to comment.

The company is close to finalizing a funding round of up to $30 billion, and it expects investor commitments to be locked in by the end of next week. Coatue Management is in talks to co-lead the round, and OpenAI has also been speaking with several funds from the United Arab Emirates, along with firms including BlackRock. At $1.25 trillion, OpenAI would be the most valuable private company ever, and well above the $852 billion valuation it carried after raising $122 billion in March from backers such as Amazon, SoftBank and NVIDIA. The company is also reportedly negotiating a separate deal to buy more computing capacity from the UAE.

The reports tie the revision to a broader rethink of AI spending. Tech stocks fell this week after mixed quarterly results from companies including Meta and Tesla, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.60% on Thursday, its steepest fall since early June. Microsoft, OpenAI's largest listed backer, slipped 2.23% to $521.08 that day, though it edged up slightly in after-hours trading. Microsoft reports fiscal first-quarter results on October 28, and the Azure contract with OpenAI, which includes an extra $250 billion of cloud purchases, matters more to its earnings than its roughly 27% stake, a figure from the October 2025 restructuring that the March round has likely diluted.

OpenAI has pushed its IPO back to next year, having confidentially filed its prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Chief financial officer Sarah Friar told employees in August that the company will be public in 2027, while chief executive Sam Altman said the following month that listing at that point would be ill-advised. Rival Anthropic is preparing an IPO expected next month, reportedly seeking $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion after raising $65 billion in May at a $965 billion valuation. Investors will be watching how the market receives Anthropic as they judge valuations across the sector. Separately, China's DeepSeek raised about 100 billion yuan, or $14.98 billion, doubling its original 50 billion yuan target, from backers including GigaDevice, Meituan and Geely.

stories.Headline: KTR urges youth to embrace AI; calls for investor-friendly ecosystem to make Hyderabad global hub
stories.Summary:
BRS Working President K T Rama Rao, known as KTR, urged young people on Saturday, October 24, 2026, to treat Artificial Intelligence as a chance for innovation and jobs rather than a danger to employment. He spoke in Hyderabad while inaugurating the India headquarters of Random Trees, a company working in data, AI and innovation. A related headline on one of the reporting sites says the company is launching operations there with 400 employees. KTR stressed continuous learning, skill development and adapting to new technologies.

He argued that every technological revolution first brings worry but later opens new avenues for growth. As an example, he recalled the resistance that met the arrival of computers in the banking sector, saying that adapting to change was essential for progress. Describing AI as a monster, he said, would only spread needless fear among people. He also pointed to the Saagu-Baagu initiative in Sircilla, where technology helps farmers spot crop pests and get timely solutions, and he cited digital platforms as business models that are creating new jobs.

On the role of government, KTR said the private sector should be the main source of employment, and that governments should concentrate on building a business-friendly climate instead of trying to give everyone a job directly. He listed reliable power and water supply, quality infrastructure, efficient transport and ease of doing business as the basics needed to draw investment. He called for coordination among governments, industries and educational institutions so that young people gain skills that industry actually wants. He added that the benefits of technology should reach every section of society.

Looking back, KTR said the previous BRS government had taken several steps to make Hyderabad a leading global IT destination and to attract international companies and Global Capability Centres. He voiced confidence that the city could grow into a major hub for AI research, data science and technological innovation. He also underlined the importance of strengthening Telangana's technology ecosystem and preparing youth for future job opportunities. The reports do not describe any specific policy measures or timeline following his remarks.
