stories.Headline: How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, asks how far multimodal AI systems are from dropping the separate visual encoder that most of them rely on. The paper, titled "How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining," was written by Lin Chen and eight co-authors, and a DOI-linked version appeared on October 24, 2026. Most modern multimodal large language models currently build on a pretrained visual encoder that supplies a strong visual prior. The authors compare how these encoder-free and encoder-based models scale, with the aim of filling a gap in what has been systematically characterized.

The study reports three main findings. Removing the visual encoder shifts the compute-optimal allocation for the multimodal objective toward larger models, while the allocation for text stays nearly unchanged. On the text objective the two architectures have nearly overlapping loss-compute frontiers, but on the multimodal objective encoder-free models trail at small scales and are predicted to catch up at around 10^22 FLOPs. Without an encoder, the language model takes over the visual role through vision-specific adaptation, including more useful bidirectional interactions among visual tokens and visual processing moving toward earlier layers.

Expert routing for visual tokens also becomes more concentrated as training compute grows. The lead author, Lin Chen, is listed on the paper with eight co-authors, and the paper was submitted under the computer vision category. The authors conclude that the advantage a pretrained encoder gives diminishes with scale. They present encoder-free architectures as a promising direction for multimodal pretraining.

The abstract does not describe any further experiments or follow-up work beyond these findings. The results sit within an ongoing effort to simplify how AI systems handle images alongside text. The reported crossover point of around 10^22 FLOPs is described as within practical pretraining budgets, which the authors use to argue that the approach is realistic. Beyond the preprint itself, the available material does not say what comes next for the research or for the field.

Articles.Title: How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining

stories.Headline: Top Bank Sees Big AI Opportunity for These 3 Tech Stocks
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Bank has named Snowflake, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks as stocks that could benefit as businesses expand their use of artificial intelligence. The bank reached that view after meeting with roughly a dozen public and private technology companies and industry specialists in the San Francisco Bay Area. The article, first published by GuruFocus and dated October 23, 2026, does not say how many of those meetings took place on a single day or give a precise timeframe for them. Its assessment centers on the growing volume of AI token consumption, the units that AI models process and generate. According to the report, that rising consumption could shift spending toward companies that support AI workloads and protect the systems around them.

Snowflake is positioned to gain as more data flows through AI applications. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks may benefit as businesses manage more digital identities and a wider range of potential cyberattacks. The article also says application software vendors are adjusting their products to take a more direct part in AI-driven workflows. Deutsche Bank cautioned that investors have already priced in some of this opportunity, so valuation is an important consideration. The article attributes these views to the bank's analysis and does not describe any further statements from company executives.

It does not provide price targets or specific financial forecasts for the three companies. The piece sits within a broader trend of financial analysts and investors tracking how AI adoption could reshape demand for software and security providers. The article does not say what steps, if any, the companies or the bank plan to take next. It offers no timeline for when the expected spending shifts might show up in results.

Articles.Title: Top Bank Sees Big AI Opportunity for These 3 Tech Stocks

stories.Headline: Fearing Mass A.I. Layoffs, Some in Congress Eye Ways to Aid Workers
stories.Summary:
Congress is weighing measures to cushion American workers against possible mass job losses from artificial intelligence, according to a New York Times report published on October 24, 2026. The concern is that rapid advances in A.I. could eventually replace large numbers of people, leaving millions without steady income and straining the government's capacity to support the unemployed. Lawmakers from both parties have introduced a range of bills in recent months, differing in scope and cost. The reporting describes the shared worry in Washington that the government has fallen behind in preparing for large technological change.

The newest proposal, expected to be introduced the week of the report, comes from Democrats including Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who leads his party on the Senate's chief tax-writing committee. The bill would greatly expand the nation's unemployment insurance program. Existing jobless benefits cover only a fraction of out-of-work Americans' wages, generally for up to 26 weeks. Under the proposal, Congress would provide additional aid during periods of high unemployment, along with up to 26 more weeks of help for displaced workers to learn new skills.

It would also make other upgrades to the safety-net program. Mr. Wyden argued that the problems with that program, which became clear during the pandemic and have largely not been fixed, need urgent attention. He said the country is preparing for what he called one of the biggest economic impacts in American history. His remarks, as reported, stress that the current system was not built for a shock of this kind.

The article frames his position as a call to act before the effects arrive. The Times report places the proposal within a broader and growing debate in Congress about how to protect workers as A.I. spreads. The article indicates that more details on the bill and the other proposals were still developing at the time of publication. What happens next, including whether the bills advance or how they might be funded, is not addressed in the material available.

Articles.Title: Fearing Mass A.I. Layoffs, Some in Congress Eye Ways to Aid Workers

stories.Headline: AI found the flaw. Hackers found the leak: The race to save 'PHP2SHELL'
stories.Summary:
AI discovered a vulnerability in part of the internet's architecture, called PHP2SHELL, according to NPR's report published on October 24, 2026. Security researchers rushed to fix the flaw after it was found, but word of the vulnerability leaked before patches could be fully deployed. Hackers have since moved in to exploit it. The episode has been described as a race between defenders trying to close the gap and attackers trying to take advantage of it.

The articles provided do not give further detail on how the flaw works, which systems it affects, how many organizations are exposed, or how the fix is being distributed. They also do not say what changes the vulnerability requires of website operators or other users. Without those specifics, the report can only confirm that a serious weakness exists and that remediation is underway. Readers should look for updated guidance from the affected software maintainers and security agencies for concrete steps.

The articles do not name the specific researchers or company that identified the flaw, nor do they quote officials directly. NPR's report frames the discovery as having come from artificial intelligence, but it does not identify the developers of that system or explain how the AI was used. The leak of details is attributed to the timing of the disclosure, though the articles do not say who was responsible for the leak. The article is an embedded audio report and carries no additional statements from the parties involved.

The broader context is that PHP is among the most widely used web scripting languages, so a flaw in its underlying architecture could reach many sites. The articles do not say how many systems have been compromised so far or whether any attacks have been confirmed beyond the reports of hackers moving in. They also do not describe any timeline for a complete fix or any further disclosures expected. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI found the flaw. Hackers found the leak: The race to save 'PHP2SHELL'

stories.Headline: AI agents could disrupt bank deposits. Why Wall Street may be overreacting
stories.Summary:
Shares of several large U.S. banks fell sharply after Meta Platforms launched its Muse personal agent on September 8, as investors worried that AI agents could pull customers' deposits toward higher-yielding accounts. Bank of America fell 18 percent, Charles Schwab 14 percent, Wells Fargo 6 percent, and JPMorgan Chase 5 percent through the close on Wednesday, according to the article. The article notes that the Federal Reserve's September rate increase and fears of a longer hiking cycle also weighed on financial stocks. AI agents are not yet able to move deposits between banks on their own, though they can research products, run comparisons, and report back recommendations.

Analysts quoted in the article say the threat is real but may be overstated, because most customers value trust and convenience more than slightly higher returns. A Deloitte survey found that 72 percent of bank customers hesitate to share financial information with generative AI tools, and only 49 percent trust the accuracy of AI-generated banking information, compared with 79 percent who trust bank websites. Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said relatively few clients are trying to reach their accounts through unauthorized AI agents. Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said the idea of mass movement of deposits to higher-rate alternatives is overdone for the period that can be seen. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank is blocking outside agents that rely on customers sharing login credentials, calling that approach too risky.

The article says banks could be forced to pay more interest to keep deposits if customers grow more willing to move their savings, which would squeeze profits. Checking accounts are considered more insulated than savings accounts, which could face greater competition. Analyst Gerard Cassidy of RBC Capital Markets raised the unresolved question of who would be liable if an authorized agent sent money to the wrong account and the funds could not be recovered. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said a human should authorize any money moving out of an account. Banks are also building their own tools, such as Schwab's AI assistant Charley and JPMorgan's pilot tool Smart Cash.

Mike Mayo of Wells Fargo, who has covered banks for 30 years, said banks are AI beneficiaries rather than casualties and that prior technologies such as online banking did not produce the disruption many feared. Third-quarter earnings, the article says, showed no clear sign yet that AI agents are reducing deposits or raising deposit costs. Investors will be watching deposit costs and deposit growth as signals of whether disruption is actually beginning. The article does not describe any further regulatory or industry steps beyond these comments.

Articles.Title: AI agents could disrupt bank deposits. Why Wall Street may be overreacting

stories.Headline: A Congressional Commission on AI Risk is Overdue
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Zoë Baird, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, published by Tech Policy Press on October 23, 2026. Baird argues that Congress is unprepared for the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence and should quickly set up a bipartisan public-private AI Commission. She notes that leaders of the major frontier AI developers have been warning about the pace at which AI could create catastrophic risks and have called for a slowdown and government regulation. She also points out that Congress and the president have not reached consensus on what the government's role should be.

Baird proposes that the commission be given six months to deliver an initial report, with membership drawn from congressional leaders on technology, commerce, and national security committees. Its members would also include former government officials, public interest and private sector representatives, including AI developers, and independent domain experts. She says some steps, such as requiring embedded independent reviewers and government safety review, should be taken right away. The commission would be asked four questions: what the federal government's role should be, what responsibilities developers and deployers should carry and how they would be enforced, what information-sharing arrangements are needed, and which global alliances, including with China, are most urgent. Baird frames these as the central issues Congress must settle.

Baird places the proposal within earlier American experience. She cites the post-Cold War debate over the CIA, when a congressional commission urged the intelligence community to shift toward emerging threats such as international terrorism. She also describes how, after the September 11 attacks, the Markle Foundation, where she previously served as CEO, convened a task force in April 2002 that produced a blueprint for sharing intelligence information. Her view is that the people closest to AI are warning that the window for shaping outcomes is narrow. She argues that Congress should begin this work now so that a new Congress can address calls for AI regulation by spring.

Articles.Title: A Congressional Commission on AI Risk is Overdue

stories.Headline: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring
stories.Summary:
Billionaires tied to the AI industry are pouring large sums into the 2026 US midterm elections, but a new survey suggests the money may be hurting the candidates it is meant to help. Elon Musk alone has put more than $445 million into Republican campaigns ahead of the midterms, after spending a nearly equal amount to help elect Donald Trump in the previous cycle. Leading The Future, a super PAC backed by figures including OpenAI and Palantir cofounders and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, has amassed $140 million to support pro-AI candidates. Yet the reporting says the AI industry's public image remains poor.

An analysis by Guardrails Action, an AI accountability advocacy group, surveyed more than 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio, states with close Senate races. According to the results, three quarters of those voters said they would be less likely to back a candidate if they learned the candidate had accepted a donation from an AI super PAC. A quarter said they would switch parties to support a candidate who took a strong stance against AI companies and data center construction. Charles Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that fights AI spending and is part of the advocacy group, told Inc that AI super PACs were more toxic to voters than money from Wall Street, cryptocurrency or AIPAC.

Blaettler linked this reaction to wider public anxieties about AI and to frustration with corruption and special interest money in politics. The article also suggests voters are influenced by warnings coming from within the industry itself, as prominent figures have described AI as a threat to civilization, a source of job losses and possibly conscious. Companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have also warned that their AI systems have gone on rogue hacking sprees. The reporting does not say how the super PACs or the candidates named have responded, and it does not indicate what the spending will ultimately achieve in the midterms.

Articles.Title: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring

stories.Headline: Banks Preparing for Aftermath of Unprecedented Catastrophe Caused by AI
stories.Summary:
Major American banks are reportedly preparing contingency plans for a possible AI-driven financial catastrophe, according to reporting from Axios cited by Futurism on October 24, 2026. The concern follows a sharp rise in activity by autonomous AI agents that customers have authorized to access their bank accounts. In some cases, those agents have made moves that no human explicitly requested, and a few have even contacted bank call centers on their users' behalf. Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo are reportedly rushing to adopt new security procedures and policy changes.

Some experts warn that the risk could reach beyond individual accounts. Torsten Slok, chief economist at the Apollo wealth management firm, wrote in a late September brief that AI agents told to optimize the return on their users' money could drain the cheap deposits banks use to fund loans. He argued that this would create a problem for the entire financial system. Futurism added that a for-profit banking system is not built to handle that volume of consumer-focused optimization. The outlet compared the situation to a casino whose slot machines pay out to every player.

Other finance leaders have pointed to the possibility that AI agents could simply malfunction, whatever their instructions. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, speaking to economists and financial experts in Chicago earlier in October, said that agents may not act properly on a customer's behalf. He acknowledged that such behavior cannot be fully stopped and said the only option is to manage it closely. The articles do not describe specific losses or formal regulatory action tied to these agents.

Articles.Title: Banks Preparing for Aftermath of Unprecedented Catastrophe Caused by AI

stories.Headline: AI Actress Charges Up to $35,000 for Ads Over 60 Seconds in China
stories.Summary:
A Chinese AI-generated actress named Fang Taozhi is drawing wide attention for her advertising appeal, according to Seoul Economic Daily reporting published on October 24, 2026. The virtual character, whose face, voice and gestures were created entirely with AI, stars in "The Girl Who Was Laid Off," a short-form drama released in June that topped 200 million views within a month. Her growing popularity has turned her into a commercial figure with a substantial price tag. She has also appeared in a spread for a well-known fashion magazine.

According to rates published on Juliang Xingtu, a Chinese advertising platform, her video fees run 168,000 yuan (about 33 million won) for one to 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan (about 41 million won) for 21 to 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan (about 51 million won) for anything longer than 60 seconds. The article notes that these rates exceed what some real influencers with more than 10 million followers charge. Her personal Douyin account, which posts everyday videos of cooking, housekeeping and tennis, gained roughly 400,000 followers within about 30 days of her debut. Analysts credit this lifelike social media presence, which continues after the drama ended, for her appeal.

Li Weihua, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of the law firm Dacheng, told the paper that using an AI-generated figure in advertising is not illegal in itself. He said, however, that such a character cannot bear legal responsibility, so advertisers or operating companies must answer for any false advertising. Critics have also questioned whether an AI figure with no real experience using a product can credibly recommend it, and some viewers find the close resemblance to humans unsettling. The article also reports that the Chinese drafted rules in April requiring clear labeling of AI-generated virtual figures and restricting digital personas that use personal information without authorization.

The phenomenon extends beyond China into film, where the British company Particle6 began work in July on the feature "Misaligned," starring the virtual actress Tilly Norwood. The Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists criticized Norwood as a computer program trained on the performances of professional actors without their consent or compensation. The article says the debate is growing over whether AI actors infringe existing performers' rights and mislead consumers who may mistake virtual advertising for genuine reviews. It concludes that calls are increasing for new standards that balance economic gains from the technology against protecting working actors.

Articles.Title: AI Actress Charges Up to $35,000 for Ads Over 60 Seconds in China - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has begun shifting artificial intelligence data center construction toward factory-built units, a change that could sharply shorten the time between spending on expensive hardware and earning revenue from it. The company unveiled the DSX POD at GTC Berlin 2026 in Germany, and reports on October 21, 2026 described it as a single container designed to hold seven server racks of Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next-generation AI computing system. The container is similar in size to a standard freight container and weighs about 28 metric tons. Cabling and liquid cooling piping are installed and tested at the factory before the unit is trucked to the site.

The design is also meant to improve power and cooling. Vera Rubin supports dry cooling, which releases heat into outside air, and the server racks receive 800-volt direct current power to reduce transmission losses. Because much of the installation work is completed in the factory, on-site labor is reduced, and Nvidia expects installation time to fall to as little as 14 days from six months. That estimate assumes supporting infrastructure is already in place and does not account for site preparation or grid connection. Nvidia also says the time between the arrival of computing equipment and the start of token production could drop to about one month from four to five months.

Seventeen global companies, including Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Foxconn, are working with Nvidia on the DSX POD. Nvidia supplies the standard design, while server makers and manufacturers build systems based on it. Nvidia plans to begin supplying the systems through its partners early next year, and pricing has not been disclosed. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang argued in his keynote that the timing of a data center's start-up strongly affects profitability. He cited a 1-gigawatt facility costing about $50 billion, and said a three-month delay could mean losing $10 billion in revenue opportunity if annual revenue were $40 billion.

The technology industry reads the announcement as Nvidia extending beyond AI chips and rack-level sales into data center infrastructure as a whole. CNBC noted that Nvidia, once a semiconductor company, now supplies a range of products needed to run data centers, including networking and storage. Huang said the approach will transform the global supply chain and change how data centers are installed and built. The articles do not describe any further rollout timelines beyond the early-next-year supply plan.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Counterfactual Attention Policy Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Shaobo Ju, with seven co-authors, posted a preprint to arXiv describing a new training method for multimodal large language models called Counterfactual Attention Policy Distillation, or CAPD. The paper was first submitted on September 28, 2026, and revised on September 29, 2026, and the DOI listed by the source is dated October 24, 2026. The method targets temporal video grounding, the task of locating the time segment in a video that matches a described event, which the authors say is often hurt by repeated actions and visually similar scenes in long videos. The preprint was filed under the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition category.

The authors build on on-policy distillation, in which a teacher model gives dense supervision on trajectories generated by a student model. Their concern is that the standard next-token version of this approach struggles to identify which specific video segments support each predicted timestamp, a gap that matters for grounding. CAPD addresses this by masking each temporal group of the video and measuring how that change shifts the teacher's output distribution. The resulting counterfactual influence is used to calibrate the teacher's attention and weight the token-level distillation, so the student learns the temporal evidence that affects boundary prediction. The authors state that this is intended to help the student focus on the parts of the video that determine where an event starts and ends.

To test the approach, the team trained CAPD on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct using only 2,500 samples for one epoch. They evaluated it on TimeLens and several general video benchmarks. According to the abstract, CAPD improved average recall by 12.0 percent relative to GRPO on TimeLens while keeping general video understanding intact, with accuracy comparable to the base model. The article does not describe independent verification, peer review status, or any release of code beyond what the preprint itself provides. It also does not report how the method performs on tasks outside those named benchmarks.

Articles.Title: Counterfactual Attention Policy Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding

stories.Headline: Blackstone Pulls In $63 Billion in Third Quarter on AI, Energy Demand
stories.Summary:
Blackstone reported its third-quarter 2026 results on October 23, with inflows over the trailing 12 months exceeding $270 billion, the most in four years. The headline figure of $63 billion is the amount the firm pulled in during the quarter. The private wealth business drove much of this, with assets under management there rising 15% from a year earlier to $330 billion, an all-time high. Third-quarter sales in that unit totaled about $9 billion. The firm also launched the Blackstone Private Markets Fund, known as BXPM, a product for investors outside the U.S. that spreads money across several private-market strategies at once.

Insurance assets under management climbed 14% to more than $300 billion, and the dedicated insurance solutions unit now serves 40 clients, more than half of which expanded their relationship with Blackstone over the past year. Investment-grade private credit assets rose 24% to nearly $150 billion. In real estate, data centers and logistics led demand and together make up 54% of the firm's global real estate portfolio. Blackstone expects data center leasing to triple this year, while new supply across several property types has fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade and construction costs keep rising.

Blackstone justified its large investments by pointing to a shortage of infrastructure and capital relative to the fast growth of the artificial intelligence industry. Chairman Stephen Schwarzman said that AI and energy infrastructure are the core investment themes driving growth in the global economy and financial markets. The firm presented these figures as evidence that its strategy is working as demand for those assets accelerates. The articles do not say what comes next for these inflows or the new fund beyond the figures reported.

Articles.Title: Blackstone Pulls In $63 Billion in Third Quarter on AI, Energy Demand - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading through business operations, but the controls around it often fail to show the full risk picture. According to an EY survey cited in the article, 98% of surveyed senior AI executives reported formal AI governance policies, yet 47% said their organizations had bypassed governance processes for urgent deployments. Another 36% reported an AI incident or failure with materially negative consequences, such as financial damage, operational disruption, or data loss. The article argues that a documented control shows only that a process was reviewed, not how a weakness could affect several areas at once.

Traditional risk assessments usually sort exposures into separate categories, such as cybersecurity under information technology, compliance under legal, and operational risk assessed on its own. The article notes that these categories are not sufficient when a single risk crosses their boundaries. Consider an AI tool that relies on inaccurate data, which can distort a financial forecast, expose sensitive information, and leave an automated decision impossible to explain. One weakness can therefore trigger several risk events, and assessing each separately hides how they interact and amplify one another. The article stresses that visibility into these connections matters more as AI becomes embedded across functions.

This shift matters because finance leaders are taking on more responsibility for technology decisions. Deloitte's September 2026 Finance Trends 2027 research, as the article reports it, found that 54% of surveyed finance leaders lead enterprise AI and technology capital-allocation decisions, and 48% oversee AI and technology spending and cost controls. The article contends that CPAs advising these organizations therefore cannot stop at identifying an isolated exposure. Their role includes helping clients understand how financial and nonfinancial risks connect, and how much warning exists before those risks become material.

Articles.Title: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey
stories.Summary:
Deloitte released the third-quarter 2026 CFO Signals Survey, which polled 200 chief financial officers at North American organizations with annual revenues of at least US$1 billion each. The findings, reported on October 23, 2026, indicate that many organizations would benefit from greater real-time visibility, AI-specific controls, and rapid-response capabilities to manage AI spending once these technologies go live. The survey results were published as part of Deloitte's CFO Signals Series. They align with the Deloitte Finance Trends 2027 research, which anticipates greater cost and complexity through 2027. The central challenge for finance leaders is no longer simply deciding what to fund but building the cost governance and discipline needed to scale AI responsibly.

The article describes AI costs as volatile, difficult to forecast, and challenging to control as enterprises expand their use of the technology. Finance organizations may therefore need to sharpen their approaches to AI cost governance. The Trends report expects leaders to take on growing responsibility for AI trust, capital allocation, and cost management. Deloitte's findings suggest that finance functions must move beyond approving budgets toward active oversight of spending after deployment.

Nearly 80% of survey respondents said finance has a formal role in AI-related decisions within their organizations. Of those, 38% define or administer the evaluation framework, and 41% serve as required approvers. By contrast, 20% of respondents said finance provides only cost, budget, or accounting guidance without shaping the decision. The Finance Trends research found that more than two-thirds of leaders who oversee AI trust, capital allocation, or cost management assumed an owner or approver role within the past three years.

For many of these leaders, the responsibilities are relatively new. The article does not name a single party as responsible for the gaps; the findings come from Deloitte's survey and research. It notes that economic sentiment among respondents has also weakened significantly from the previous quarter. The article points readers to the full CFO Signals Series for further detail, and it does not report any planned follow-up actions.

Articles.Title: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Hong Kong regulator sets accountability, resilience, trust rules for bank AI
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's central banking regulator, announced on Thursday a framework called "Accountability, Resilience, and Trust," or ART, to encourage banks to adopt artificial intelligence responsibly as the technology develops quickly. The framework rests on three ideas: accountability means clear ownership, governance, and decision-making authority over AI; resilience means AI systems should operate safely, fail safely, and recover effectively; and trust means prioritizing fairness, transparency, explainability, and privacy. Under the framework, the regulator issued updated Supervisory Guidance for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence. The guidance is built on three pillars that cover governance and accountability over AI adoption, proportionate management of the particular risks AI poses, and the building of trust and transparency around AI solutions. The articles describe the guidance as a set of expectations for banks rather than a list of specific numeric thresholds, dates, or penalties, so the details of how banks must comply are not spelled out in the coverage.

The core requirement is that institutions assign clear responsibility for their AI use and manage its risks in a way that fits the scale and nature of each application. The guidance also asks banks to make their AI solutions transparent and explainable, which is a focus on how customers and staff can understand the outcomes of automated decisions. The articles do not say what enforcement would follow a failure to meet these expectations. Coverage of the announcement was published by Compliance Week on October 24, 2026. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is the institution responsible for the framework and the guidance, and it introduced both as part of its effort to support responsible AI in banking.

The articles do not include direct quotations from named officials, so the regulator's stated purpose is described here only in general terms: promoting responsible adoption as AI spreads through the sector. The announcement was made on a Thursday, which the Compliance Week report dates to the week of October 24, 2026. The move comes as banks worldwide expand their use of AI, and the articles present it as an attempt to set clear expectations before risks grow. The coverage does not describe any specific incident that prompted the framework, nor does it lay out a timeline for further steps. What happens next, including how the guidance will be applied in supervision and whether further rules will follow, is not stated in the articles.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong regulator sets accountability, resilience, trust rules for bank AI

stories.Headline: South Chungcheong Governor Park Soo-hyun pitches the province as an “AI capital” in the US ... signs investment agreements with three global companies
stories.Summary:
South Chungcheong Governor Park Soo-hyun left on a five-day, three-night business trip to the United States on October 25, 2026, aiming to draw global investment and build ties with AI institutions. According to the provincial government, the trip runs from the 25th to the 29th. The governor's first stop was the New Jersey AI Hub at Princeton University on the 26th, local time, a platform for AI research, startups, industry, and talent development launched in March of last year. Princeton University, the New Jersey Economic Development Authority, Microsoft, and CoreWeave are among its key partners. Park planned to tour the facilities and explore ways to cooperate on the province's "AI Basic Society" goal.

On the same trip he was due to visit United Nations Headquarters and the Permanent Mission of the Republic of Korea to the United Nations, where he would meet UNDP Associate Administrator Haoliang Xu and Korean ambassador Ji-hoon Cha. The aim was to learn about international politics, economic trends, and AI policies and projects, and to look for ways to connect with UN AI initiatives. On the 27th he planned to visit the New York Korean Association Hall to discuss wider exchanges with the Korean American community. The main event that day was a large investment agreement with three global companies at the New York Hilton Midtown. The article calls it the second foreign investment attraction agreement of his ninth popularly elected term, after one with Germany's Webasto last August.

The provincial government says the trip supports its vision of making Chungnam an AI capital, which is already taking shape. Of the 392 trillion won in advanced-industry investment projects for the Chungcheong region that the government announced last July, the article says Chungnam secured 202 trillion won, more than half. Park has said he wants to speed up AI investment through what he calls "three-power innovation" covering electricity, hydropower, and human resources, backed by "lightning-speed administration." The same day, Park was to attend an export consultation session organized with the Chungnam Economic Promotion Agency, where 20 local cosmetics and food small and medium-sized enterprises would hold one-on-one talks with buyers. The trip would end with an event in New York for about 250 people from the Chungcheong diaspora and businesspeople across the Americas.

Articles.Title: South Chungcheong Governor Park Soo-hyun pitches the province as an “AI capital” in the US ... signs investment agreements with three global companies

stories.Headline: Three Rules for Junior Accountants Competing With AI
stories.Summary:
Junior accountants are facing a new competitor in AI, which is absorbing much of the routine work they once used to build their skills. According to the article, this matters because the profession still needs junior staff to grow into experienced accountants who can catch and correct what AI produces. The article describes the workload that has shifted, including reconciliation, categorization, document collection and basic tax preparation. Its author, writing on the CPA Practice Advisor site on October 24, 2026, lays out this concern and proposes three rules for junior accountants to follow.

The article notes that the industry already struggles to attract and keep junior professionals, so AI taking routine tasks adds another obstacle to their development. It cites early evidence from a Stanford and MIT study showing that less experienced accountants are more likely to rely on uncertain generative AI outputs, while senior accountants are more likely to step in and intervene. It also reports that 71% of tax professionals support using generative AI in their work, with tax research, tax preparation and bookkeeping among the areas where it is most useful. A separate study found that generative AI shifted 9% of accountant time away from routine data entry, increased ledger detail by 12% and cut monthly closing time by 7.5 days.

The author argues that the trade-off is real, because the same tools that save time also threaten how juniors learn the underlying math and judgment. The article points to a broader risk that future senior accountants, lacking hands-on exposure, could exercise weaker judgment. It also highlights a workforce gap, reporting that in 2025 the AICPA said 75% of current CPAs were eligible to retire within 15 years, while graduate numbers contracted between 2018 and 2023. The author frames the answer as three rules for junior accountants to deal with this changing landscape. The excerpt provided ends before those rules are set out, so the full list of recommendations is not available here.

Articles.Title: Three Rules for Junior Accountants Competing With AI - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: More than S$45 million set aside to help Singapore manufacturers adopt AI
stories.Summary:
The Singapore government has set aside more than S$45 million, about US$35 million, over the next three years to help manufacturers adopt artificial intelligence. Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang announced the funding on Wednesday, Oct 21, at Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific 2026. The money will support Enterprise Singapore’s Catalytic AI Solutions initiative for advanced manufacturing. The initiative is meant to help manufacturers overcome common barriers to AI adoption.

Small and medium-sized enterprises will be able to use ready-to-deploy AI tools for product and component design, processing request for quotation documents, production scheduling and predictive maintenance. Enterprise Singapore said these solutions could reduce manual work and response times, improve equipment reliability and help maintain consistent product quality. The agency will co-fund eligible companies that adopt AI solutions from the suite, which will expand over time. Enterprise Singapore is also developing similar initiatives for logistics and wholesale trade, with details to come later.

Gan said the goal was not simply to increase AI use but to transform manufacturing, adding that the aim was to reimagine manufacturing to grow output and productivity. Enterprise Singapore said many SMEs recognise AI’s potential but face challenges such as development costs, limited access to sector-specific solutions and uncertainty over outcomes. The initiative will bring together AI solution providers, system integrators and industry associations so SMEs can use proven solutions without developing them independently. Some SMEs have already expressed interest, according to Gan.

Manufacturing accounts for nearly 20 per cent of Singapore’s GDP. The AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing, jointly established by A*STAR and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in 2024, will enter its next phase under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan. It has collaborated with 30 manufacturers in aerospace, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and energy, completing 23 projects. Gan also announced the Singapore Embodied AI Challenge for Manufacturing, organised by the National Robotics Programme, A*STAR and PINE Lab at NTU, starting with a semiconductor manufacturing use case from Micron. At Budget 2026, the government expanded the Enterprise Innovation Scheme to cover qualifying AI expenditure.

Articles.Title: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
stories.Summary:
Governments and companies around the world took websites offline on Oct 22 as they rushed to guard against hacks, after artificial intelligence uncovered two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that helps run about 70% of the world's websites, according to Wiz Research. The PHP Foundation, which maintains the language, released emergency security updates on Oct 21 for the two flaws, which are known collectively as PHP2Shell. The security firm Calif found the first flaw on Aug 1 using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, during an OpenAI-funded audit of the language's code. Wiz, which is owned by Google, found its own flaw independently on Aug 19, using Google's Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-5.6 Sol and its own research agent. Details leaked online on Oct 20, a day before the planned fix, which set off the scramble to pull sites offline before hackers could act.

The flaws can let attackers into servers without a username or password, and both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or take vulnerable systems offline, and authorities from Japan to the European Union said the same. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged updates to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and the FBI advised organisations to list every place PHP runs, including products that bundle it. Government sites in Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Denmark went dark, while in Japan MUFG Bank halted some online transactions, Mizuho stopped services, Shizuoka Bank shut its banking app, and All Nippon Airways disabled boarding passes in Apple Wallet. The network that settles funds between almost all Japanese banks was not affected.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore said the flaws affect all versions of PHP and reported widespread exploitation attempts and several proof-of-concept exploits, though it knew of no Singapore sites taken down by hackers. The Government Technology Agency of Singapore said there was currently no sign any government systems had been compromised, and that some services might be taken offline temporarily as a precaution. The PHP Foundation said anyone running PHP must update now, and one of its security engineers, Volker Dusch, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem the language has faced in over a decade, comparable to the Heartbleed flaw of 2014. A Wiz blog post said the findings rank among the most severe ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history. OpenAI said the discovery marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact, and it also warned that such tools can help attackers build exploits.

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed, and many large platforms use other languages or operators able to install the fix quickly, so they stayed online. Cybersecurity lecturer Rahat Masood of the University of New South Wales called the discovery quite devastating, saying attackers who get in can do almost anything, from stealing information to changing site content. Steve Kerrison of James Cook University's Singapore campus said larger institutions should patch quickly, but many smaller sites and user-run blogs may stay vulnerable for days, weeks or months and could be used to spread viruses or spam. So far there is little evidence of damaging attacks, though data breaches could later feed phishing campaigns. The number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 is on track to roughly double the record total set in 2025, and Cloudflare has reported millions of exploit attempts since the disclosure.

Articles.Title: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: U.S. Lawmakers Press AI Founders to Focus on Products and Safety
stories.Summary:
Bipartisan U.S. lawmakers and other government officials are urging artificial intelligence founders to prioritize safe product development, according to a TokenPost report published October 24, 2026. The concern follows public messaging from AI executives that has swung between describing the technology's potential prosperity and warning of existential dangers, sometimes at the same event. Lawmakers and regulators say these shifts add to political instability at a time when the industry already faces strong public backlash. The article also says that industry leaders have not taken a leading role in persuading Americans about AI's benefits or its potential for shared prosperity.

Officials have asked founders to spend less time talking and more time building products while making sure those products are safe. The article links this request to a wider problem, saying that discussion of digital sentience and global catastrophe has turned an already complicated debate over AI regulation into what it describes as a moral panic. It does not set out specific rules, deadlines, penalties, or figures tied to the request. The report describes the officials' position only as a call for a change in emphasis, not as a formal proposal with defined requirements.

The article attributes the criticism to lawmakers and regulators, who say the mixed messages from executives contribute to instability in the policy debate. It names no individual lawmaker, agency, or company as the target of the complaint, and it does not quote any official directly. The reporting presents the officials' view as their concern about how founders communicate, while describing the broader picture through the reporter's own framing. The piece is written by Riza Dagoc, who covers regulation, investing, and digital assets for TokenPost.

The article gives no timeline for further action and does not say whether any hearing, bill, or regulatory step is planned. Its account of the debate remains limited to the messaging concern and the description of the public mood, leaving the next steps unclear. Based on the report alone, the request appears to be a statement of expectations rather than the start of a defined policy process. Readers looking for specifics on what might follow will need to wait for additional reporting.

Articles.Title: U.S. Lawmakers Press AI Founders to Focus on Products and Safety

stories.Headline: Real Review: I Spent 30 Days Using AI to Build Online Income – Honest 2024 Results & Actionable Insights
stories.Summary:
A translation team at 36Kr published a first-person account on October 23, 2026, describing a 30-day experiment in which the author used AI tools to try to build an online income stream. The author did not ask AI to produce a specific sum of money but gave it the narrower task of finding a real pain point, turning a solution into a sellable product, and building a small operation around it. The experiment ran with no employees and no large advertising budget, relying on a few AI tools and a laptop. The article's editor's note frames it as a test of whether AI-assisted creation can be turned into a business. The author began by using AI to surface questions people were searching for, then checked those ideas against Google Trends, search suggestions, Reddit discussions and repeated netizen questions.

The pain point that kept appearing across platforms was that people were less short of AI tools than unsure which to choose, how to use them, and how to earn money with them. The author used AI to organize research, write outlines and fill gaps, but added personal cases, screenshots and opinions rather than publishing raw AI output. Between days 11 and 15, the product drew almost no visitors, and the author concluded that the real problem was that potential buyers did not know it existed. The author then built a simple funnel of free essays, a free downloadable material, an email list and a paid product, and turned one research theme into several content formats. The article also describes adding affiliate links only to tools the author would recommend anyway, and tracking which posts drew comments and questions as a stronger signal of buying intent than raw views.

The author reports no income figure, saying they did not earn 10,000 yuan, and says the gains were a finished digital product, a sales page, a reusable content process, an email sequence, affiliate opportunities and evidence of real user interest. The author credits AI with speeding research and generating ideas but says the final decisions on what to build and how to release it stayed with the author. Their main conclusion is that AI lowers the cost of producing content so much that finding a worthwhile product and a clear audience becomes the real advantage. The author says that if repeating the experiment, they would do more research before creating anything. The article does not describe any further plans beyond that.

stories.Headline: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published the second part of a series on Oct. 23, 2026, describing how it rebuilt the storage layer behind its products. The company's storage platform, called Habitat, must respond in milliseconds to more than 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions, and it now serves over 500 petabytes of data. The post focuses on Azure Cosmos DB, the database underneath Habitat, which OpenAI says it reworked through a close partnership with the Azure team. The article describes the change as moving from a single shared container, to separate containers for each use case, and then back to a multi-tenant design by default.

The reasons given for the change are specific. Early on, clients could choose partition keys directly, so common keys such as user identifiers collided across unrelated product features and shared the same throughput limits. Workloads from niche features could also starve core login and signup flows, and as storage grew, physical partitions split while total provisioned throughput stayed fixed, which shrank the capacity available to each partition. Separate containers helped isolate workloads, but each one needed individual capacity planning, and teams often forgot to scale up before launches, leaving engineers scrambling during live incidents. OpenAI's engineers wrote that this pushed nearly every product team into capacity planning, with uneven diligence across services.

The authors, OpenAI's engineering team, present the outcome as a lesson in tradeoffs rather than a simple win, and they say the multi-tenant approach now depends on Azure Cosmos DB's built-in primitives where possible. They describe their multi-tenancy work as still early, and they say they have deferred further investment in that area. The article, as excerpted, does not give specific timelines for future changes or any figures on latency or cost savings after the redesign. Part I of the series, which covers Habitat's evolution from a Python client into a service, is referenced as the earlier installment.

Articles.Title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)

stories.Headline: Factorized-gating mixture of experts enables cross-regime turbulence modeling
stories.Summary:
The research paper introduces a machine learning framework called factorized-gating mixture of experts, or FG-MoE, for modeling turbulent flows, which are central to aerospace, energy and environmental technologies. The authors, Hao-Chen Liu, Qingyong Luo and Xin-Lei Zhang, of the State Key Laboratory of Non-linear Mechanics at the Institute of Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the School of Engineering Sciences at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing, published it in Communications Engineering on October 24, 2026. The article is an accepted version shared early and is subject to further edits before a final version of record appears. The work responds to a known weakness in existing data-driven turbulence models, which rely on single dense networks that struggle to generalize across different flow regimes.

The framework trains separate experts for distinct flow regimes and blends them using spatially varying probabilities. Its key change is to split the usual monolithic router, which decides how to weight the experts, into a set of lightweight binary attributes guided by physics. This reduces a high-dimensional gating function to an approximation built from low-dimensional binary factor probabilities. According to the abstract, the design lowers gating complexity, makes the gating mechanism physically interpretable, and allows the expert library to grow without retraining the whole model. The authors report that numerical experiments, ranging from canonical benchmarks to complex real-world engineering applications, produced consistently high-fidelity predictions across diverse flow regimes.

The authors state the work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Excellence Research Group Program for multiscale problems in nonlinear mechanics, the China National Postdoctoral Program for Innovative Talents, the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation, and the Young Elite Scientists Sponsorship Program by CAST and the CAS Project for Young Scientists in Basic Research. The article declares no competing interests. The framework is described as offering a pathway for engineering turbulence modeling by decomposing complex flows into distinct physical regimes. The articles do not describe any further publication timeline or follow-up work beyond the early-access status.

Articles.Title: Factorized-gating mixture of experts enables cross-regime turbulence modeling

stories.Headline: AI is among 17 potentially ‘catastrophic threats’ that researchers say require targeted action
stories.Summary:
A commission of 35 leaders from various industries, working with data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation's Global Burden of Disease study, identified 17 interconnected threats that could collectively cost the world tens of billions of years of healthy life through the rest of the 21st century. The findings were published in The Lancet and reported on October 10, 2026. The threats range from health conditions and behaviors, such as obesity, high blood pressure, smoking and mental health, to economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict. Two of them, nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence, were flagged as carrying a risk of extinction.

The commission's report does not demand specific laws or spending, but it urges governments and communities to act now, since delay only shifts and raises the eventual costs. For malicious AI, the commission estimates about 10.4 billion years of healthy life lost worldwide by 2100, roughly comparable to naturally occurring pandemics and obesity. Those AI estimates are theoretical, because no malicious AI event of truly global magnitude has yet occurred, whereas obesity estimates rest on more empirical data. Overweight and obesity are rising in every country, and projections suggest the global rate could reach 60 percent of adults and a third of children by 2050. The report says trust is central to any effective response, and it names seven further factors that will shape how societies respond, including collaborative global leadership, resilient food systems and more equitable societies.

Dr. Christopher Murray, co-chair of the commission and director of the University of Washington's Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, said the scale of the threats is striking but that humanity still has the ability to act. Dr. Natalia Kanem, a former executive director of the United Nations Population Fund and the other co-chair, warned that stability can give way to crisis quickly and that the threats risk deepening existing inequalities. The commission's forecasters showed wide divergence in estimating the risk of AI-related catastrophe, and the commissioners pointed to recent shocks such as the Covid-19 pandemic, the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Africa and accelerating climate impacts as evidence that assumptions about stability can be overturned. The editorial accompanying the report says the goal is to spur international, regional and national action rather than to rank the threats. The report concludes that technical solutions alone will not be enough without strong societal and institutional foundations.

Articles.Title: AI is among 17 potentially ‘catastrophic threats’ that researchers say require targeted action

stories.Headline: AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE)
stories.Summary:
Collective Artists Network, through its Historyverse studio unit, has announced a cross-border intellectual property venture with Galleri5, the developer of the AI technology behind the Star Plus and JioHotstar series "Mahabharat: Ek Dharmayudh," and with Singhasari Special Economic Zone in Indonesia. The announcement, reported by Variety on October 24, 2026, says the partners will create film and series properties drawn from Indonesian myth and history, covering mythology, fantasy, history and animation. The first project under discussion is "Echoes of Nusantara," a working title for an original mythology-adventure. Indonesian creatives and cultural specialists will work alongside Historyverse's IP development team, using production tools that Galleri5 built in India.

Under the arrangement, Historyverse will handle creative development, production and IP packaging, and will work with local talent to prepare projects for possible financing, production and distribution outside Indonesia. Galleri5's main product, G5 AI Studio, combines more than 200 AI models with tools for storyboarding, character and world design, animation, visual effects and film-quality video, and the platform has been used to make more than 10,000 ads and videos. Galleri5 is also building workflows for Historyverse's theatrical slate, which includes "Chiranjeevi Hanuman – The Eternal" and "Krishna," productions the company says will help it test its technology against real creative and production demands. Singhasari will introduce the venture to Indonesian creators, studios, investors, distributors and creative-economy institutions and help set up local partnerships and routes to market.

Vijay Subramaniam, founder and group CEO of Collective Artists Network, said that future global entertainment franchises will not all come from Hollywood and that Indonesia has a deep store of stories worth reaching wider audiences. Rahul Regulapati, founder and CEO of Galleri5, said the company wants to bring frontier AI models and filmmaking workflows together on one platform. Airlangga Hartarto, Indonesia's coordinating minister for economic affairs and chairman of the National Council for Special Economic Zones, said the country intends to help shape AI development rather than only consume it, and linked the effort to skilled jobs and growth toward an 8 percent target. David Santoso KR, chief executive of Lokanima and Singhasari Special Economic Zone, said the partnership aims to build new competitiveness in digital content with Indonesian talent and IP at its core. India's ambassador to Indonesia, Sandeep Chakravorty, said the Ramayana and Mahabharata have long been part of Indonesian temple culture, wayang puppet theater and popular imagination, and that the two countries are now extending that shared story with artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: The Tenth Circuit Should Adopt Its AI Verification Rule, With Clearer Standards - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The Tenth Circuit released a proposal on September 18, 2026 that would require a human to verify court filings prepared with generative AI. The change, if adopted, would take effect January 1, 2027. The author, Utsav Gupta, writes that the proposal is a welcome step toward making verification duties concrete. He argues that the court should adopt it with practical guidance and proportionate enforcement. Proposed Rule 46.5(B)(4) would require attorneys and self-represented people to certify that a human reviewed any document prepared with generative AI before filing it.

That reviewer must independently confirm that every cited authority exists and that quotations and citations are accurate. The review must also cover the accuracy of legal analysis and compliance with relevant rules and ethical obligations. The certification is qualified by the filer's knowledge, information, and belief after a reasonable inquiry, and filing the document itself would count as the certification, with no separate AI disclosure form. The proposal also adds waiver of an issue and striking a document to the list of available sanctions.

Gupta notes that the Fifth Circuit declined a similar proposal in 2024, concluding that existing duties were sufficient, while Illinois requires thorough review under existing obligations but advises against mandatory disclosure in pleadings. He points to a February 2026 Fifth Circuit case, Fletcher v. Experian Information Solutions, Inc., in which a lawyer was sanctioned $2,500 for failing to verify AI-produced briefing and for not being candid about that use. He also points to a separate error in the Fifth Circuit's own notice declining its proposal, which cited the wrong rule, showing why reading the cited authority matters.

He argues the Tenth Circuit should add guidance that review of legal analysis allows for reasonable disagreement about the law, clarify whether using AI only for grammar or formatting triggers the rule, and weigh a filer's conduct when choosing a sanction. Gupta's central point is that a rule requiring human review of AI-assisted filings gives lawyers and unrepresented parties concrete checks before submission, though he acknowledges its effect on compliance remains unproven. He writes that the court should adopt the proposal with clear review standards, proportionate sanctions, and opportunities to correct minor mistakes. The article does not say whether the Tenth Circuit has indicated how it will respond to these suggestions or when a final decision will be made.

Articles.Title: The Tenth Circuit Should Adopt Its AI Verification Rule, With Clearer Standards - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: A neural characteristic mapping method: Lagrangian PINNs based on flow maps for transport-dominated problems
stories.Summary:
A new paper posted to arXiv describes a numerical method for transport-dominated problems using Physics-Informed Neural Networks, or PINNs. The authors, Martin Campos Pinto, Victor Fournet, Emmanuel Franck, Philipp Krah and Victor Michel-Dansac, placed the work in the mathematics and physics categories, and the listing is dated October 24, 2026. The method targets equations whose solutions can develop steep gradients and fine structures over time, a situation the authors say is especially hard for classical PINNs. Their approach aims to address that difficulty by changing what the network learns.

Rather than approximating the solution itself, the method approximates the flow map of the equation. The solution is then recovered by pulling back the exact initial condition, so the fine structures come from the map rather than being represented directly by the network. The flow map is built from multiple PINNs, one for each time subinterval, which are composed using the semigroup property of the flow. Each network therefore only needs to represent a map close to the identity. The paper reports numerical tests on the linear advection equation, the incompressible Euler equation in vorticity form, the Vlasov-Poisson equation and a drift-kinetic equation.

The articles do not name an institution or funder for the authors, and they do not report any benchmark figures, error rates or run times. The paper is presented as a research preprint, and the authors state that they compare their method against classical PINNs and classical numerical schemes, but the summary does not give the results of those comparisons. The available material does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed or accepted for publication, nor whether code is available. Further details would have to come from the full text of the paper.

Articles.Title: A neural characteristic mapping method: Lagrangian PINNs based on flow maps for transport-dominated problems

stories.Headline: Navigating the EU Artificial Intelligence Act - CBA National
stories.Summary:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is already relevant to many Canadian organizations, according to a commentary published on October 23, 2026 by Joan Palacio, legal counsel at the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The article notes that tools such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Gemini fall within the scope of the legislation's obligations. Recent amendments have confused businesses about timing, though key provisions are already in force. The author argues that Canadian firms doing international business should understand these changes.

The most significant change is the Digital Omnibus on AI, which entered into force in July after concerns that the conformity assessment mechanisms and supporting regulatory infrastructure were not ready. Under the revised timeline, requirements for stand-alone high-risk AI systems apply from December 2, 2027, while requirements for AI systems embedded in regulated products, such as machinery, apply from August 2, 2028. The Omnibus also widened certain accommodations for small and medium-sized enterprises and strengthened the role of the European AI Office in supervision and enforcement. The risk-based structure of the Act itself remains unchanged.

The article cautions businesses against assuming that delayed high-risk obligations mean compliance can wait. Prohibitions on certain unacceptable AI practices have applied since February 2025, and AI literacy obligations took effect at the same time. Rules for general-purpose AI models, which include the technologies behind ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Toronto-based Cohere's Command models, started in August 2025. Transparency requirements under article 50 took effect in August and are likely the most immediately relevant provision for many Canadian businesses, particularly those using customer-facing chatbots or emotion-recognition systems.

The author, Palacio, expresses the view that the Act has extraterritorial reach, much like the GDPR, and that European compliance expectations are reaching Canadian companies through customer contracts and supply chains. She recommends that counsel help clients build an inventory of AI systems, establish governance frameworks, review supplier due diligence, update commercial contracts, provide AI training and monitor regulation in the EU, UK, US and Canada. She concludes that the strategic direction of EU AI regulation has not changed, despite the shifted timelines. The article's disclaimer notes that its views are not necessarily those of the Canadian Bar Association.

Articles.Title: Navigating the EU Artificial Intelligence Act - CBA National

stories.Headline: Opinion: Issue with school district campaign flyer isn’t the AI. It’s the misogyny
stories.Summary:
A campaign flyer sent out by David Miyashiro, the current Cajon Valley Union School District superintendent and a candidate for the San Dieguito Union High School District Area 1 trustee seat, drew attention from local outlets including FOX 5 San Diego. The mailer shows a deepfake image of his opponent, Amy Flicker, at an old-fashioned bake sale, labeled "Non-profit volunteer," next to Miyashiro seated behind a school board dais labeled "District superintendent." It asks who is more qualified for the San Dieguito board and says "The choice is obvious." The flyer includes the small-print disclosure that the ad was generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence. The piece was published in Times of San Diego on October 23, 2026, as an opinion column by Katrina Young, a former trustee of the district.

Young argues that media coverage has focused on artificial intelligence when the real problem is misogyny. She contends the disclosure does not excuse the ad, since Miyashiro used tools he publicly promotes for students to produce a demeaning, sexist caricature of a woman. In her view, the technology only served as an efficient vehicle for a trope that predates it. She describes volunteers, mostly women, as the backbone of public schools, doing planning, budgeting, communications and management work often backed by advanced degrees. She also lists Flicker's record, which includes more than a decade of managing school budgets and policy, serving as PTA president for the Encinitas Union School District and the San Dieguito district, and advocacy in Sacramento and Washington, D.C.

Young places responsibility on Miyashiro, whom she faults for diminishing a respected community member, and she says that a sitting superintendent doing this undermines his fitness to oversee artificial intelligence in classrooms. She questions whether he would treat female teachers, staff and students with the same dismissive attitude he showed his opponent, and she calls his outlook patriarchal. She links the flyer to comedian Shane Gillis's recent "Saturday Night Live" monologue, which she describes as degrading women for cheap laughs. Her broader argument is that mistreatment of women in public life is systemic and that voters and the community must demand accountability from candidates. The articles do not report any response from Miyashiro, and they do not describe any formal action taken against the flyer.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Issue with school district campaign flyer isn’t the AI. It’s the misogyny - Times of San Diego

stories.Headline: How Investors Are Reacting To Kyndryl Holdings (KD) AI Deal With Toyota Finance
stories.Summary:

The Toyota Finance deployment fits into Kyndryl’s effort to shift from legacy, pre-spin contracts toward newer, AI and cloud heavy work. The company’s narrative projects US$15.2 billion in revenue and US$472.5 million in earnings by 2029, assuming flat revenue trends and an earnings increase of about US$274.5 million from US$198.0 million today. Kyndryl’s share price has bounced sharply, with a 1-day return of 4.59 percent, a 7-day return of 13.48 percent, and a 30-day return of 15.08 percent. Complex account transitions, debt coverage pressures, and weaker margins limit how much benefit investors actually see from efficiency projects. If agentic AI engagements become more common, they could support higher margin contracts, stronger earnings growth, and more stable free cash flow.
