stories.Headline: AI in the middle market: High satisfaction, limited enterprise adoption
stories.Summary:
The RSM US published its 2026 Middle Market AI Survey, which found that middle market organizations are adopting artificial intelligence and reporting high satisfaction with it, yet many have not scaled it across the enterprise. The survey, which aggregated responses from 827 U.S. and 203 Canadian middle market executives across a variety of industries, was published on October 24, 2026, with the page dated July 21, 2026. Reported findings show that 86% of respondents said AI is integrated into operations, but only 36% have it fully embedded across core processes. Another 97% reported satisfaction with AI's business value, though many organizations are measuring early wins rather than enterprise-wide outcomes.

The survey identifies the main obstacles to wider deployment. Data quality was cited as a top barrier by 34% of respondents, followed by security and privacy concerns at 30% and legacy systems integration at 28%. The report also found that 85% of respondents said leadership is more enthusiastic about AI than employees are, which it describes as a sign that change management and workforce readiness need attention. The articles present these as areas that require governance, measurement, integration and change management before AI can produce lasting business value. The report argues that spending alone will not deliver that value, and that organizations need an operating model connecting strategy, technology and talent.

RSM US attributes the analysis to its consulting team. Ana Minter, the firm's Consulting AI Go-to-Market Leader, is quoted as saying that AI is not failing in the middle market, but that scaling it requires prioritizing issues, identifying how AI can address them and then executing on those ideas. Minter said the next phase requires more than tools and pilots. The report is promoted as a guide for leaders seeking to move from productivity gains to repeatable, enterprise-wide value, and the page links to industry snapshots covering manufacturing, financial services, health care, technology, professional services and real estate.

Articles.Title: AI in the middle market: High satisfaction, limited enterprise adoption

stories.Headline: ‘Tech debt coming due’: AI-found flaw signals chaos ahead
stories.Summary:
Companies and government agencies rushed last week to patch two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language that runs a large share of the world's websites. The vulnerability was found using a powerful model from OpenAI, in what the article describes as one of the most high-profile demonstrations of AI's cyber capabilities. Reporters spoke with Michael Daniel, who is president of the Cyber Threat Alliance and a former White House cybersecurity coordinator under U.S. President Barack Obama. The conversation focused on what the episode means as AI tools find software flaws faster than ever.

Daniel's remarks, as the article presents them, centered on the speed at which these tools can now locate weaknesses in widely used software. The flaws were serious enough that organizations across the private and public sectors moved quickly to apply fixes. The article's framing, reflected in its headline, suggests that older code and accumulated shortcuts, often called technical debt, are now surfacing at a pace that could create disruption. Details beyond the two patched PHP flaws, such as exact dates of discovery or specific affected organizations, are not provided in the text available here. The article does not give a precise count of affected websites.

The article attributes the analysis primarily to Daniel, whose background in U.S. cybersecurity policy lends weight to his comments. The discovery itself is credited to OpenAI's model, and the article presents that as a notable example of AI being applied to cybersecurity work. Beyond this, the text available does not include direct statements from OpenAI, PHP maintainers, or affected companies. The page content is largely navigation and unrelated headlines, so the fuller reporting is not included.

The broader context is that AI systems are increasingly able to scan code and identify vulnerabilities that might previously have taken human researchers far longer to find. The article does not say what steps regulators or software makers plan next, and it offers no timeline for further disclosures. Whether this episode leads to new standards or practices is not addressed in the text. More to follow.

Articles.Title: ‘Tech debt coming due’: AI-found flaw signals chaos ahead

stories.Headline: APEX: Active Protection at Execution Boundaries for LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
A team of ten researchers posted a preprint on arXiv describing APEX, a defense against indirect prompt injection in large language model agents. The paper, arXiv:2610.06966, was first submitted on 3 October 2026 and revised on 7 October 2026, and the DOI record shows an update dated 24 October 2026. The authors include Xinran Zheng, Xin Fan Guo, Zhiqiang Hao, Fan Yang, Xingzhi Qian, Jiawei Du, Jinfeng Xu, Zheng Xing, Shuo Yang and Xingjun Wang. The paper is listed under Cryptography and Security, with a secondary category in Artificial Intelligence.

The authors argue that existing defenses, which try to recognize specific attack patterns, fall behind as agents combine more kinds of tools, servers and skills that can carry hidden instructions. APEX instead enforces two checks at the point where an agent turns its internal state into an external action or output: whether the action is authorized, and whether the information behind it is endorsed by the trusted task. Both are drawn from a single authorization contract compiled before the agent handles untrusted content. The method combines evidence-gated prevention, which allows an action only when the contract justifies it, with deception-based exposure, which is meant to make unendorsed use reveal itself before the action commits. According to the abstract, the approach needs no attack-specific policies or taint tracking.

The authors report results against 13 baseline defenses. APEX reached 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56% on the sixth, and stayed at 0% under adaptive attacks across three types of capability units. The abstract also says it remained effective across different defender backbones. The authors have made the code available, and the paper is a preprint that has not been described in the articles as peer reviewed. The articles do not say how the results compare with the methods in the broader research community, nor do they describe any deployment or any planned next steps beyond the code release.

Articles.Title: APEX: Active Protection at Execution Boundaries for LLM Agents

stories.Headline: Crusoe: Building AI Factories at a US$30.9bn Valuation
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, an AI infrastructure company, raised US$3.9bn in a Series F round in September 2026 at a post-money valuation of US$30.9bn. The article reports that the company now has more than US$140bn in total contracted value and over 6GW of gross contracted capacity, with about 1GW delivered and operational. Its best-known project is a campus in Abilene, Texas, where OpenAI trained its model Astra, and Crusoe designed and built the site. The company was founded on using wasted natural gas to power computing and has since grown into a major builder of AI infrastructure.

The company's strategy is vertical integration, meaning it controls every stage from power supply to the rental of computing capacity through Crusoe Cloud. In practice, it secures energy, designs and builds data centre campuses, manufactures some of its own equipment, and sells compute to customers. Its energy deals span grid, battery, nuclear, thermal and renewable sources. The Armstrong County campus near Amarillo, being built for Google, connects directly to two adjacent 265.5MW wind farms. Aalo Atomics has a partnership aimed at delivering the first nuclear-powered AI factory in 2027, and ON.energy will supply 5GW of AI UPS systems across several hyperscale campuses.

Chase Lochmiller, Crusoe's co-founder and CEO, has described the strategy as controlling the infrastructure from electrons to tokens. The article attributes the company's growth in cloud business to bookings that are up more than 20 times year on year in 2026 so far. Its Managed Inference product has passed US$100m in contracted annual recurring revenue within a year of launch. Perplexity signed a multi-year deal in September 2026 for dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 clusers, and Thinking Machines Lab agreed a US$65m-a-year contract for open-model inference days later.

The Series F was co-led by Atreides Management, Mubadala Capital and Valor Equity Partners, and the funds are intended for the next wave of campuses and cloud capacity. Crusoe now employs more than 1,800 people across five countries and has added board members including Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert. In October 2026 it pledged US$50m in compute credits to the White House AI Science Initiative. The article does not describe any specific regulatory or market challenges facing the company.

Articles.Title: Crusoe: Building AI Factories at a US$30.9bn Valuation - AI Magazine

stories.Headline: Hitachi Energy develops power system simulation with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help accelerate AI factory deployment
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Energy has announced a new simulation capability built on integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, which lets data center teams test how future AI factory power systems might perform before they are built. The tool was announced in Berlin on October 23, 2026, and it joins the wider NVIDIA DSXSim partner ecosystem. It brings AI load scenarios and power system models into one shared digital environment. Teams can compare alternative designs, assess resilience, and reach more informed decisions earlier in planning.

Power infrastructure is a critical factor in how quickly and at what scale AI factories can be deployed. According to the article, electricity demand from data centers rose 17 percent in 2025, and consumption from AI-focused facilities grew faster still, well ahead of overall global demand growth. Operators must make key design choices that affect their ability to deliver with speed, reliability, scalability, and long-term resilience. The initial focus of the simulation is 800-volt direct current architectures, which are being developed to meet the rising power density and efficiency needs of next-generation AI factories. Grid-to-rack simulation can give insight into how such systems behave before they are deployed at scale.

The capability is part of a close collaboration between Hitachi Energy and NVIDIA on 800 VDC AI factories. Using OpenUSD-based workflows powered by NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, engineering data and Hitachi Energy power system models can be evaluated together in the shared environment. Marco Berardi, Head of Grid & Power Quality Solutions and Service at Hitachi Energy, said that as AI factories scale, access to electricity and the ability to deploy infrastructure quickly are becoming more important, and that combining Hitachi Energy's electrification expertise with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries lets customers explore and optimize power architectures before deployment. The development also follows the recent qualification of Hitachi Energy's battery energy storage system as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS, which helps customers identify components that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements.

The article gives context on the companies involved. Hitachi Energy describes itself as a global leader in electrification, with an installed base in over 140 countries, around 56,000 employees in 60 countries, and revenues of around $20 billion USD. Hitachi, its parent group, reported revenues of 10,586.7 billion yen for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The article does not describe specific next steps or delivery timelines for the simulation capability.

Articles.Title: Hitachi Energy develops power system simulation with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help accelerate AI factory deployment

stories.Headline: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in Washington are weighing a series of bills to protect American workers from job losses that artificial intelligence could cause. Their proposals vary in scope, though many focus on training programs for workers whose roles are eliminated. On a Friday in late October 2026, Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, a Democrat, backed a bill called The Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act. The measure would extend unemployment benefits during high-unemployment periods, and it would also provide education and retraining for higher-paying jobs to workers displaced by AI.

The Oregon senator's bill would extend unemployment benefits to 52 weeks once the unemployment rate reaches 8.5%, which is double the current standard of up to 26 weeks. Other proposals are more varied in their approach. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act last month, which would create three excise taxes on the AI industry, including a 5% tax on digital advertising revenue, an AI usage tax and a 50% excess profits tax. Those revenues would go into a fund that could be used to retrain displaced workers. Representatives Greg Casar, Valerie Foushee and Sara Jacobs introduced the AI Tax and Work Protection Act in August, which would tax AI companies based on token usage at a rate that rises as unemployment rises.

The concerns behind these bills come from warnings by AI industry leaders and other prominent figures. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10% to 20% within one to five years. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates also warned in a recent essay that AI could put millions of jobs at risk. Economists note that those projections have not yet materialized, and that AI-related layoffs so far have mostly been concentrated in the tech industry. Still, a recent Associated Press-NORC poll found that nearly 80% of Americans said protecting workers in the age of AI is extremely or very important.

Another proposal, the AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act, is aimed at transparency rather than direct support. Senators Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat, and Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, introduced it last year, and it would require major companies and federal agencies to report AI-related layoffs to the Department of Labor. The Labor Department would then make that data public. A House version was introduced in July by Representatives Steven Horsford of Nevada and Sara Jacobs of California, along with James Moylan, the delegate for Guam.

Articles.Title: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Says AI Agents Have Sent Token, GPU Demand ‘Through the Roof’: Gene Munster Sees 15 Million Bot Users Soaring to Billions
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that token consumption and demand for graphics processing units have gone "through the roof" because of artificial intelligence agents. He made the remarks during his keynote address in Berlin on October 21, 2026, when he pointed to personalized agents such as Meta Muse, Grok Bot and Gemini. Huang argued that agents think, reason, iterate and use tools, which consumes a large amount of tokens. He added that this demand had flowed directly into GPU demand as well.

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, echoed that view and said rising agent use is one of the clearer reasons compute demand should keep climbing for the next few years. He estimated that agents can consume ten to fifteen times the tokens a chatbot uses. Munster noted that about 15 million consumers use bots daily today, but said that in a few years that figure could reach the billions. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist, also said agents already consume roughly five times more tokens than human users on the OpenRouter platform.

Huang outlined five elements of an AI agent: a model, a harness that he called an exoskeleton, a sandbox for isolation, memory and tools. He said this architecture requires dedicated computing power to run the language model, manage the agent's knowledge and execute its tools. He also said the industry is moving from consuming AI toward manufacturing it inside large data centers, which he called AI factories. Those requirements are the basis for his expectation that compute demand will keep growing.

The article notes that Nvidia shares were down about 2.4 percent in premarket trading on the Thursday it was published, after closing up 2.54 percent at $221.97 the previous day. Over the past year the stock had risen about 22.5 percent, and it was up about 19 percent for the year to date. Benzinga's ratings describe a weak short-term price trend but a strong long- and medium-term trend. The piece is a market commentary and does not describe any further announcements or events beyond these remarks.

Articles.Title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Says AI Agents Have Sent Token, GPU Demand ‘Through the Roof’: Gene Munster Sees 15 Million Bot Users Soaring to Billions

stories.Headline: Tech bills of the week: Preventing AI model theft; Regulating AI-generated political content; and more
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers this week introduced several technology bills, two of which target threats tied to artificial intelligence. Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., proposed legislation aimed at preventing "distillation attacks," in which copies of U.S.-made AI models are created by flooding them with millions of prompts. Separately, Rep. Shontel Brown, D-Ohio, introduced a bill on Monday addressing AI use in elections. The articles do not give a specific date for the Harrigan and Whitesides proposal beyond the week it was reported.

The Harrigan and Whitesides proposal would direct the National Institute for Standards and Technology to develop voluntary industry standards and best practices, working with private-sector model developers. It would also create an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable to foster partnerships between critical infrastructure operators and technology firms. The proposal names Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, along with entities tied to them, as actors of particular concern. Brown's bill would prohibit using AI to intentionally deprive or defraud someone of the right to vote, and would require campaign ads using AI content to carry a disclaimer stating that the output was generated by artificial intelligence. Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., reintroduced a separate bill last week that would also require disclaimers on political ads containing AI-generated photos or video.

Harrigan argued that leading AI development is happening in America, that the country has a responsibility to keep the technology secure, and that adversaries are already seeking ways to exploit these systems. He said companies developing the technology should work directly with those defending power grids, hospitals and financial systems. Brown said voters deserve to know whether the campaign content they see is real, and that people who knowingly use AI to spread false information should be held accountable. The articles do not describe any committee action or vote on these measures.

The same roundup also covered a bill from Reps. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., introduced Wednesday, called the SCREENS Act, which seeks to make cancer screening recommendations easier to understand. It would direct the Department of Health and Human Services to develop a national digital framework for screening and risk assessment recommendations that could be built into electronic health records, and would authorize research and pilot projects. Scholten said navigating complicated health guidance can lead to missed screenings. The articles do not indicate what happens next for any of these bills.

Articles.Title: Tech bills of the week: Preventing AI model theft; Regulating AI-generated political content; and more

stories.Headline: Hierarchical Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization
stories.Summary:
This is a preprint posted to Research Square on October 24, 2026, at 05:00 UTC, titled "Hierarchical Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization." The paper introduces what its authors describe as the first hierarchical version of Deep CFR, called HDCFR, aimed at imperfect information games where players lack complete information. The article does not name the individual authors, and it has not been peer reviewed by a journal. The method combines skill-based strategy learning with counterfactual regret minimization, the family of algorithms that has been among the most successful for these games.

Under this design, low-level components represent skills for solving subgames while a high-level component manages the transitions between them. The authors say this can improve learning efficiency in tasks with very large state spaces and deep game trees, and that it allows predefined human expertise to be built in and skills to be extracted for use on similar tasks. The paper also describes a variance-reduced Monte Carlo sampling extension for settings where backtracking is not possible, and it extends the approach to large-scale problems through deep learning objectives. The article gives no specific benchmark numbers or performance figures.

The authors present the work as their own, and the article reports no competing interests. The abstract states that code is available at an anonymous repository link, which suggests the authors are withholding their identities during review. The preprint is a proposal and theoretical account, so its claims about efficiency and transferability remain untested by independent peer review. The articles do not say whether the work will appear in a journal or be revised based on feedback.

Articles.Title: Hierarchical Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization

stories.Headline: Real-world user interactions with large language models for explaining home electrocardiogram reports
stories.Summary:
A study published in npj Digital Medicine on October 24, 2026, examined how real users interact with large language models that explain home electrocardiogram reports. The researchers, a team led by Shun Huang and Shenda Hong at Peking University and affiliated institutions, retrospectively analyzed 109,017 conversational sessions containing 323,470 dialogue turns. These came from 26,419 users of the Wen-Xin-Wu-Yang system over a period of 16 months. The work was designed to address a gap that appears when portable ECG devices give people heart data at home but they lack the medical knowledge to interpret it.

The analysis found that 60.01% of interactions happened outside regular working hours, showing that people turned to the tool when they were at home and not in clinical settings. Another 57.90% of users came from lower-tier cities and regions. Users showed relatively high retention and moderate interaction depth. Their questions moved over time from simply interpreting results toward medical knowledge, action-oriented guidance, and general health management.

The researchers also tracked how users expressed confirmation of the system's reliability and concern, and how they repaired interactions when things became unclear. The authors report that explicit confirmation of system reliability decreased during transitions from action questions to knowledge questions. Expressions of concern rose during the middle stages of conversations and then partly declined. In uncertain exchanges, users tended to simplify how they phrased their messages.

The paper concludes that LLMs built into AI-ECG systems can connect physiological data with medical knowledge. It suggests design implications including progressive explanation, recognition of risk-related concerns, support for repairing misunderstandings, and continued review by physicians. The study is one of several recent efforts to evaluate AI tools for heart monitoring, and the authors frame it as real-world evidence rather than a controlled trial. The articles do not describe any follow-up plans beyond the design suggestions, and the paper is an accepted early version that is still subject to further edits before its final publication.

Articles.Title: Real-world user interactions with large language models for explaining home electrocardiogram reports

stories.Headline: AI Can Now Read Court Records at Scale. Courts Should Let It.
stories.Summary:
AI Can Now Read Court Records at Scale. Courts Should Let It. is an opinion series finale by data analyst David Stasior, published by JURIST on October 23, 2026, that argues artificial intelligence can strengthen the rule of law while cases are still pending, not only measure it after the fact. Over five parts, Stasior used AI to read roughly 4,000 Massachusetts attorney disciplinary decisions, more than 10,000 federal statistical tables, federal supervised release orders, and the findings and exhibits of a contested civil trial. The series found that Massachusetts discipline looked inconsistent, that a federal court's "rocket docket" reputation rested on only 16 trials in 2025, and that federal judges applied contradictory standards on early release from supervised release.

The most striking case study involved a civil trial lasting nearly a dozen days. Stasior's analysis found that about 55 of every 100 sentences in the judge's findings were copied, word for word or nearly so, from the plaintiff's proposed findings, compared with about 11 from the defendant's. The copied defense material was mostly background and undisputed facts, while the plaintiff's copied material went to the heart of the dispute. AI also flagged that some adopted findings contradicted the trial exhibits, and every error favored the party that proposed it. Stasior argues that similar errors likely go unnoticed across many decisions because no one compares findings to the record at scale, and that judges, clerks, or the parties could run that check before a ruling is signed or filed.

The second example came from a small claims courtroom Stasior visited with a relative. Her bank had allowed four of 20 fraudulent card charges through, costing thousands of dollars, and the bank's investigation ended in repeated form-letter denials, so she sued. Stasior found that the court held small claims sessions only about once a month, that more than 40 people were waiting that morning, and that most cases were follow-up hearings because parties had not completed tasks ordered at earlier sessions, such as financial affidavits and accountings. He proposes that AI could read orders, identify each party's deadlines, send reminders, flag problems in filings, and let courts schedule follow-ups in days rather than a month. The relative's case could not be heard until sometime in 2027.

Stasior closes by arguing that reading is no longer the bottleneck and access is. He cites a state court that refused to release electronic divorce files, Massachusetts' disciplinary authority closing about 95 percent of attorney complaints without investigation and leaving no public record, and federal court records kept behind PACER's paywall. He urges courts and disciplinary authorities to release records in bulk, check filings against the record before decisions issue, and read orders and submissions electronically rather than waiting for the next court date. The article's text ends mid-list, so the full set of recommendations and any further responses from courts are not available in the material provided.

Articles.Title: AI Can Now Read Court Records at Scale. Courts Should Let It.

stories.Headline: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations
stories.Summary:
Ohio federal judges have published standing orders that restrict the use of artificial intelligence in preparing court filings, and a commentary from the law firm Epstein Becker Green, dated October 23, 2026, examines what those orders cover and how a violation could be proven. Some orders ban AI use outright. In the Northern District of Ohio, Judge Christopher A. Boyko's standing order bars attorneys and self-represented parties from using AI in preparing any filing, while exempting information drawn from legal and internet search engines such as Westlaw, LexisNexis, Google, and Bing. District Judge Charles Esque Fleming takes a substantially similar approach, and potential sanctions under these orders include striking a pleading, monetary penalties, contempt, and dismissal.

The restrictions do not match one another. Magistrate Judge Jonathan D. Greenberg's order also bans generative AI in preparing filings and allows information from legal search engines, but it expressly prohibits Google and Bing AI Overviews, so a search allowed under the Boyko and Fleming orders could return output that Greenberg's order forbids. The orders also leave open whether AI used for summarizing testimony, suggesting arguments, proofreading, or other non-drafting work counts as "preparation." The authors note that the provisions do not separately address these uses or exempt work a lawyer later verifies. The orders require parties to notify the court immediately upon discovering AI use in a filed document, but they do not explain how disputed allegations should be resolved or require counsel to run detection software on opposing filings.

The authors say that counsel should not infer AI use from a brief's writing style or an incorrect citation, since neither proves AI use on its own. They cite National Institute of Standards and Technology reports noting that detection tools struggle with text that mixes human and AI writing and with AI-generated text that has been paraphrased. Even when AI use is confirmed, a violation depends on what the tool produced, how it was used, and what the applicable order permits, and a detector's score alone cannot establish those facts. The authors, Maurice Wells and James P. Flynn, advise litigation teams to check each assigned judge's requirements at the outset, communicate them to everyone contributing to filings, and document how supporting research was prepared. The article does not describe any specific enforcement action or pending dispute.

Articles.Title: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations

stories.Headline: Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params
stories.Summary:
Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint, its first model, a coding model built for local use by software agents. Flint is a mixture-of-experts system with about 39.8B total parameters and roughly 2.5B active per token, and the company says its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights were published on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. A second article, dated two days later, reports that Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro, a mixture-of-experts model with 2.8T total and 104B active parameters and a 1M context window, though the text supplied for it cuts off before any further detail.

Flint is a text-only, decoder-only Transformer that supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Its model card documents a context of 262,144 tokens, while the company's blog cites up to 512k. It has 49 layers, two dense and 47 mixture-of-experts, each with 256 routed experts, of which a router picks six per token alongside one always-active shared expert. Thirty-five layers use a 513-token sliding window and 14 use full attention, with 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 4-bit weights take about 23 GB, so the model runs on 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs, and Recursive claims up to twice the speed of comparable models, over 125 tokens per second on a MacBook Pro and over 150 on RTX Spark.

All benchmark scores are self-reported by Recursive. The 16-bit version scores 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89.7% on SWE-bench Pro v2, 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3% on LiveCodeBench v6, 89.2% on IFBench and 95.1% on IFEval. The 4-bit NVFP4 version stays close at 53.7%, 88.5%, 74.1%, 80.8%, 88.1% and 94.6% on the same tests, within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model overall. Recursive's chart puts Flint ahead of other mixture-of-experts models under 50B on agentic coding, including Qwen 3.6, which scores 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Flint trails the strongest dense models, with dense Qwen 3.8 reaching 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 75.6% on SWE-bench Verified.

Recursive attributes much of the design to the Eureka Machine, which proposes ideas, implements and tests them, and chooses what to try next. Starting from a baseline of 35B total and 3B active parameters, it searched expert configurations and widths and arrived at the final 40B and 2.5B figures. It also quantized the output layer to 4 bits, against common practice, and used offline distillation with the 16-bit model as teacher to recover accuracy, nearly halving training steps compared with a quantization-aware training baseline. It wrote specialized kernels as well, including a Metal megakernel that fuses the whole decode forward pass on M4 and M5 chips. The supplied articles do not describe any planned next steps for either release.

Articles.Title: Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro: A 2.8T Total/104B Active Params (MoE) Model with 1M Context

stories.Headline: Mining Regulatory Shifts, Profits, AI, and Environmental Rules
stories.Summary:
Mexico's mining sector is being reshaped by a regulatory push, a profit surge at Grupo México, and a new federal ban on mining inside protected natural areas, according to a weekly roundup published by Mexico Business News on October 23, 2026. The federal government is clearing permit backlogs for US$2.7 billion in mining capital projects while enforcing tighter environmental limits at the same time. Grupo México reported a 56% rise in net profit to US$2 billion for the third quarter, on a 38% revenue increase to US$6.33 billion, though its copper output fell 1.9% because of operational problems in Peru and the United States. The company lowered its full-year copper production target to 1.026 million metric tons as a result.

SEMARNAT, Mexico's environment ministry, published a regulation barring environmental permits for mining exploration and extraction inside federally protected natural areas. The rule applies retroactively, reaching concessions granted before 2023. Backed by Supreme Court rulings, the decree makes the technical assessments of CONANP, the national protected areas commission, binding. Legacy concession holders inside protected zones must submit mine restoration and closure plans within 15 business days.

The article also reports that SEMARNAT has resolved 85% of pending permit applications while updating core rules, including NOM-157 on mine waste management, and that a proposed overhaul would replace the General Law on Ecological Equilibrium and Environmental Protection, known as LGEEPA. That draft would remove automatic administrative approval, expand protected territorial categories, and strengthen state enforcement powers. The article does not name a single official who made these decisions beyond the agencies themselves, but it credits SEMARNAT with the permit clearances and the protected-areas ban, and it describes CONANP's assessments as binding under the new decree. Legal analyst Santiago Suárez Sevilla is quoted in the piece on the proposed LGEEPA overhaul, and he is described as arguing that mining firms will need proactive preventive compliance strategies.

Elio Céspedes Bravo of Datamine is cited as arguing that successful AI adoption in mining depends more on data quality, system integration, and governance than on advanced algorithms, since mining data sits in separate silos. The same roundup also covers Capitan Silver, which reported a carbonate replacement deposit discovery at its Cruz de Plata project in Durango, with high-grade assays and a fourth drill rig added to its 60,000-meter drilling campaign. Taken together, the articles suggest that companies will face tighter compliance demands while commodity prices stay strong. The articles do not say when the proposed LGEEPA overhaul will be finalized, so the next steps on that front remain unclear.

Articles.Title: Mining Regulatory Shifts, Profits, AI, and Environmental Rules - Mexico Business News

stories.Headline: AI boom fuels investment activity in Asia: Citi - CNA
stories.Summary:
Citi's Head of Investment Banking for Asia Pacific, Kaustubh Kulkarni, has said that strong demand for artificial intelligence is pushing companies across Asia to seek more funding. He said valuations remain reasonable, which is keeping deal activity healthy. The comments were reported by CNA on October 20, 2026. The rest of the article's details, including any figures on deal volumes, are not included in the material available to me.

Kulkarni also said Asian firms are expanding overseas to spread out their supply chains. According to the same report, China continues to be a major source of deals across the region. The article does not give specific numbers, company names, or deal sizes to support these points. It is also unclear from the material whether any new rules or changes are involved.

Kulkarni is the speaker quoted, and the report presents his views as Citi's assessment of the regional market. The article does not describe any reaction from regulators, investors, or other banks. It also does not say how long these trends are expected to last. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI is unearthing internet’s hidden flaws – and more outages may follow
stories.Summary:
Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a growing stream of software vulnerabilities, and cybersecurity professionals warn this will bring more disruption like the outages that spread across government websites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on October 21. Those outages followed the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a long-established programming language that powers a large share of the internet. VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm, says AI helped double the number of flaws discovered year-on-year, with research due to be published in the coming days. The same week also brought disclosures involving Node.js, Plex, LiteLLM, Railway and the Indian certificate authority eMudhra.

Operators rushed to fix their software before attackers could exploit it, and some who felt they could not patch in time simply took their sites offline until they were safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble over PHP came during an already busy week, and he expects many more urgent fixes for internet-exposed software. Experts say AI has shortened the time needed to find bugs and turn them into working attacks, which once took weeks or months of skilled effort and now can take hours. Shane Fry of RunSafe Security said the change is in how quickly both discovery and weaponisation now happen. The article notes that the timescale defenders once relied on has effectively collapsed.

Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince says he knows of several other severe vulnerabilities in critical software and predicts that "every single week" may feel alarming for a couple of years. Daniel Stenberg, lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argues that AI-found bugs tend to be exotic and hard for attackers to exploit, and Ramy Rahman of ArmorCode says more disclosed flaws do not automatically mean more successful attacks. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io has seen aggressive attempts to exploit the PHP bug, though its research head Esteban Borges says the criminals it tracks appear not to have built a working tool yet. Prince has seen anecdotal evidence of compromises tied to the PHP flaw, but he argues the wave of discoveries will ultimately be a net positive, since the flaws are being cleaned up rather than left hidden.

Articles.Title: AI is unearthing internet’s hidden flaws – and more outages may follow - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: Africa AI & Data Protection Regulation Report | October 2026
stories.Summary:
The articles in this report cover a broad set of AI and data protection developments across Africa in October 2026, with 33 updates spread over seven markets. One theme runs through many of them: AI strategies have multiplied faster than enforceable rules and funding. Egypt is approaching a data protection compliance deadline in November 2026, while its parliament is reviewing a draft AI law built on a four-tier risk model. Both moves are meant to reshape how businesses, banks and public agencies handle personal data and automated systems. In Ghana, the Bank of Ghana is drafting a directive on AI use in the financial sector, announced by Governor Johnson Pandit Asiama on October 11, 2026.

The proposed rules would address data quality, model risk, cybersecurity and consumer protection. On October 15, 2026, the Data Protection Commission flagged six companies in the Kaneshie North Industrial Area and Tudu for operating without registration, using expired certificates, or failing to renew. Separately, Minister Sam George appointed AI focal persons across all government ministries on October 17, 2026, supported by an AI readiness assessment carried out with UNESCO. Kenya presents a more contested picture. The Senate ICT Committee has recommended abandoning the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, citing concerns about regulatory powers, penalties and compliance costs that could hinder local innovation, and officials are now turning toward a national AI policy instead.

The Africa Public Interest AI Council is meanwhile focusing on the risks AI poses to democratic integrity ahead of Kenya's 2027 general election. Kenya has also signed an AI partnership with Anthropic in September covering public-sector AI, research and skills, though the agreement is described as a starting point rather than a record of delivered results. Across these markets, the central open question is whether regulators can build rules that protect citizens and clarify responsibilities without placing burdens that local developers cannot meet. The articles suggest that enforcement is already tightening in some areas, such as Ghana's registration checks and Egypt's approaching deadline, while broader AI frameworks remain in draft or under review. Reports from the coming months will show whether draft directives and bills become binding law and whether the funding and institutions needed to enforce them follow.

Articles.Title: Africa AI & Data Protection Regulation Report | October 2026 - Wansom AI

stories.Headline: Meta Expects Up To $145 Billion In Capex As AI Investments Expand
stories.Summary:
Meta has said it expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026 as it keeps investing in AI infrastructure and new products. The company released its third-quarter financial results on October 21, 2026, and the figures were reported by Analytics India Magazine. Meta says its AI investments are already producing extra advertising revenue through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetisation. It expects these investments and new product launches to support revenue growth through 2027, even while it keeps spending heavily on infrastructure.

Revenue for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 came to $64.60 billion, up 26% from a year earlier. Advertising revenue rose to $63.06 billion from $50.08 billion in the same quarter last year. Ad impressions across Meta's family of apps increased 10%, while the average price per ad rose 14%. The company also pointed to the launch of Muse and Muse Wonder, which it described as its first frontier model. Meta expects total expenses for 2026 to range from $175 billion to $179 billion.

Those expense projections include a $9.9 billion charge tied to legal proceedings recognized in the third quarter. The charge relates to an August agreement with 52 US state attorneys general to resolve litigation over teen mental health and social media. Total costs and expenses reached $51.61 billion in the quarter, up 68% year-on-year. Excluding the legal charge, Meta's third-quarter operating income would have been $22.88 billion, compared with the reported $12.99 billion. The reported operating margin was 20%, down from 40% a year earlier.

Meta also expects Reality Labs losses of $18 billion to $19 billion in 2026, and it anticipates those losses narrowing to around $15 billion in 2027 as it redirects investment toward other priorities, primarily AI. The company's infrastructure capacity and planned additions, it said, will let it allocate resources across model training, core business growth, and new product development and support. The results show a company spending heavily on AI while its advertising business continues to expand. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Meta Expects Up To $145 Billion In Capex As AI Investments Expand - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: CCH Axcess Adds Agentic AI for Tax Preparation
stories.Summary:
Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting has added agentic tax return preparation to its CCH Axcess Tax system, announced October 23, 2026. The feature is built into the cloud-native platform where firms already manage their tax work, and it is meant to reduce repetitive preparation work and increase firm capacity. For individual Form 1040 returns, CCH Axcess Tax powered by Expert AI prepares and calculates the return and then flags exceptions that need attention before professional review begins. Unlike tools that automate a single task, the feature coordinates work across several steps of the return process, using prior-year information and current source documents.

Tax professionals have traditionally spent considerable time gathering documents, entering information and checking work before review can start. Under this approach, firms get a clearer view of which returns are ready for review and which exceptions still need attention. The agentic capabilities are built into the platform rather than sold as separate products, and they work inside CCH Axcess Tax from source documents through preparation, calculation, review and handoff. Expert AI agents use the firm's own data, authoritative CCH content and each firm's permissions and controls to move the work forward.

The company says the agents prepare, check and advance the work, while professionals review, decide and approve the final return. Cathy Rowe, Executive Vice President and Segment Leader for the U.S. Professional Market at Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting, described CCH Axcess as an agentic platform for tax and accounting. She said agentic tax preparation marks a significant shift in how tax work gets done and helps firms add capacity without sacrificing quality or control. Rowe said the goal is to let professionals focus their expertise where it matters most.

The company also states that professionals remain responsible for deciding and approving the final return. The feature is part of a broader push by Wolters Kluwer to extend CCH Axcess beyond tax preparation, since firms already use the platform to collect client documents, extract data, manage workflow and identify advisory opportunities. Wolters Kluwer plans to share more about how CCH Axcess moves work forward across tax, planning and audit at CCH Connections 2026, which begins October 26 in Orlando. More details are available on the CCH Axcess Tax website.

Articles.Title: CCH Axcess Adds Agentic AI for Tax Preparation - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization for Data-free Mixture-of-Experts Compression
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on October 24, 2026, introduces a method called Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization (SLBF) for compressing mixture-of-experts large language models without needing any training data. The authors are Tianxiao Cao, Jiahe Shao, Yuning Qiu, Kyohei Atarashi, Hisashi Kashima and Qibin Zhao. The paper addresses the storage and serving burden created by the very large parameter counts of these models. Mixture-of-experts models separate capacity from computation through sparse routing, which lets them hold many parameters while activating only some of them for each input.

The authors examined three existing families of compression techniques: expert pruning, expert merging, and weight reconstruction. According to their analysis, pruning and merging can produce errors that do not shrink to zero, and those errors are tied to how inputs are routed and how different the experts are from one another. Weight reconstruction avoids these structural costs because it keeps the expert structure and the routing intact. SLBF is a data-free weight reconstruction method that uses rank-k bases shared among the experts, which allows richer sharing across experts, faster convergence and lower reconstruction error. The paper also describes a post-hoc gauge fixing step that removes redundant parameters without reducing what the model can represent.

The authors report testing SLBF on five mixture-of-experts architectures ranging from 16 billion to 122 billion parameters. In those tests, the method consistently outperformed representative methods from all three compression families. The abstract presents these results as the authors' own findings, and the article does not describe independent verification. The paper is listed as a preprint on arXiv, so it has not been described as peer reviewed in the material provided. The articles do not say whether the code will be released or whether the method will be adopted in production systems.

Articles.Title: Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization for Data-free Mixture-of-Experts Compression

stories.Headline: Customers Bank Uses AI to Close Commercial Loans in 7 Days
stories.Summary:
Customers Bancorp, the parent of Customers Bank, said on October 22, 2026, in its third-quarter earnings results that it is scaling an AI-powered commercial loan closing process after a pilot closed select loans in seven days. The bank had earlier said in its July second-quarter release that the pilot closed loans in that time, compared with a typical wait of 30 to 60 days. The bank also doubled its deployed AI agents during the quarter, a count that includes custom GPTs and similar tools. The pilot used a multi-agent credit underwriting process built by bank engineers, which cut the time to readiness to close by 85 percent.

The bank's parent says the scaled process has produced an estimated 76,000 cumulative hours of saved employee time, up nearly 65 percent from the second quarter, and more than $15 million in annualized capacity. That capacity figure counts salary and benefit savings from positions not backfilled and open positions reduced this year. Customers Bancorp listed broad deployment of the seven-day loan tool among its 2026 AI priorities in July. Its chief executive, Sam Sidhu, has said that engineers build each tool on the bank's own data and systems, then measure results before an agent joins daily operations.

He also said that OpenAI engineers work alongside the team to build proprietary tools in-house. Sidhu leads a 40-person team, about 5 percent of the workforce, focused on AI workflow transformation. Sidhu said the larger builds still take quarters rather than weeks, and that the underlying technology is about six months old. The articles note that the bank finished the pilot one to two quarters ahead of schedule, according to its July release.

The bank's figures are its own, and the articles place them alongside a PYMNTS Intelligence survey of 60 senior technology executives at companies with at least $1 billion in revenue. That survey found that only 5 to 10 percent of large companies report a full return on new AI tools, so the self-assessed figures are not independently verified. Other large lenders, including TD Bank Group, Bank of America and Lloyds Banking Group, have also reported their own AI gains. The articles do not say how the bank plans to expand the process beyond its current scope.

Articles.Title: Customers Bank Uses AI to Close Commercial Loans in 7 Days

stories.Headline: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards
stories.Summary:
Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., introduced the bipartisan AI Cyber Defense Act on Oct. 22, 2026. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop voluntary standards for protecting artificial intelligence models from foreign exploitation and for using AI to strengthen cybersecurity defenses for critical infrastructure. It would give NIST 180 days after enactment to begin engaging private-sector AI stakeholders and to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable.

That roundtable would include AI companies and critical infrastructure owners and operators, and it would develop voluntary standards and best practices for defensive uses of AI. Harrigan said the companies building this technology need to work directly with those responsible for defending power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. NIST would also work with industry to define distillation attacks, which let outside actors extract valuable capabilities from advanced AI models. Together with industry, the agency would develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing those attacks.

NIST would have to publish these standards on its website within one year after they are established, though the bill sets no separate deadline for their development. Within one year of creating the roundtable, NIST would also have to publish its voluntary standards and best practices for defensive AI use. The bill defines eligible private-sector stakeholders broadly, covering businesses that develop, train, deploy, offer, sell, or license AI systems, along with providers of substantial computing infrastructure, data, or technical services. It excludes entities of concern, including foreign businesses headquartered in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or Cuba, or whose parent companies are based in those countries.

Whitesides said the proposal would help protect American AI development while supporting infrastructure operators facing evolving cyber threats. He argued that every month that keeps China and other adversaries from stealing American progress is a month gained to build needed safeguards. The bill has been referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology. The article does not say when the committee will take it up or whether a companion bill is planned in the Senate.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards

stories.Headline: AICPA & IRS AI Risk Framework
stories.Summary:
Randy Johnston and Brian Tankersley, hosts of the Accounting Technology Lab Podcast, discussed a proposed AI tax risk framework in an episode published October 24, 2026, by CPA Practice Advisor. The framework is linked to materials associated with former IRS Commissioner Danny Werfel and sorts risks for tax preparers into five categories: technical, practice, legal and regulatory, business, and workforce and strategic. The hosts framed the question of who is responsible when AI gets a tax matter wrong as central to the discussion. They treated the framework as a proposal rather than a binding new IRS rule.

The hosts walked through specific hazards, including AI hallucinations, inaccurate document extraction, client data leakage, and overtrust of AI-generated tax advice. They also described how AI-driven productivity can outpace conventional human review procedures. Additional concerns included shadow AI, professional liability, client disclosure, vendor dependence, erosion of professional expertise, and preservation of institutional knowledge. They distinguished the risks facing practitioners from those facing tax authorities, while noting that hallucinations, overtrust, skill erosion, data leakage, and vendor dependence overlap for both.

The practical message was that faster preparation does not remove professional accountability. According to the discussion, firms need independent verification of AI conclusions, meaningful human oversight, reliable source documentation, and protection of confidential taxpayer information. They also need clear thinking on liability, disclosure, and governance, along with contingency plans in case a vendor fails or changes terms. The episode's summary lists these as the core action items for tax practices. The articles do not name a deadline or indicate when, or whether, the framework would take binding effect.

Articles.Title: AICPA & IRS AI Risk Framework – Accounting Technology Lab Podcast – Oct. 2026 - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: AI's Dark Cash, the Oregon Massacre, Erin's Law & a Kid With a Camera
stories.Summary:
Pro-AI super PACs are spending heavily to influence 36 House and Senate races, mostly in Georgia, New York and Texas, according to Scripps News reporting featured in this episode. The reporting describes the spending as aimed at each candidate's perceived weak spot rather than at artificial intelligence itself. The reporting follows the money behind these campaigns, which are tied to regions where data center construction is concentrated. The episode is hosted by Jon Leiberman, with national investigative reporter Patrick Terpstra following the funding.

The same episode features Erin Merryn, who was abused as a child and kept quiet because her abuser told her no one would believe her. Her advocacy led to Erin's Law, which the episode says is now on the books in 38 states. The law requires schools to teach children body safety once a year. Merryn's story is presented as an example of breaking that kind of silence after abuse.

The episode also covers a range of other news items, including a count of protesters marching across France, President Trump's endorsement of Benjamin Netanyahu, a Supreme Court decision declining to revive the 9/11 plea deal, and Trump's call for New Mexico to rename itself. Andrew Rafferty offers a midterm update with under two weeks to go, and a panel discusses the push to bring back the Redskins name, newly unsealed records in the O.J. Simpson case, and the New Mexico proposal. Viewers can text the word Scripps to 202-968-2449 to comment or join an upcoming panel discussion. The episode is a roundup format rather than a single breaking event, and the articles do not indicate further developments on the AI spending story beyond the episode itself.

Articles.Title: AI's Dark Cash, the Oregon Massacre, Erin's Law & a Kid With a Camera

stories.Headline: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, published an article on October 23, 2026 titled in substance as a discussion of how law firms can turn the time AI saves into better results for clients. The piece reports on a panel at Harvey FORUM in Sydney, where Hilary Goodier of Ashurst Perkins Coie, Michelle Mahoney of Mallesons and Michael Griffith, Deputy General Counsel at Telstra, discussed how AI is changing the value firms can deliver and how clients judge it. The article frames the central question as what faster work makes possible for a client, such as an earlier business decision, a wider view of risk, or more time for judgment. It presents the panel's views as a guide for firms thinking about pricing, service and how lawyers spend their time.

Griffith said Telstra, which the article describes as Australia's leading telecommunications and information services company, still judges firms by the same standards it used before AI, but the range of benefits a firm can offer has widened. He suggested clients ask whether AI could lower the cost of the work, bring specialized advice sooner, or allow more documents to be examined and more risks found. The article notes that the right answer depends on the client's goal, since a deadline tied to a business decision may make speed more valuable than a fee reduction. Goodier described an obligations mapping project for a global investment bank that her team finished in five weeks using AI, compared with an estimated six months by conventional methods, and said the client expected to enter a new market five months earlier. She also said that hourly targets and bonuses can discourage lawyers from using time-saving methods, which firms need to address.

Mahoney said her team now spends less time gathering and organizing data and more time examining what it shows, such as checking one clause across thousands of arrangements instead of a small sample. Goodier pointed to contract remediation, portfolio reviews and compliance projects that clients may once have judged too costly to pursue. Griffith cautioned that faster analysis should not compress the time needed for hard decisions, and the article suggests firms can use AI for first-pass review while leaving lawyers time to test findings and weigh tradeoffs with clients. The article closes by saying the most valuable use of AI depends on the matter, and it points readers to an RSGI report, The Accelerating Impact of Legal AI, on how legal organizations measure AI's impact.

Articles.Title: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value

stories.Headline: Beyond the LLM: Why I’m Betting on Smaller, Sovereign AI for Law Firms

Watts, of Watts Law Firm, spoke at the Mass Torts Made Perfect conference in Las Vegas earlier in October 2026. stories.Headline: Pa. bill that would crack down on sexually explicit AI deepfakes heads to governor's desk
stories.Summary:
A bill that grew in part out of an investigation at a Lancaster County private school is now heading to the governor's desk in Pennsylvania. The bipartisan measure is meant to protect children from sexually explicit artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes and from hazing. It adds AI-generated content to the list of offenses that mandated reporters must report to the state's Child Protective Services. The story it grew from involved two students at Lancaster Country Day who, in 2023, used AI to create sexually explicit deepfake images of dozens of their classmates. The articles provide few details beyond that.

They do not give a vote count, a date the governor is expected to act, or the bill's number. They also do not describe penalties for creating or sharing such images beyond the reporting requirement. The school's response and the legal fallout are mentioned only through related headlines, which note that parents have taken legal action, that two people have been charged in connection with the AI-generated nude photos, and that two administrators left their posts. The article also points to the bill's bipartisan backing, though it names no specific sponsors or officials making statements about it. Because the articles do not attribute any quoted remarks, the piece cannot report what any lawmaker or official said about the measure.

The reporting describes the bill's aims and its reporting requirement without assigning responsibility for the underlying incident beyond the two students and the school's own administration. The broader context is a growing concern over AI tools that can produce realistic sexual images of real people, particularly minors. The articles do not say what will happen next beyond the governor's review, nor when or whether the bill will take effect. More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korea Fair Trade Commission opens public consultation on AI advertising guidelines
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Fair Trade Commission, the country's antitrust regulator, announced on 22 October 2026 that it has opened a public consultation on draft guidelines on labelling and advertising related to artificial intelligence. The consultation runs until 11 November 2026. The commission says the draft is meant to identify and address misleading advertising that exaggerates the use of AI, a practice it calls "AI washing." It cites a Korea Consumer Agency survey, conducted in November, in which 57.9 per cent of respondents said they would pay more for a product marketed as AI-powered, with an average premium of about 21 per cent above the standard price.

The draft sets out four major categories of potential violations of the Act on Fair Labelling and Advertising, along with a self-assessment checklist and a frequently asked questions section. The FTC gives examples such as electric hot-water heating mats, cat litter boxes, AI-labelled pillows and weight-control shakes marketed as AI products. It also voices concern about AI-generated virtual people and fabricated reviews used to promote food and pharmaceutical products to older consumers. The guidelines apply the existing principles of truthfulness, completeness, fairness and verifiability to AI-related claims, and they are not legally binding. Failing a checklist item does not by itself amount to a violation, and the guidelines create no new regulatory obligations.

The commission, which is responsible for the draft, says the guidelines will help businesses avoid breaching the advertising law, help consumers make informed choices and support fair competition in AI-related markets. In judging whether an advertisement is misleading, the FTC says it will weigh the conduct involved, the likelihood of consumer confusion and the potential harm to fair trade. Once the comment period closes, the commission plans to finalise and distribute the guidelines, consult the relevant ministries and update them periodically as technology and rulings change. The development reflects a broader concern that AI has become a common marketing term that can be used to overstate what products can actually do.

Articles.Title: South Korea Fair Trade Commission opens public consultation on AI advertising guidelines

stories.Headline: AI Not Only Failed To Kill The Billable Hour, It’s Looking Like Its Bodyguard
stories.Summary:
A new report on small and mid-size law firms suggests that artificial intelligence has not reduced the billable hour, and may even be helping to keep it in place. The SMB Law Billing and Payments Report, drawn from more than 60,000 firms using the products MyCase and LawPay, found that flat fees made up 15 percent of all bills sent, down from 16 percent a year earlier. Nearly half of firms still bill entirely by the hour, while only one in ten bill purely on flat fees. Firms with 11 or more employees cut back on flat fees the most, falling from about 16 percent to 14 percent. The report's data came from the software vendor's own customers, so the author notes it is not representative of the whole U.S. legal market.

The figures also show that the amount of billed work grew. Billing per month rose 5 to 8 percent across firm sizes, and three of the four size groups did not raise their hourly rates at all, which points to more hours being billed rather than higher prices. Firms with 11 or more employees billed nearly 12 percent more hours while logging fewer, raising the share of tracked time that reached a bill from 44 percent to 49 percent. Earlier 8am data had found hours per case climbing in nearly every practice area, even as surveys showed lawyers using generative AI more and reporting time savings. The article suggests that AI can produce drafts quickly, but lawyers must still verify citations and arguments, and that the tools also surface new lines of research that would not otherwise have been pursued.

The author, Joe Patrice, a senior editor at Above the Law, argues that the billable hour is more durable than expected because AI expands the work rather than shrinking it. He draws a comparison to the economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed that more efficient steam engines led Britain to burn more coal, and suggests that cheaper exploration of legal questions leads lawyers to explore more of them. He also notes that the trend appears at the other end of the market, citing Citi data showing demand for Biglaw lawyers' time grew 4.2 percent in the first half of the year, nearly triple the normal pace. The Bloomberg Law reporter Roy Strom is quoted as saying that clients insist AI saves time on legal work yet are paying for more hours than ever. The article's own earlier coverage noted similar patterns, and the report itself advises weighing whether a matter is predictable enough for a flat fee before choosing between flat and hourly billing.

Articles.Title: AI Not Only Failed To Kill The Billable Hour, It’s Looking Like Its Bodyguard

stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: India plans AI law, homegrown mobile phone brands by 2028
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said at an NDTV event in New Delhi that the government is preparing to start a consultation process on artificial intelligence legislation in the coming weeks. He said the risks of AI have crossed a threshold that calls for a law and new regulations. The same day he also set a target for locally designed and manufactured mobile phone brands and a first made-in-India chip, both by October 2028. The report is based on a PTI wire story carried by The Hindu BusinessLine.

The proposed AI consultation paper is still being drafted, and it is intended to gather inputs from society, citizens and industry. Vaishnaw said AI has been adopted very aggressively by industry, and the government wants to hear from AI users. On mobile phones, he said the target date is October 23, 2028, when Indian-designed, Indian-manufactured and Indian-branded phones are expected to be ready. The government has an incentive scheme to boost mobile production and to promote designed and made-in-India brands. The article does not give the value of that scheme.

Vaishnaw is the Electronics and IT Minister, and he made these statements himself at the event. He said global AI giants, which he described as among the top three or four AI ecosystems in the world, need to work jointly on fundamental principles for the technology. He also said the 12 plants approved under India Semicon Mission 1.0 will become operational very soon, with the sixth to be inaugurated shortly. He described the second phase, Semicon 2, as aiming to make India the design capital of semiconductors, citing about 300 universities as a talent pipeline.

Vaishnaw put the context in terms of manufacturing, saying the previous Congress government ignored manufacturing for several decades. He said electronics have become India's third largest export and could soon be the second. He expressed confidence that India would be able to match some of the largest electronics manufacturers and designers in the world in the coming years. The articles do not say when the AI consultation paper will be published or whether any draft law has been fixed, so the next concrete step is the release of that paper.

Articles.Title: India plans AI law, homegrown mobile phone brands by 2028

stories.Headline: Nigeria’s AI Bill Targets Sovereignty, Investment, Power - Voice of Nigeria
stories.Summary:
Nigeria's proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill aims to protect national data assets, attract computing investment and balance innovation with risk management, according to Dr. Olubunmi Ajala, National Director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics. He spoke in an interview with Voice of Nigeria on the sidelines of BUILD 2026 in Abuja, published on October 23, 2026. Ajala said the framework would strengthen digital sovereignty and create room for African leadership, private-sector investment and regional cooperation. He described the bill as having two parts, one covering sovereignty and the other opening opportunities for leadership within Africa.

The bill would allow Nigerian businesses to invest in computing infrastructure and let international technology firms, known as hyperscalers, invest in the country as well. Ajala said Nigeria hopes to host other African countries' datasets or build shared infrastructure through twin data parks. On regulation, he said the bill addresses transparency, responsibility and accountability while avoiding restrictions that could stifle innovation. Regulatory sandboxes would let AI applications be tested before wider deployment. The articles give no figures for investment or cost.

Ajala linked the data park plans to electricity supply, saying sustainable and alternative power, including solar and gas, must be considered. He said a privately owned power plant had indicated it could supply 200 megawatts as demand grows, using capacity it does not currently use. He also pointed to decentralised generation and mini-grids, including research involving Professor Muyiwa and the ministry responsible for power, supported by UK Research and Innovation. He said decentralised power solutions would help ensure electricity constraints do not hold back AI adoption. The article does not say when the bill is expected to be passed.

Articles.Title: Nigeria’s AI Bill Targets Sovereignty, Investment, Power - Voice of Nigeria

stories.Headline: Democrats Please: AI is NOT Too Big to Fail. Regulation Yes, Bailouts No
stories.Summary:
The article is a community opinion post on Daily Kos, published Friday, October 23, 2026, by a user identified as "this is only a test." The author argues that Democrats should publicly commit, before the election, that they will not bail out the AI and Wall Street industries if an AI-driven financial crash occurs. The post cites an interview with analyst Ben Hunt and states that investors widely believe the federal government will rescue the industry on national security grounds and to avert another deep recession. The author says this belief is part of why AI-related valuations are so high relative to economic fundamentals. The author adds that the Democratic Party has a political opening to reject that expectation and reshape investor behavior.

The post describes the scale of the AI buildout as requiring $5 to $10 trillion in capital expenditures over the next several years. It argues this would require large amounts of new debt on top of a federal deficit of about $2 trillion per year, strain electricity supplies, push up real interest rates and inflation, and crowd out other investment. The author notes that AI already accounts for about half of U.S. economic growth while non-AI investment is falling. According to the post, the industry seeks four things in exchange for accepting "guard rails" or slower frontier development: federal guarantees for its loans, relief from state and local data center restrictions, relief from liability for harmful actions involving AI, and protection from cheaper open-source competition, mostly from China. The author calls this arrangement absurd and recalls that the Bush and Obama administrations bailed out Wall Street in 2008.

The author places the responsibility for the potential bailout on Wall Street investors and the federal government, which the post says would be expected to step in if the AI debt collapses. The author argues that Democrats should state clearly that they will not bail out Wall Street and the technology industry this time, and says doing so would let policymakers redirect resources from AI spending toward the consumer economy and other needed investment. The post itself is labeled as community content not reviewed by Daily Kos staff before publication, and it presents the argument as the author's opinion. The article does not report any official response from Democratic leaders or the industry, and it does not describe any scheduled policy action or next steps beyond the author's call for a public pledge.

Articles.Title: Democrats Please: AI is NOT Too Big to Fail. Regulation Yes, Bailouts No

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open Small Language Model for Local Voice Agents, Game Characters and Robots
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model built for fast conversational agents. The model is aimed at voice assistants, game characters and robot interfaces that run locally on RTX, Jetson and Spark hardware. It is post-trained from Google's Gemma 4 E4B using reinforcement learning, without supervised fine-tuning. According to the articles, it is designed to deliver agent behavior within roughly 4GB of VRAM, leaving room for speech and vision models.

The model has 8 billion total parameters, 4 billion of them effective, and a 64K context window. NVIDIA says its Q4_K_M build used 3.1 to 4.3 GB of VRAM on RTX in its tests. In NVIDIA's own measurements, Bolt topped 15 of 21 benchmarks against Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen3.5-4B and Nemotron 3 Nano 4B. It scored 84.8 on IHEval, compared with 67.0 for Gemma 4 E4B and 60.6 for Qwen3.5-4B. It trailed on Tau2-Bench, where it scored 55.1 against 75.1 for Qwen3.5-4B.

NVIDIA's research team developed the model, and the articles credit it with the training approach. The team used RLVR and RLHF through NeMo-RL and NeMo-Gym, and it said supervised fine-tuning improved tool calling but hurt conversational quality and verbosity. The datasets and full recipe are public. A demo described in the report pairs Bolt with the Cosmos 3 Edge vision model on a Reachy Mini robot, with Bolt handling speech replies and tool calls.

The articles place the release in a crowded field of small models, where Bolt wins some categories and loses others. Qwen3.5-4B leads on Tau2-Bench, RULER 64K, LongBench v2 and BFCL-v3, and Gemma 4 E4B keeps a narrow edge on EQ-Bench v3. NVIDIA also reports faster speeds, with Bolt paired with its DFlash drafter reaching 272.6 tokens per second on an RTX 5070, compared with 225.9 for Gemma 4 E4B. Most performance figures come from NVIDIA's own testing, and the articles say the model's full recipe and datasets are publicly available for developers to examine.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open Small Language Model for Local Voice Agents, Game Characters and Robots

The Reserve Bank of India has issued an alert about cyber risks linked to artificial intelligence, and banks are taking steps to close the gaps those risks could exploit.
