Their letter asks Google to provide its research on AI harms to children's mental wellbeing, explain why AI integration is the default and cannot be turned off on education devices, disclose concerns raised by districts, teachers, or parents and the company's responses, and detail its promotional programs and spending. It also asks what steps Google took after its internal ethics research, and how it has prevented sycophantic or emotionally dependent conversations with minors, with answers requested by November 2, 2026. The articles do not say whether Google has responded to the letter.

Articles.Title: Answers Demanded From Google About AI Classroom Push - DoingItLocal

stories.Headline: Minuttia Study Finds Vendors Write Up to Half of AI-Cited Best Tools Lists
stories.Summary:
On October 24, 2026, Minuttia, an SEO and AEO agency for software companies, published the Self-Promotional Content Data Study, its second large-scale look at how Google and AI assistants answer questions about software. The team asked 18,084 software questions across Google Search, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity in August 2026, then read every cited page, 311,766 in total, and labelled who had published it. Its central finding is that between a third and a half of the "best alternatives" listicles these platforms cite are written by a vendor in the category they sell in. For "X vs Y" comparison questions, the share rises to between 56% and 65%.

The study shows that vendors' own lists are almost always built to favor the vendor. Across the platforms, 93% of these lists highlight the vendor's product, 87% rank it first, 90% criticize competitors, and only 16% clearly disclose that the vendor wrote the page. The shares by platform range from 34% for ChatGPT to 47% for Google and Gemini on alternatives questions. Minuttia notes these figures are a floor, since pages the team could not read were counted as not self-promotional. The study also found that the level varies widely by category, from 12% in Audio Production to 76% in AI Security Operations Center, while the 20 most-cited vendors account for only 6% of citations.

Minuttia attributes the pattern to how each platform selects its sources. According to the study, ChatGPT searches the vendor's own website before answering, with 92% of its "site:" searches targeting that site, and vendors' own sites make up 42% of its alternatives citations. Perplexity, by contrast, cites pages that rank well in its search results and offer useful features such as a comparison table or a stated selection method, not promotional language. Zacharias Xiroudakis, Managing Director at Minuttia, said that each platform picks its sources differently and that the company published its data so software teams can check the work for their own categories.

The study carries stated limits. It is a snapshot taken in August 2026, and when Minuttia re-asked Perplexity 2,000 of the questions in September, only 28% of the pages it listed had appeared in the August answer. The findings describe shares of page types and sites rather than which individual page wins. The full study, methodology and CSV data are available at self-promotional-content-data-study.minuttia.com. Minuttia conducted the study with Convex Works, and the release lists Xiroudakis as the media contact.

Articles.Title: Minuttia Study Finds Vendors Write Up to Half of AI-Cited Best Tools Lists

stories.Headline: Kentucky Sheriff Nixes AI-Assisted Report Writing After Trial
stories.Summary:
The Ulster County Sheriff's Office in New York has decided not to move ahead with artificial intelligence-assisted report writing after a trial period. The office also dropped plans to add more Motorola automatic license plate reader cameras. The decision came as the public and local officials pushed back on AI surveillance tools. The sheriff's office said its own 90-day pilot of the Axon Draft One product concluded on Oct. 9, and it chose not to continue. The change affects how the office spends federal money.

On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Justice announced a $794,000 grant to modernize the office's technology, which included expanding the Motorola license plate reader program and implementing the Axon report tool. Axon Draft One attaches to body cameras, transcribes field conversations and produces a first draft of police reports, and it can also translate languages. Lt. Collin Reynolds said the office will keep its existing Motorola cameras and will not add more. The sheriff's office will instead direct the money toward computers, radio equipment and dedicated software for the O.R.A.C.L.E. system.

Reynolds said the trial showed a number of limited uses for the draft tool, but the office decided on a cost-benefit basis. He said the value did not justify the cost, and that the benefits did not outweigh the negatives. County Executive Jen Metzger, who said she was highly opposed to first-draft technology, signed an executive order banning AI surveillance technologies within her administration, and the sheriff supported that order. Reynolds said the sheriff strongly respects individual rights, while describing license plate readers as a crucial law enforcement tool that must be used legally, ethically and responsibly. He also said the office's Motorola cameras, which are fully owned by the office, differ from those made by Flock Technology.

Reynolds framed the decision as a response to community concerns, saying "this is just not the time" for expansion. He also argued that law enforcement must keep adapting to new technology because criminals often find new methods first, and that promising tools would still be examined. Sheriff Juan Figueroa had earlier backed the new technologies, calling license plate readers "huge" and crediting them with helping resolve a homicide case. Figueroa said his office would release a full statement on its approach to AI and privacy.

Articles.Title: Kentucky Sheriff Nixes AI-Assisted Report Writing After Trial - GovTech

stories.Headline: If we compare the robot industry to artificial intelligence (AI), we are now in the GPT-3 phase. It'..
stories.Summary:
The article reports an interview with Andrew Kang, CEO of RoboStrategy, a robot-focused investment company listed on Nasdaq in May under the stock code BOT. Kang told Maeil Business Newspaper that the robot industry is now in a phase comparable to GPT-3 in artificial intelligence, and that robots with capabilities similar to later AI models are only a matter of time. The interview was published on October 24, 2026. RoboStrategy invests mainly in unlisted robot companies such as Figure AI, Dynamic Robotics, and Standard Bots, allowing individuals to gain indirect exposure through the BOT shares.

Kang described rapid progress in the general-purpose AI models that serve as the "brain" of robots, saying a robot can now follow similar movements after being shown a demonstration. He noted that these changes are happening mostly in research institutes and factories and are not yet easily visible to the public. He also said U.S. venture capital firms are shifting money from software toward physical AI because investors are pressing them to change strategy. Commercialization is already under way in manufacturing and logistics, with a welding-only AI model from Pass Robotics cited as having been used in the field for more than two years.

Kang singled out Figure AI, a humanoid robot developer founded in 2022, which was valued at $39 billion (about 55 trillion won) in a funding round last year with participation from Nvidia and Intel. He said the company is already producing hundreds of robots a month. On Korea, he pointed to large affiliates such as Samsung and LG, which are working with U.S. robot companies as distribution partners and developing robots themselves. He praised Korean engineering and robot AI talent, but said RoboStrategy has not yet invested in Korean unlisted robot companies, though it is reviewing early-stage firms.

Kang also warned that Chinese humanoid robot companies look less attractive to him because of excessive competition, citing roughly four to five serious humanoid companies in the United States against hundreds in China. He argued that such crowding would push down selling prices and profits, and he noted that in July the U.S. Federal Communications Commission banned the sale of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots in the United States. He estimated the combined value of unlisted physical AI companies worldwide at only about $200 billion, and cautioned individual investors that failure rates among early companies are significant, so they should study deeply or invest through experienced operators. More to follow.

Articles.Title: If we compare the robot industry to artificial intelligence (AI), we are now in the GPT-3 phase. It'..

stories.Headline: AI’s Boom is Paid in Water - Columbia Political Review
stories.Summary:
Google planned to draw 7.6 million liters of water a day to cool its servers in a Chilean city that has lacked enough water for 15 years, according to an opinion piece in the Columbia Political Review published October 24, 2026. After local outrage and legal challenges, a Chilean environmental court partially reversed the permit that allowed Google to build a data center in the country and asked the company to account for climate change. The article describes the project as sited in Cerrillos, a district of Santiago where residents and environmental groups argued that one facility should not pump millions of liters a day from an already stressed aquifer. The partial reversal forced regulators to treat climate change and groundwater stress as central issues, and it pushed Google to redesign the facility by moving away from the most water-intensive cooling systems toward fan-based cooling. The article calls this a rare win for local institutions against a global technology company.

It also notes that the permit fight sits within Chile's National Data Centers Plan, which aims to make the country Latin America's AI hub and which officials say could create more than 80,000 jobs. The article points out that Chile has been in a megadrought for more than a decade, with river flows and reservoirs shrinking and some rural communities relying on emergency tanker deliveries for drinking water. The author, Meredith Anlan Wang, a student at Columbia, argues that Chile's government has prioritized foreign technology investment over equitable access to water. She ties this to the 1981 Water Code enacted under dictator Augusto Pinochet, which turned water into a market commodity, and to studies showing that water rights remain highly concentrated among a small number of people. According to the article, desalinated seawater mostly goes first to mining and green export industries such as lithium and hydrogen rather than to the households most affected by scarcity.

The piece also describes protests in Quilicura, where volunteers staged "human-powered chatbots" in early 2023 to highlight how much digital convenience matters compared with access to drinking water. The article frames Chile's case as a warning for other communities and for AI regulation generally, since the European Union's AI rules focus mainly on energy efficiency and algorithmic risk while US debates center on innovation, competition with China, and national security. The author contends that until AI regulation treats water as seriously as energy use and bias, AI development will deepen inequality in places least able to bear the cost. The article does not describe any further legal steps or a final outcome for the Google project.

Articles.Title: AI’s Boom is Paid in Water - Columbia Political Review

stories.Headline: Good news, photographers: Two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made is better than GenAI
stories.Summary:
Surveys by the stock platform Storyblocks, published by Digital Camera World on October 24, 2026, found that around two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made works are better than AI-generated content. The buyers surveyed are people who license photos, videos, graphics, audio and other content through stock platforms. The company ran four surveys over the summer, covering more than 1,400 people who regularly license content for their jobs. Although a large majority favored human-made work, 87 percent of respondents said they had used AI-generated visual or audio content in the past year.

The findings point to a split between what buyers prefer and what they actually do. About half of respondents said they had rejected a piece of stock content because it was AI-generated. Across the four surveys, between 74 and 94 percent called for AI-generated content to be labeled, a demand Storyblocks described as near-universal, and even respondents open to AI reportedly agreed on labeling. About 63 percent said their organizations now have policies on AI-generated content. When asked what mattered most in a stock platform, the availability of AI-generated content ranked last in every survey.

Storyblocks, a stock platform for photos, videos and audio, conducted the surveys and reported the results, which the article presents as the company's own findings. The article notes that content made by computers, unlike content made by humans, cannot be copyrighted in the United States. Between 33 and 37 percent of all respondents believed AI content may be of better quality, but among those who already use a non-AI platform for their content, that figure fell to between 5 and 8 percent. The article does not say what further steps the company or the industry plans to take.

Articles.Title: Good news, photographers: Two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made is better than GenAI

stories.Headline: AI adoption by country: the 25 economies using AI most
stories.Summary:
The Microsoft report on global AI diffusion, published September 21 by its AI Economy Institute, ranks 147 economies by the share of working-age people who used a generative AI product. In June 2026, 18.8% of the world's working-age population used generative AI, up from 17.8% in the first quarter, and the gap between rich and developing regions kept widening. The estimate counts people aged 15 to 64 using anonymized Microsoft telemetry, adjusted for device and operating-system market share, internet access and population. The United Arab Emirates ranks first with 73.3% of its working-age adults using generative AI, while Singapore is second at 64.3%, the only two economies where more than half of adults use AI.

Ireland is third at 49.9%, France fourth at 49.6% and Norway fifth at 49.4%, a spread of just half a percentage point. Microsoft says the metric is imperfect because it counts how many people use AI, not how often they use it, and it does not yet include several newer tools. The company says it will widen the set of tools it measures in its next report and expects that change to raise measured usage nearly everywhere, especially in China. The United States, home to major AI developers, ranks only 21st on this measure.

The report attributes the leaders' strength to a mix of factors rather than to any single cause. The UAE has pursued state AI policy since 2017, including a national strategy with a 2031 horizon and a graduate university devoted to the field, and its workforce is heavily employed in finance, aviation, logistics and professional services. Singapore has run national digital and AI programs since 2014, and its economy leans on finance, shipping and corporate software, with English as the main language of business. Ireland hosts the European headquarters of many U.S. technology firms, and France has become a center for AI development, with Mistral AI founded in Paris in 2023.

Microsoft is itself a stakeholder in this picture. The company invested $1.5 billion in G42, an Abu Dhabi AI company, in 2024, though the report applies the same method to every economy it ranks. The articles do not say how the rankings will change once the broader tool set is included. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI adoption by country: the 25 economies using AI most - qz.com

stories.Headline: EPFL Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab Opens Research Opportunities for Postdoctoral Fellows, PhD Students and Interns in Switzerland (Fully Funded)
stories.Summary:
The Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab at EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, has opened applications for postdoctoral fellows, PhD students, summer research interns, and bachelor's and master's students. The announcement was published on 25 October 2026 by Global South Opportunities. The lab works on artificial intelligence methods that help researchers understand biological systems and make new scientific discoveries from complex biological data. Applicants can pursue research projects or thesis work, depending on their qualifications and interests.

Postdoctoral candidates should hold, or be close to completing, a PhD in computer science, computational biology, statistics, applied mathematics, or a closely related field. Those applying must email a CV with a publication list, a one-to-two-page research statement, the names and contact details of two references, and a preferred start date to mlbio.postdoc@epfl.ch, using the subject line "Postdoctoral application." Prior experience with biomedical data is preferred but not required for candidates with a strong AI background. PhD applicants must apply through EPFL's doctoral programmes in computer and communication sciences or computational and quantitative biology, where admission is managed centrally. Bachelor's and master's students may apply for research projects through a designated form, and EPFL master's students can contact the lab directly about theses.

The lab's research areas include single-cell foundation models, multimodal learning, generative models of biology, cell engineering, and agentic AI for scientific discovery. Lab leaders named in the listings include Yist Yu, Siba Smarak Panigrahi, and Yulun Jiang, each a contact for a specific student project. The lab also has access to substantial GPU computing resources through the Swiss AI Initiative and collaborates with programmes such as the CIFAR Multiscale Human Program. The listed project descriptions were last updated on 15 November 2025, so applicants must confirm that projects remain open for the relevant period.

The announcement does not give a universal application deadline, salary, stipend, or funding package, and the article notes that these vary by programme and opportunity. Candidates are advised to check the official application pages and the lab's Join Us page before applying. The article also points to external fellowships such as the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowships and the EPFL AI Center Postdoctoral Fellowship. The source states that Global South Opportunities does not own or verify the opportunities it shares.

Articles.Title: EPFL Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab Opens Research Opportunities for Postdoctoral Fellows, PhD Students and Interns in Switzerland (Fully Funded)

stories.Headline: As news traffic collapses, Nevada outlet puts AI to work without handing over editorial control
stories.Summary:
Nevada News & Views, a smaller outlet in Nevada, has said it is using artificial intelligence to help its reporters work faster while keeping human journalists in charge of sourcing, judgement and final copy. The move comes as major publishers face a steep fall in traffic. According to Similarweb data reported by Axios, U.S. traffic to around 100 major news sites dropped sharply in July compared with the previous year. Media Copilot separately reported that traffic to the top 50 US news websites fell by 37% between July 2024 and July 2026, and that generative AI still accounted for only a small share of visits.

The collapse is linked to changes in how people find information, since search engines now answer more questions on the results page and AI assistants can offer quick summaries that reduce clicks to publisher sites. The articles describe a familiar squeeze of fewer clicks, weaker advertising revenue and newsroom cutbacks that can reduce the depth and pace of coverage. Against that background, the outlet presents AI as a research aid that sifts public records, checks figures and speeds up document-heavy work. It insists that reporters still chase leads, question filings and decide what matters.

A survey by the Associated Press found that most journalists and newsroom leaders have used generative AI in some form, even as they call for clearer rules, training and oversight. The outlet points to its coverage of Republican congressional candidate David Flippo as an example of this approach in practice. It says senior political writer Brittany Sheehan used federal election filings, supported by AI-assisted research, to examine campaign loans and donor refunds, including repeated contributions from some of the same names. The publication argues that such tools speed up the routine parts of reporting without replacing human verification.

The articles do not describe any penalty, regulation or formal change tied to this coverage. Industry groups and trade outlets describe a broader shift from testing to wider deployment of AI across newsroom production and audience strategy, including faster service journalism and routine updates. Critics continue to warn that speed alone cannot substitute for judgement, verification and trust. The tension now runs between legacy brands losing traffic and leaner outlets trying to use the same technology to work efficiently and build direct readership.

Articles.Title: As news traffic collapses, Nevada outlet puts AI to work without handing over editorial control

stories.Headline: CFTC Forms Innovation Task Force To Build Crypto and AI Rules
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has created a new Innovation Task Force to develop regulatory frameworks for crypto, artificial intelligence, and prediction markets. CFTC Chair Michael Selig announced the group on Tuesday at the Digital Asset Summit in New York. The task force is meant to give founders, developers, and other builders a structured way to engage with CFTC staff. Selig said in a prepared statement that a clear regulatory framework would foster responsible innovation at home. He also said American market participants should not be left on the sidelines.

Michael J. Passalacqua will lead the task force as senior adviser to Selig. Passalacqua joined the CFTC in January after handling crypto and blockchain matters at the international law firm Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. The new group will work alongside the CFTC's Innovation Advisory Committee, which was formed in February and has more than 30 members. Those members include Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour and Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman. The task force will also coordinate with the Securities and Exchange Commission and its own crypto task force, which launched last year.

The announcement follows an SEC interpretive notice published last week, which indicated that most crypto assets would not be classified as securities under federal law. SEC Chair Paul Atkins described that guidance as a temporary bridge while Congress works toward broader digital asset legislation. The CLARITY Act, the primary market structure bill, passed the House of Representatives in July 2025 but has stalled in the Senate. Disagreements over stablecoin yield, ethics rules, tokenized equities, and other provisions remain unresolved. No timeline has been confirmed for a full Senate floor vote as of Tuesday.

The CFTC has also been asserting jurisdiction over prediction markets, and several states have challenged that position. Those states argue that sports-linked contracts on such platforms may conflict with local gaming laws. The articles do not say how or when these disputes will be resolved. They also do not describe specific rules the task force will propose or a schedule for releasing them.

Articles.Title: CFTC Forms Innovation Task Force To Build Crypto and AI Rules - CoinMarketCap

stories.Headline: Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung urges AI, drone ties with Europe
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung called on Taiwan and Europe to build trusted supply chains in artificial intelligence and drones, speaking on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at the opening of the annual conference of the Formosa Club in Taipei. The Formosa Club connects pro-Taiwan parliamentarians across Europe. Lin said Taiwan's semiconductor, AI server and emerging drone industries complement Europe's expertise in precision manufacturing and industrial technology. He argued that these fields require trusted partners because they directly involve national security and critical infrastructure. Lin said Russia's war against Ukraine had shown how excessive economic dependence could become a tool of coercion, and he presented Taiwan as a partner grounded in trust and shared values.

Taiwan is developing a complete drone supply chain covering hardware, critical components and cybersecurity standards. As an example of industrial cooperation, he cited a proposed technology park in Poland being planned by the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers' Association. The project would focus on AI data centers, smart cities and electric vehicles. Lin described economic cooperation as one pillar of Taiwan's "integrated diplomacy," alongside partnerships with fellow democracies.

Lin also urged like-minded countries to work together against transnational repression, accusing China of using domestic legislation to extend its jurisdiction overseas and threaten freedom of expression. He said no country should be allowed to use domestic law to spread a chilling effect beyond its borders. Michael Gahler, a member of the European Parliament who chaired the conference, called for parliamentary support for Taiwan to develop into broader, institutionalized cooperation at the government level. He advocated arrangements that would facilitate investment in both directions, saying their substance mattered more than their names.

Gahler also said Europe could deepen practical engagement with Taiwan while keeping its own "one China" policies, which he distinguished from Beijing's "one China" principle. According to the report, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Formosa Club, which was founded in 2019, are scheduled to co-host a forum on Tuesday focusing on cooperation between Taiwan and Europe in AI and drone technology. Gahler added that democracies need to coordinate their responses to the long-term threats of war, hybrid warfare and economic coercion from Russia and China. The article does not give the specific outcomes of the forum or any agreements reached at the conference.

Articles.Title: Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung urges AI, drone ties with Europe

stories.Headline: Oklahoma Local News Summit explores AI’s role in journalism
stories.Summary:
At an Oklahoma Local News Summit in Tulsa, journalists and media experts gathered to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping reporting, with concerns about accuracy, public records access and press freedoms at the center of the conversation. The event was organized by Freedom of Information Oklahoma, the Oklahoma Media Center and the Oklahoma Pro Chapter of the Society of Professional Journalists, and coverage was published on October 23, 2026. A panel titled "Are We Truly Free 250 Years Later?" was moderated by Griffin Media's Scott Mitchell and examined how AI and political polarization are affecting First Amendment freedoms. Three speakers joined the discussion: Leslie Briggs, Oklahoma attorney for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press; Wendy Suares, evening anchor and investigative journalist at KOKH Fox 25; and Mark Thomas, executive vice president of the Oklahoma Press Association.

The panelists described both the promise and the risks of the technology. Briggs pointed to a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigation into missing persons cases in Chicago, produced by a journalist with the Invisible Institute, which used machine learning to analyze more than one million public records and documents. She also warned that government agencies could use AI to answer public records requests in ways that shield information, since the models can be steered toward particular search results. Suares said AI cannot replicate the human judgment, relationships and context that reporters bring, but it can help sift records and court cases for new developments. Thomas urged journalists not to let the ease of AI replace the hard work of reporting.

The panel also raised the question of copyright and policy. Briggs asked where the line falls between copyrightable work and output produced by analyzing large volumes of documents, and she suggested that the issue may need to be addressed at the federal level. Thomas framed the broader purpose of journalism as seeking and telling the truth so communities can make informed decisions about daily life, from voting to road closures. The articles do not report any specific policy proposal, legislative action or ruling that emerged from the summit, and they do not describe next steps beyond the discussion itself.

Articles.Title: Oklahoma Local News Summit explores AI’s role in journalism

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and advanced computer vision to recover more textile waste
stories.Summary:
Tecnalia, a Spanish research and technology organisation, has announced that it has developed and validated a technology that combines advanced computer vision and artificial intelligence to automatically identify and sort textile waste under real conditions. The work is part of the CIRTEXCAM initiative and was carried out with the company Valoriza, with the announcement published on 23 October 2026. The system uses a mix of sensors, including RGB imaging, near-infrared (NIR) imaging and 3D imaging, to gather complementary information about each item of waste. Its purpose is to detect, identify and characterise textile waste so that it can be sorted and recovered more effectively.

The article explains that greater circularity in the textile sector depends on more than better recycling technology, because materials must first be properly identified, sorted and prepared. It notes that the wide variety of garments, compositions and formats, together with other waste mixed in, makes textile sorting difficult and limits reuse and recycling. To test the technology, the team ran a pilot at a waste management plant in collaboration with Valoriza, working with pre-sorted textiles, non-textile waste and combinations of both. Footwear waste was also added to make the tests more complex. The pilot was designed to assess performance in conditions similar to those a future industrial solution would face and to generate new datasets for improving the artificial intelligence models.

The article attributes the work to Tecnalia, and its author is listed as Nerea Campos. The organisation says the aim goes beyond sorting pre-separated materials to also identifying textiles that currently go unnoticed and are often left out of reuse or recycling processes. It describes the combination of sensing, computer vision and artificial intelligence as a way to automate textile waste recovery and increase the supply of materials for a more circular economy. The article presents this as a step toward recovering materials that are still being lost today. It does not state a timeline for an industrial rollout, and it gives no further details on next steps beyond continuing to improve and validate the models.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and advanced computer vision to recover more textile waste

stories.Headline: How much artificial intelligence should be included in art?
stories.Summary:
A Quebec author is facing backlash after his publisher found evidence that he used artificial intelligence in his work. The controversy has prompted a wider question about what place AI should have in the creative world. Global News ran a video report on the matter, reported by Elizabeth Zogalis and published on October 23, 2026. The piece is a video segment with a brief description, and the article text available does not name the author or publisher or describe the evidence in detail. Some artists and academics quoted in the report say the technology does not have to replace human creativity.

Their position, as the description presents it, is that AI needs to be used responsibly. The page does not spell out what responsible use would require, and it does not set out any rules, limits or policy changes. It also gives no further details of how the publisher reached its conclusion. Beyond the author himself, the articles do not identify anyone formally responsible or record any statement from the author, the publisher or an industry body.

The description attributes the views to unnamed artists and academics, so it is not possible to say who holds which position. The surrounding page is largely unrelated news about Montreal, Quebec and national affairs, which gives no further context on the AI dispute. The articles do not say whether the author has responded, whether the publisher has taken any action, or whether any further debate or policy discussion is planned. Because the available material is limited to a single video description, More to follow.

Articles.Title: How much artificial intelligence should be included in art?

stories.Headline: Not Intel. Not CoreWeave. This Underappreciated Nvidia-Backed Company Is Growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) Revenue by 123%. Here's Why It's a Buy Today for $8.
stories.Summary:
Nokia, the Finnish company best known for its early brick phones, is being reshaped around artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis published on October 23, 2026. The article's headline and pitch frame Nokia as an underappreciated Nvidia-backed stock with AI revenue growing 123%, priced at about $8 per share. The author, Adam Spatacco, argues the company is leveraging its telecommunications infrastructure to become a supplier of AI networking equipment. The piece appeared in two versions, one on Yahoo Finance and one on fool.com, with the same core content.

Nvidia invested $1 billion in Nokia last October, acquiring a 2.9 percent stake, and the two companies are collaborating on artificial intelligence radio access networks, which combine wireless networking equipment with accelerated computing. The article explains that these networks would turn telecom infrastructure into distributed AI platforms for edge uses such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation. It cites data compiled by Omdia projecting the AI-RAN market will exceed $200 billion by 2030. Nokia's acquisition of Infinera is described as strengthening its optical networking and high-speed connectivity for AI infrastructure.

The article points to Nokia's third-quarter results as evidence of the shift. Revenue reached 5.2 billion euros, up 9 percent year over year on a constant-currency basis, while operating profit rose 35 percent to 605 million euros and earnings per share climbed 50 percent to 0.09 euros. Revenue from the AI and Cloud division rose 123 percent to 631 million euros, order intake grew 118 percent, and Nokia secured about 1.5 billion euros in new orders during the quarter. The author notes Nokia is working with Alphabet, which is pursuing a 13 billion-euro investment in Finland, along with telecom players such as Zayo and neocloud providers.

Spatacco writes that he sees Nokia as a compelling long-term AI infrastructure investment at a price-to-sales ratio of about 2.6. He argues that investors focus on GPUs and memory chips, while the buildout also requires optical networking and connectivity equipment that Nokia supplies. The article notes that Wall Street expects hyperscaler spending to keep accelerating, which he says may mean Nokia's AI story is still early. The Motley Fool, which publishes the piece, also promotes its Stock Advisor service, and the author discloses positions in several large technology companies, not Nokia.

Articles.Title: A Surprising New Rival Is Threatening CoreWeave (and It's Not Best Known as an AI Cloud Company)

stories.Headline: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?
stories.Summary:
America has lost more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries over the last four years, with roughly 50,000 lost in the last year alone. Analysts call it one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, comparable in intensity and duration only to the recessions of 2001 and 2008. Unlike those periods, there is no general recession today, and the losses coincide with the spread of AI systems that can produce novels, images, music and other digital art cheaply and at scale. The article asks whether this marks a broader decline of the creative class.

Measuring how much of this is caused by AI is difficult. Media firms are reluctant to disclose their AI use, partly to avoid public backlash and partly to protect the legal basis for their copyrights. AI's effects are also tangled up with other pressures on arts businesses, including Hollywood consolidation, offshoring of production and the shift toward social media creators. Still, every digital subsector is shedding jobs while in-person entertainment keeps growing, which the article treats as the clearest sign of AI's influence. Movie and sound recording has been hit hardest, losing more than 100,000 jobs, nearly a third of its total, and written publishing has lost more than 70,000.

The article draws on the past to consider what comes next. When Napster spread music for free around 2000, Metallica and the Recording Industry Association of America sued and won, but the broader technology kept undermining copyright and pushed music toward streaming, where the value of individual songs fell sharply. Musicians adapted by treating recordings as advertising for concerts and merchandise, a route that video and newspapers lacked. Video revenue has been squeezed as well, with movie ticket sales in 2025 down 25% from their 2019 peak and cable revenue down 18%. Newspapers, which once employed about half a million people, have cut their payrolls by nearly 85%, and the article presents that as the worst-case model for creative work under AI.

The article also notes limits to its conclusions, since it is hard to predict how new technology will interact with arts businesses. Book sales, for example, rose about 70% over the last six years, helped by BookTok, even as fewer people read overall. Roughly 32% of workers in arts, entertainment and recreation use generative AI to some extent, compared with 62% across all industries, and the article suggests AI is seeping into production in ways studios may struggle to control. Whether further AI development will keep displacing creative workers remains an open question that the data does not yet settle.

Articles.Title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?

stories.Headline: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
stories.Summary:
Bayer Crop Science has built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent natural language interface over its Connected Decision Engine (CDE), which runs hundreds of machine learning model configurations for plant breeding. The system was built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with help from AWS Unified Operations, and the article describes it as an article published on the AWS blog on October 23, 2026. Bayer built ADE because users struggled to understand workflow results, since answers meant piecing together information from APIs, documentation, dashboards, and logs. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop.

ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources they call. A supervisor agent classifies each request and routes it to one of 22 specialist agents running in production, each scoped to a single domain. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to the agents as tools while keeping authentication and authorization out of agent code. Bayer's team also chose a framework-agnostic approach so it could run its own LangGraph orchestration and choose its models. In one example, a diagnosis of a failed phenotyping workflow that once took over an hour now takes under 10 minutes.

Bayer's team worked through five design decisions with AWS staff who took part as members of the working team. These covered storing orchestration state in DynamoDB so workflows could resume after restarts, separating user identity from service authorization, and treating model selection as an interface contract after a newer model version proved incompatible with ADE's tool use and structured output. The team also limited the tool catalog available to each agent, since CDE manages more than 500 model configurations and each tool definition adds tokens. Visualization was moved from a tool into its own specialist agent once it needed retries, error handling, and presentation decisions.

Before launch, the team found that its exception handlers returned responses that monitoring counted as successful even when agent tasks had failed. It responded by adding custom CloudWatch metrics and alarms for tool errors, throttling, model timeouts, and structured output failures. The article says the team also began working on attributing inference cost to individual requests, since one request can invoke several models and tools. The article does not give further details on that cost work or on the platform's broader rollout plans.

Articles.Title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations

stories.Headline: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services published a hands-on guide on October 23, 2026, explaining how to run Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI. The method trains a model on tasks that involve a sequence of actions, where the only feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which calls the policy model being trained, acts over as many turns as the task requires, and returns a single reward when the episode ends. The guide uses the word game Wordle as its example, because its rules are simple and its outcomes can be scored objectively.

The pipeline depends on two IAM roles and a deployed agent. The agent runtime role trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and carries the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, while the training job role must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession. The author warns that using the generic sagemaker.amazonaws.com principal makes job creation fail with a "Could not assume role" error. The agent is deployed with the AgentCore command line tool, and the guide recommends that route over uploading a code package in the console. Training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to update a Low-Rank Adaptation adapter, and the reward gives 1.05 to 1.55 for a solve depending on speed, -0.5 for a loss, and -1.5 for never making a valid guess.

In the authors' run, the method raised gpt-oss-20b's solve rate on held-out words from 61 to 84 percent at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at. The 100-step run cost about $339 in training tokens across 105,486 rollouts over 12 hours and 40 minutes, plus roughly $79 in AgentCore runtime charges. The guide says the training stage accounts for most of the token cost and scales with trajectory length. It also says the trained data, agent and model remain in the user's AWS account and are not used to train the base models. The service is offered for Amazon Nova 2 Lite, GPT-OSS-20B, Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.6 27B, in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), though the article states that the Region list may change.

Articles.Title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide

stories.Headline: Enterprises face evolving insurance landscape for artificial intelligence risks
stories.Summary:
Insurers are increasingly weighing how to cover artificial intelligence risks, according to a brief from SC Media published on October 23, 2026, which draws on reporting from Dark Reading. The piece says enterprises are seeking coverage for potential harms from rogue AI agents and automated system failures, and that the insurance market has not settled on how to respond. Some specialty firms sell purpose-built policies or affirmative endorsements that address these threats directly. Many large carriers, however, are adding strict exclusions to their policies.

Major insurers named in the brief, including Chubb, Travelers and AIG, have adopted Verisk/ISO endorsement language that limits their liability for damages tied to generative AI. The article notes that this leaves many organizations exposed, since standard cyber or errors and omissions policies often do not cover these emerging threats. Experts quoted in the reporting advise companies to carry out thorough policy reviews to find gaps in their current protection. Companies that want specialized coverage are expected to show strong security controls, and underwriters are paying closer attention to how businesses monitor their AI applications. The article says underwriters treat these applications much like critical service accounts.

The brief places responsibility for closing these gaps mainly with the enterprises themselves, which must demonstrate guardrails, human oversight and supply chain management to qualify for better terms. It says executives need to deal with shadow AI, meaning unsanctioned AI use inside the organization, and to secure infrastructure, data pipelines and third-party contracts against both malicious attacks and non-malicious system failures. The reporting attributes these recommendations to experts and underwriting practice rather than to any single regulator. The article does not report any formal rule change or deadline. Its framing is that the insurance landscape for AI remains in flux, with coverage terms likely to keep shifting as adoption grows.

Articles.Title: Enterprises face evolving insurance landscape for artificial intelligence risks

stories.Headline: CISA, Allies Warn of Denial-of-Wallet Risks in AI Token Guidance
stories.Summary:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and four allied cyber agencies released joint guidance on a Thursday in October 2026 to help organizations keep artificial intelligence token consumption from inflating costs, exhausting service quotas and disrupting critical services. The guidance, titled "Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience," was published by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and co-authored by CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre, and the national cyber security centers of New Zealand and the United Kingdom. The agencies said usage-based AI pricing is hard to forecast and that token demand will rise as AI becomes more embedded in operations. They noted that agentic workflows, which reprocess earlier content at each step, add to that demand. The guidance proposes a three-tier model for allocating AI capacity.

Cyber defense and incident response sit at the top tier, compliance, policy analysis and other core business functions form a monitored middle tier, and routine productivity tasks such as email drafting could be throttled when demand peaks. The agencies acknowledged that reserving capacity for the top tier adds cost but said the tradeoff strengthens continuity. The document also describes denial-of-tokens attacks, which aim to lock out legitimate users by burning through an organization's token supply or tripping its rate limits. A related tactic, denial-of-wallet, targets an organization's budget through complex queries or loops that force a model to repeatedly process its own output. The agencies suggested feeding token telemetry into security information and event management platforms, since unusual spikes may also signal data exfiltration.

The agencies advised organizations to learn how token pricing works before committing to service-level agreements and to evaluate providers on reliability and quota constraints. They also recommended spreading workloads across multiple providers so they can be rerouted during outages, and matching smaller or locally run models to simpler tasks. Critical infrastructure operators were urged to keep manual fallbacks ready in case AI becomes unavailable. The publication follows joint guidance on securely adopting agentic AI services that intelligence and cybersecurity agencies from the same five countries released in May, which outlined privilege, behavior and accountability risks tied to autonomous AI agents.

Articles.Title: CISA, Allies Warn of Denial-of-Wallet Risks in AI Token Guidance

stories.Headline: “The Home Edition” sees how AI is changing the real estate market
stories.Summary:
A television program has taken a look at how artificial intelligence is changing the real estate business in Arizona. The episode of "On Your Side: The Home Edition," hosted by Susan Campbell, aired on the Arizona's Family streaming sites and was published on October 24, 2026. The show features a tour of a timeless Arcadia home at the base of Camelback Mountain, along with a look at what $500,000 can buy in Mesa. The articles do not say how many episodes the show has aired or whether its schedule has changed. Agent Jill Laurell shows viewers a 6,000-square-foot home built in 1968, which includes a pool that resembles a tropical resort.

Agent Yvonne Faustinos explains that AI is simplifying many of her daily tasks, which gives her more time to connect with buyers and sellers. Agent Jennifer Sturgeon then shows a $500,000 home in northeast Mesa, close to nearby mountains and hiking trails. The episode airs every Friday at 7 p.m., and past episodes can also be watched on demand. The segment presents these agents as the source of the information on how AI is being used in their work. The articles describe their comments in general terms and do not give specific tools, costs, or measurable results.

They also do not identify any official or outside expert who comments on the broader effects of AI on the housing market. The program is produced by Arizona's Family, which is operated by KTVK and KPHO. The article is a television preview rather than a news report on a policy change or market event. It does not say whether AI adoption is widespread among Arizona agents, nor does it report sales data tied to the technology. The episode's broader market context is limited to the single Arcadia and Mesa properties shown, so viewers should look to other sources for statewide trends.

Articles.Title: “The Home Edition” sees how AI is changing the real estate market

stories.Headline: PHP Warning Highlights Battle Between AI Speed, Cyber Hygiene
stories.Summary:
On October 21, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an urgent alert about a pair of web server vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws affect the PHP programming language, which reportedly runs on about 70 percent of the world's websites, and could let an intruder run code on an affected server without logging in and steal or alter data. CISA said it had not observed exploitation as of the time of publication, but warned that unpatched systems remained at risk. Security researchers at Wiz and Calif used Google Gemini and OpenAI models to find the flaws, which they said had been present for decades across multiple PHP versions.

CISA directed organizations to immediately update their PHP code on internet-facing systems, or take those systems offline until they could be patched. Reports said some government services were taken down in countries including the United Kingdom, Japan and Finland. No federal government websites in the United States reported outages from php2shell, though one security executive cautioned that a site still running does not mean it is secure. The article also describes CISA's broader shift toward faster remediation, including a risk-based approach that gives agencies no more than three days to deploy patches for serious mitigations. The agency has also rolled out a cloud-based monitoring platform, Security Information and Event Management-as-a-service, through its Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation program.

David Williams, founder and CEO of the UK-based Fior Group, said the immediate priorities are patching, investigating possible compromise and replacing exposed credentials. He argued that governments should design security on the assumption that some vulnerabilities will be exploited before they can be patched, and that the key question is what an attacker can do once inside. Katie Chrisman, federal solutions engineering team lead at NinjaOne, said at a GovCIO Media & Research forum on October 8 that three days should be seen as a new baseline, and that the organizations that succeed will be those that patch quickly while also trusting their underlying data. A CISA spokesperson said on Friday that the agency had no information beyond its October 21 alert.

The episode shows how AI is changing the pace of both attack and defense. Because the technology can locate weaknesses far faster than before, it has also removed the resource constraints that once kept attackers from finding long-standing flaws, so officials must now patch and monitor for exploits on a much shorter timeline. The article does not say whether any exploitation has since been confirmed or what further guidance CISA may issue. It also does not say whether the three-day patching requirement applies to php2shell specifically. More to follow.

Articles.Title: PHP Warning Highlights Battle Between AI Speed, Cyber Hygiene

stories.Headline: REDESCA Calls for the Protection of Labor Rights in the Face of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation
stories.Summary:
The Special Rapporteurship on Economic, Social, Cultural, and Environmental Rights (REDESCA) of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights issued a press release on October 23, 2026, calling for stronger public policies and rules so that the spread of artificial intelligence, algorithmic management, and other digital tools in work respects human rights. The office says these changes can raise productivity and open new economic activities, but they can also widen inequality, create new forms of precarious work, and weaken the effective exercise of basic rights. REDESCA notes that automated systems are already used in hiring, task assignment, supervision, performance evaluation, pay, and dismissal in both the private and public sectors. It warns that such use can affect the right to fair working conditions, social security, health, equality, privacy, freedom of expression, freedom of association, and collective bargaining. The office also says that access to effective protection and redress must be guaranteed.

REDESCA states that the duties to respect, protect, and guarantee human rights apply to the design, acquisition, and use of new technologies at work, and it points to the American Convention on Human Rights, the Protocol of San Salvador, and IACHR and Inter-American Court standards as guidance. It calls for transparency that gives workers and their representatives understandable information they can use to verify, negotiate, and challenge decisions. The office also urges safeguards against disproportionate surveillance, improper use of personal data, algorithmic discrimination, and automated decisions that lack clear explanations, meaningful human review, or appeal mechanisms. It says governments need integrated policies covering labor law, data protection, equality, occupational safety and health, social protection, and corporate responsibility. Public institutions, in its view, should be able to identify which systems are in use, access documentation, audit their operation, and order corrective measures.

REDESCA also stresses that workers and their organizations, through social dialogue and collective bargaining, must take part in these responses. The office draws attention to Latin America and the Caribbean, where high levels of informality, outsourcing, non-standard employment, structural inequality, and limited social protection can magnify the risks, with women and migrants facing disproportionate effects. It says training, retraining, protection against unfair shifting of risks and arbitrary loss of income, and fair sharing of productivity gains must be part of a just digital transition. In this context, REDESCA describes the adoption in June 2026 of International Labour Organization Convention No. 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy as significant, since it is the first international labor standard dedicated to this issue. According to the office, the convention addresses labor rights, automated management systems, personal data, compensation, social security, and review of certain automated decisions, and it will serve as a reference once it is ratified and enters into force.

REDESCA also notes that a technical workshop it held with the Special Rapporteurship on Freedom of Expression during the 196th Session in August 2026 examined these issues, and that it will support a side event at the 197th Session in Panama. REDESCA says it will keep contributing, within its mandate and in coordination with other IACHR bodies, to analysis of how digital transformation affects economic, social, cultural, and environmental rights. It calls for continued dialogue with states, workers' organizations, civil society, businesses, international bodies, and academics on monitoring, technical cooperation, research, and regional discussion. The office frames the goal as a digital transition that is just, inclusive, and respectful of human rights. The Special Rapporteurship is an office of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which is an autonomous principal organ of the Organization of American States.

Articles.Title: REDESCA Calls for the Protection of Labor Rights in the Face of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation

stories.Headline: Why the ideology of AI looks so much like religion
stories.Summary:
In 2017, Anthony Levandowski, a former Google and Uber engineer who was later convicted of trade-secret theft, filed paperwork in California to establish a religious organization called Way of the Future. Its stated purpose was to develop and worship an artificial superintelligence he called "the Godhead." The organization has since dissolved, but the article argues that the impulse behind it has not. It appears, the author writes, in the way people describe AI's future, especially in the idea of an uploaded mind as a form of immortality or resurrection. Effective altruism, in several of its forms, also works as a redemption narrative in which believers give and calculate in hope of a technologically secured future.

The article draws on Charles Taylor's book A Secular Age (2007) to explain why this pattern keeps emerging. Taylor argues that modernity changed the structure of the self, turning a "porous" self open to a meaningful cosmos into a "buffered" self sealed off from external authority. The buffered self sees itself as sovereign and self-sufficient, yet it still carries a longing for transcendence that does not simply disappear. According to the article, that longing, which Augustine described as a restless heart, will seek new forms when traditional ones are set aside. Taylor's view is that secular spiritualities are not the absence of religious feeling but its displacement into new settings.

The author applies this to AI, arguing that a buffered self encountering a system of apparently unlimited knowledge reaches for theological vocabulary, which is why ideas like the Singularity take on the language of rapture. The article presents the ideology of AI as a form of religion rather than a post-religious outlook, one that has inherited the hunger without the tradition that gave it discipline and meaning. It contrasts this with the Aristotelian-Thomistic view of the person as relational, embodied, and ordered toward truth and God. Citing Magnifica Humanitas, the article says AI systems cannot know from within what love, work, friendship, or responsibility mean, and so cannot long for anything.

Leo XIV's engagement with AI is described as a question of anthropology rather than technology. The article does not report any new event, deadline, or policy change, and it gives no further developments or next steps. Its content is an analytical essay rather than a news report, so it offers no specific timelines or figures beyond the 2017 filing and the 2007 publication date. The argument is presented as the author's own reading of Taylor and of Church teaching.

Articles.Title: Why the ideology of AI looks so much like religion

stories.Headline: Did Texas use artificial intelligence to call fourth-down play against Florida?
stories.Summary:
A report from the Austin American-Statesman said that during the fourth quarter of Texas's game against Florida at Royal-Memorial Stadium, the Longhorns used a new artificial intelligence data analytics platform called Bevo Lab to help decide a fourth-down play. Trailing 20-17 and facing fourth-and-2, coach Steve Sarkisian and his staff reportedly turned to the tool. Texas failed to convert after quarterback Arch Manning lost three yards on the play. The report appeared on a Friday, the same day the school announced the Bevo Lab, a 25,000-square-foot AI facility on campus. The announcement describes the lab as a space where artificial intelligence informs coaching decisions and daily athletic department work, and the school has been building tools with Google for areas such as revenue-sharing and roster management.

The Statesman report framed the fourth-down moment as a pivotal use of that new technology. Fans reacted quickly on social media, many of them suggesting the coaches had simply asked an AI which play to run. The article notes that the frustration followed consecutive losses to unranked teams and an underwhelming season from Manning. Athletic Director Chris Del Conte responded roughly an hour after the report was published, telling Bobby Burton that the story was wrong in its implication. He said the decision to go for it on fourth-and-2 was not based on Bevo Lab analysis.

Del Conte explained that he had used the play only as an example of what the platform could suggest, not of what it actually did during the game. The outlet's reporter also argued that the fan speculation was overblown and that Sarkisian was not likely reading AI-generated instructions to Manning. The episode comes as Texas prepares to face Ole Miss on Saturday night, with the team's season under scrutiny. The articles do not report any further investigation or any formal response beyond Del Conte's clarification. They also do not say whether the Statesman will issue a correction or update its reporting.

Articles.Title: Did Texas use artificial intelligence to call fourth-down play against Florida?

stories.Headline: HP (HPQ) Stock May Be 33% Undervalued As AI Workstation Launch Lands
stories.Summary:
HP Inc. shares were described in an October 24, 2026 Yahoo Finance piece by Bailey Pemberton as possibly undervalued by about 33 percent, with the stock trading at US$33.64 as the company's AI-focused workstation launch took hold. The article notes that HP's shares had risen 52.1 percent year to date, drawing fresh attention to whether that price matches the cash the business is expected to produce. The analysis is framed around the company's AI-focused ZGX Fury workstations and related offerings, which the piece says may help move heavier and potentially more profitable workloads onto HP devices. Investors have been focusing on AI hardware and PC refresh themes, so the question is how much of HP's future cash flow the market has already priced in.

The valuation in the article rests on a discounted cash flow model, which projects the cash HP can return to shareholders and discounts it back to today. According to the piece, HP generated about $3.88 billion in free cash flow over the last twelve months, and analysts feeding into the model expect that figure to stay in the multi-billion-dollar range over the coming decade. The outer years assume a gentle decline rather than aggressive growth. On that basis, the estimated intrinsic value sits well above the current share price, which is why the stock screens as undervalued using this method. The article also mentions a price-to-earnings ratio of 12.4 times as another way investors might judge the stock.

The article is a Simply Wall St analysis syndicated on Yahoo Finance, and its content is presented as general commentary rather than investment advice. It describes two competing narratives about HP: a bull case that sees roughly fair value, with the acquisition of Humane and the CosmOS AI platform extending across AI PCs, printers and peripherals, and a bear case that puts the shares about 23 percent overvalued. The bear view argues the price already assumes AI PCs, services and cost savings will offset weakness in print and PC sales. The piece also flags two warning signs, one of them major, that readers should weigh before reaching a conclusion. The article does not say what HP itself has announced about future guidance, and it offers no timeline beyond the multi-year model.

Articles.Title: HP (HPQ) Stock May Be 33% Undervalued As AI Workstation Launch Lands

stories.Headline: 2026 IMPACT | SHINKO Reveals the Next Evolution of AI Advanced Packaging Substrates: From ABF and Glass Core to Hybrid RDL - semivision
stories.Summary:
At the 2026 IMPACT conference, Kinsus Interconnect Technology explained how AI chip substrates are changing from passive carriers into active system interconnect hubs. The company said modern AI packages must handle multiple chiplets, high-bandwidth memory stacks, high-density interconnects, and more complex power delivery networks. Substrate makers now need to join chip architecture discussions much earlier, working with foundries, IC designers, packaging providers, and system manufacturers. Kinsus also noted that AI accelerator power consumption approaching or exceeding one kilowatt makes substrates essential parts of the power delivery network.

SHINKO Electric Industries presented its technology roadmap at the same 2026 IMPACT conference under the theme “Advanced Semiconductor Package Substrate for AI and HPC.” The Japanese manufacturer said packaging substrates are becoming critical integration platforms that connect computing dies, HBM, high-speed interconnects, power delivery networks, and possibly optical I/O technologies. SHINKO reported that glass-core experiments show significant warpage reduction, but effective coefficient of thermal expansion remains dependent on structure. Glass cracking and thermal cycling reliability are critical barriers to commercialization, and future differentiation will depend on low-CTE materials, high-stiffness cores, high-density redistribution layers, and advanced assembly technologies.

KINTEX said on October 21 that TEX+VISION 2026, the International Textile and Sewing Industry Exhibition, opened at KINTEX Exhibition Center 2 in Goyang. The show is co-hosted with Seoul Messe and the Gyeonggi Textile Industry Association and runs through October 23. This year’s exhibition focuses on industrial textiles and high-performance materials for mobility sectors such as automobiles, along with smart manufacturing, AI technologies, and eco-friendly sustainability solutions. KINTEX CEO Lee Min-woo said the event goes beyond a simple exhibition to serve as a business platform where participants can see the convergence of advanced materials and manufacturing technologies and generate actual deals.

The TEX+VISION Conference 2026 is being held alongside the exhibition to help the industry respond to new technologies and environmental regulations. On the opening day, participants heard about strategies for responding to eco-friendly regulations and the circular economy, as well as a road map for advanced materials including ultra-high-temperature ceramic fibers. On October 22, sessions will cover AI- and 3D data-based manufacturing and the digital transformation of the textile and fashion value chain. Other events include a technology seminar by the Korea Laundry Association, a briefing on MMS certification standards, and a seminar on innovation in the textile and fashion industry in northern Gyeonggi Province.
