stories.Headline: Three insights into agentic AI security and cyber resilience
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, SiliconANGLE published a feature by Victoria Gayton summarizing three insights from theCUBE's coverage of Oracle's virtual event "AI Cyberattacks Are Escalating: How to Secure Your Data Now." The piece says agentic AI, software that can access sensitive data and act on users' behalf, is forcing enterprises to rethink where they place their trust. Security is no longer just about controlling individual requests, because governing actions that span multiple systems and business processes has become the harder problem. Analysts Krista Case and Dave Vellante examined these pressures during the coverage, which brought together Oracle executives and technology experts.

The first insight concerns where data security must be enforced. Juan Loaiza, executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies, argued that protections should sit beneath applications and AI agents, inside the database itself, so that each end user sees only their own data regardless of the prompt. Vipin Samar, senior vice president of Database Security at Oracle, said controls must hold across the entire fleet of databases, users and data, and that Oracle pairs database-level controls with centralized management tools. The article also describes Accenture Enkitec Group using Oracle Deep Data Security to let dozens of agents, possibly 40 or more, query a shared repository at different authorization levels. Roger Cornejo of Accenture Enkitec Group said testing showed the setup could handle 300 simultaneous queries, returning most results in 15 seconds or less.

The second insight is that agentic AI security depends on modernized systems and accountable oversight. Holger Mueller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research, warned that delaying adoption leaves organizations exposed while technical debt compounds, and predicted that next year's focus will be scaling backend systems. Johnnie Konstantas, group vice president of Oracle Cloud Engineering, said enterprises need to know where agents are built and which sensitive assets they can reach, and that agents carry identity permissions for the people they act for. Brennan Baybeck, senior vice president and chief information security officer of Oracle Customer Success, said governance and clearly understood responsibilities remain gaps, and that humans are now an essential link in controlling powerful automated systems.

The third insight addresses cyber resilience, which requires trusted recovery and continuous improvement. Ashish Ray, senior vice president of Oracle Database product management, said both production systems and backups may become targets, and that backups must be validated because unverified data may prove unusable when restored. Ray pointed to separate administrative controls, network segregation and Oracle's Zero Data Loss Recovery Appliance as ways to protect and check recovery assets. Zulfikar Ramzan, former chief technology officer and chief digital officer of RSA Security USA, urged defenders to learn from every incident and near miss and feed those lessons back into security programs on a regular basis. The article is a summary of event coverage and does not describe any single breach or new regulatory requirement.

Articles.Title: Three insights into agentic AI security and cyber resilience - SiliconANGLE

stories.Headline: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone
stories.Summary:
Cristian Volpato, a 22-year-old Socceroo who plays for Italian Serie A club Sassuolo, struck a deal in mid-September with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI likeness. Under the agreement, Callandor received exclusive rights to Volpato's digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals and taking a cut, and it will help restrict content that lacks his approval. The article, published by the Guardian on 24 October 2026, describes a social media video in which Volpato's AI clones appear in different settings around the world.

Callandor co-founder Michael Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, said the company creates "synthetic twins" that brands could use around the clock. Fisk described plans for AI-generated book voiceovers in foreign-language editions and an app that would give fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin, such as one that offers real-time football coaching. Callandor was founded in February and has a small roster that includes Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole, with its campaigns still in a pilot phase. Volpato follows Brazilian star Neymar, who in June licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that published short videos during the FIFA World Cup.

The article notes that player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI, and that governments worldwide are still considering basic AI regulation. Earlier this month the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without consent, after a complaint from the players' union, which is considering stricter rules. Sydney start-up Hyperknown, led by William Saunders, is pursuing similar licensing deals and argues that athletes must establish their rights before others decide how their identities are used. Jonathan Harlen, an intellectual property law expert at Southern Cross University, said copyright generally requires human authorship and does not cover AI reproductions, while celebrities' protection against unauthorised use under passing-off laws requires proof of economic loss.

The article reports that deepfakes have proliferated, and that last month a UK campaign backed by the global players' union Fifpro, featuring footballers including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, raised concerns about them. An offshore casino also used a deepfake of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year. Fisk suggested a heavy crackdown on fan-made AI content could backfire, while acknowledging the need for care around sensitive topics. The article ends by noting that the consequences of this emerging industry may be hard to predict.

Articles.Title: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone

stories.Headline: If Critical AI Fails, Who Keeps The Country Running? – OpEd
stories.Summary:
A government adopts artificial intelligence to allocate emergency resources more quickly, but months later the automated service begins producing unreliable recommendations. Officials suspend it as a precaution and find that the backup procedure relies on the same cloud account, data feed and staff who have stopped doing the work by hand. The article presents this as a hypothetical case rather than a report of a real failure. It points to a gap in planning, since an institution may have a way to stop a machine without a funded way to keep its mission running. The author, Burak Oktenli, writes in an opinion piece for Eurasia Review published on October 25, 2026.

The article proposes that every consequential AI investment come with a continuity budget. That budget would name the minimum service level that must survive an outage, the people authorized to make decisions without AI, the independent information they would use, and what live exercises would cost. It would cover training, secure access to current records and alternative communications rather than just software subscriptions. The author also proposes a scenario-coverage ledger that maps failure pathways and shared dependencies without presenting uncertain scenarios as measured probabilities.

Verification would come through live exercises that withdraw automated tools and test staff handovers, not through documents alone. The author says governments disagree about how likely catastrophic AI failures are, and cites the 2026 International AI Safety Report on expert disagreement about how quickly capabilities will advance. He also notes that a United Nations scientific panel reviewed documented cases of AI agents acting beyond intended boundaries in September, while declining to estimate how likely severe loss of control is. On October 16, NIST, the National Security Agency and CISA issued voluntary incident-readiness practices for highly capable AI systems in training and evaluation, which the author treats as a starting point rather than a mandatory continuity rule.

He points to the European Commission's Preparedness Union Strategy as an existing setting in which AI-dependent services could be assessed, and to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, which brought together delegates from 163 countries in July 2026 and is scheduled to reconvene in May 2027. The article does not report any follow-up action by governments or the bodies it mentions, and it offers no timetable for adopting its proposals. Its main suggestion for the next Global Dialogue is to compare how public institutions document critical AI dependencies and verify fallback arrangements. The author's central argument is that a country is prepared for AI disruption only when its institutions can keep serving people after an automated system is removed.

Articles.Title: If Critical AI Fails, Who Keeps The Country Running? – OpEd

stories.Headline: Nvidia targets local AI assistants with a model built around a 4GB memory budget
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, a small AI model built for local voice assistants, game characters and robots, on October 23, 2026. The model comes with downloadable weights and works with tools including Ollama and LM Studio. It is designed to leave memory free for the rest of an application running alongside it. The company's benchmark comparisons rely on tests and hardware configurations that it selected itself.

The model is built on Google's Gemma 4 E4B and includes Nvidia's additional training for multi-turn conversation and actions. It can call application tools, keep a character's persona consistent, and use a conversational mode that produces shorter answers suited to speech. The name reflects a memory budget that depends on the workload. In one Nvidia test on an RTX 5070, the compressed model used 3.5GB of graphics memory with about 3,000 input tokens and 50 output tokens.

A test that retained 32,000 tokens of context used 4.3GB, and measurements on a Jetson Orin Nano ranged from 4.2GB to 4.9GB. The model supports a context window of up to 64,000 tokens. The official model page offers the compressed GGUF release and instructions for running it in local inference tools. Nvidia also publishes training recipes and a separate drafter model meant to speed up generation.

Reasoning can be turned on for harder requests or off for faster replies. The release targets GeForce RTX PCs, Jetson systems, RTX Spark and DGX Spark, extending the local AI work of Nvidia's larger DGX Spark setups to smaller conversational tasks. Nvidia says the model posts higher average benchmark scores than its previous Nano 4B model, though its own tables show competitors ahead on some individual tests. Developers still need to verify that the model performs reliably on their specific tasks.

Articles.Title: Nvidia targets local AI assistants with a model built around a 4GB memory budget

stories.Headline: The American AI Exports Program Risks Stifling Smaller Competitors
stories.Summary:
The American AI Exports Program, created by executive order in July 2025 and run by the Department of Commerce with the State Department, is meant to help American firms win overseas AI contracts. Under its current rules, companies are organized into consortia that must offer a complete five-layer AI package covering hardware and infrastructure, data pipelines, models, cybersecurity, and applications, even if a customer wants only part of it. Designated packages can receive priority consideration for diplomatic help, export-license review, and federal financing referrals, though each financing decision still needs the relevant agency's approval. The Commerce Department received 78 applications before its June 30, 2026, deadline for the first round. Huawei's offer to build AI data centers for Egypt, with about 2,000 Ascend chips, is cited as the kind of market the program targets.

The author argues that the structure favors large American firms, because an anchor member that must have international experience chooses its partners and can leave out a smaller rival whose product would fit a customer better. A small firm could bid separately, but getting designated would mean assembling its own consortium, which it may lack the resources to do. The Business Software Alliance and the Institute for Progress raised similar concerns in filings before applications opened. Amazon Web Services confirmed it is among the applicants, and a Commerce official said several small companies also applied, but the agency did not name them and the reporting gives no breakdown of their roles. The article also notes a practical case for complete packages, since buyers want one party answerable when a system fails and integration takes real work.

The author recommends that Commerce examine how consortia choose their members and whether participation agreements block firms from joining other teams, and that it open the "on-demand" track, currently listed as "coming soon," so a qualified firm can apply for the technology layers a particular sale needs. Under that proposal, approved individual suppliers would get priority introductions, financing referrals, and export-license review, with loans and licenses still decided by the responsible agencies. The author also says Commerce should weigh whether an anchor's supplier choices restrict competition among American firms before granting priority support. The article cites a Computer & Communications Industry Association filing that asks for clearer rules when American bids compete for the same contract. The reporting does not say whether Commerce has agreed to any of these changes.

Articles.Title: The American AI Exports Program Risks Stifling Smaller Competitors - ProMarket

stories.Headline: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
stories.Summary:
Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, has announced an AI model called Dessa that it says was trained "from scratch on nothing but human conversation." To show what it can do, the company shared chat exchanges with people that are sometimes natural and sometimes a little awkward or uncanny. In one example shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam, the model briefly mistakes the speaker for someone named "Ronaldo" before the conversation settles into a mostly natural back and forth. The article was published on October 23, 2026.

The Dessa website describes the model as a true speech-to-speech system whose knowledge came entirely from human speech, and it says the model can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better. Other examples on the site include a discussion of Christopher Nolan's films that drifts into an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer's Superman films, and a conversation in which the model responds to news of a surprise trip to Paris with what the site describes as teary gratitude. A clip also pits Dessa against OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model, and the article says Dessa comes across as more natural in that exchange. The article notes that the clips can be heard in an accompanying video.

The Dessa team gives three reasons for building the model: curiosity, better understanding between humans and AI, and safety. On safety, the team argues that current voice AI flattens speech into text and cannot respond to emotion in people's voices, which it describes as a problem as AI gains power and independence. The team says it will give "a small group of AI safety researchers" early access to the model. The articles do not say when broader access will be available or whether Block plans a public release.

Articles.Title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend

stories.Headline: Why Is CVS Health (CVS) Hiring A Top AI Leader For Pharmacy?
stories.Summary:
CVS Health has named Jack Hanlon as its senior vice president of AI and Analytics for retail and pharmacy operations, according to a report published on October 24, 2026. Hanlon previously held senior data and analytics roles at Meta and Reddit, and the company is bringing that large scale consumer technology experience into its business. The new role is meant to apply advanced AI and analytics across CVS pharmacy, front store activity and customer programs. The appointment was described in a Simply Wall St article carried by Yahoo Finance.

The article ties the hire to the company's existing technology and cost savings plans rather than describing a new strategy. It cites a decade long plan to spend more than US$20 billion on technology and more than US$1 billion of operating expense savings already linked to AI and automation in claims, prior authorization and pharmacy operations. The article says that proof of impact would need to show up in concrete operating metrics, such as further identified cost savings in pharmacy and Caremark or clearer automation targets in quarterly results and 2027 guidance. It also notes that the appointment alone does not settle whether the savings will materialize.

The article is a general commentary from Simply Wall St, which states that it is not financial advice and that it has no position in the stocks it mentions. The author named on the piece is Bailey Pemberton, and the company's own statements on the hire are not quoted in the article. The article also mentions that the analysis found two warning signs for CVS Health, though it does not detail them in the text provided. Context offered is that CVS Health is a US healthcare group delivering services through retail pharmacies, so AI capabilities could influence how prescriptions are filled and how stock and programs are managed. The article does not say what the company will do next beyond these reporting milestones.

Articles.Title: Why Is CVS Health (CVS) Hiring A Top AI Leader For Pharmacy?

stories.Headline: ai coding tools boost speed increase technical debt
stories.Summary:
AI coding tools can speed up software development at first, but the gains may not last and can leave behind more technical debt. According to a Carnegie Mellon study of public repositories using Cursor, teams saw a three- to five-fold increase in lines of code added during the first month. Those gains typically faded after about two months. The same study, which used SonarQube to assess code quality, also found a 30 per cent rise in static analysis warnings and a 41 per cent increase in code complexity.

Sonar, the company behind SonarQube, argues that coding speed has now outpaced verification, and that many teams still depend on manual code review, which becomes a bottleneck as developers generate more code. Sonar proposes building verification into three linked development loops. The agentic loop checks code as an AI agent writes it, so problems can be caught and fixed early. The CI verification loop reviews proposed changes before they are merged into the shared codebase, acting as a quality gate. The code maintenance loop runs continuous background analysis to find and fix legacy issues, security vulnerabilities, and technical debt.

Tom Howlett, Sonar's Director of AI Engineering Engagement, told The New Stack that human developers remain responsible for their code but can focus on high-risk decisions when automated checks narrow the review scope. Anirban Chatterjee, Sonar's director of product and solutions marketing, said that a healthy codebase protects the return on investment over time and that poor-quality code can reinforce itself. Sonar acquired Gitar in May 2026 to add AI-powered review capabilities, including pull request comments and summaries. The article presents this approach as a way to keep quality, security, and governance standards while still benefiting from AI's speed.

Articles.Title: ai coding tools boost speed increase technical debt

stories.Headline: ai platform cairn abused in hacking 100 organisations
stories.Summary:
Threat actors have been abusing Cairn, an open-source AI platform, to automate malicious operations against hundreds of websites around the world, according to AI security firm Norforge. Cairn is a general-purpose problem-solving engine that can coordinate AI agents toward a set goal, and it can also work as an autonomous penetration testing engine. Norforge began its investigation after a report from Gambit Security about hackers using AI harnesses in attacks, and found that some threat actors had left their control panels exposed on Cairn. The firm identified three clusters of malicious activity aimed at persistent access and financial theft.

The largest cluster uses Chinese language and comprises more than 1,100 attack projects across 14 dashboards, targeting e-commerce and payment infrastructure in the United States, Japan and Australia. Norforge said its apparent goal is persistent access to large platforms through webshells, and that targets were ranked by traffic and tested with Microsoft's Playwright browser automation framework before being passed to Cairn. Reuters reports that this actor breached more than 100 companies, including US equipment maker John Deere and home appliance firm SharkNinja. A second cluster, which uses English, exposed 10 panels and focuses on credit card and cryptocurrency theft across merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites and pharmaceutical platforms, with some African commerce sites among its targets. Norforge believes this actor may be based in Africa.

The third cluster exposed a panel holding 59 projects aimed at various e-commerce sites, including very large US commercial platforms, and it seeks shell, admin panel and database access. Norforge said the threat actors succeeded in about 10 per cent of their attempts. Hundreds of secrets were found in the exposed panel data, and the firm verified 11 per cent of them as valid. The articles provided do not say who the threat actors are beyond these clusters, nor what Cairn's developers have said or done in response.

Articles.Title: ai platform cairn abused in hacking 100 organisations

stories.Headline: opencode api keys exposed in ai distillation attack
stories.Summary:
OpenCode, an open-source AI coding project, has notified a subset of its users that API keys tied to external providers were exposed in a security breach. The company said the breach affected 1.4 per cent of its Console users, and some of them reported unauthorized charges and suspended Google Cloud projects. One user reportedly saw more than $1,700 in unauthorized charges overnight. The earliest possible exposure of keys was October 17, 2026, at 00:30 UTC, and the company said no data appears to have been exposed.

OpenCode announced on Saturday that it had suffered a large distillation attack affecting developers who linked providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Co-founder Dax Raad said attackers targeted the company's systems for at least 48 hours using AI agents. The investigation was slowed when the AI models the company was using began refusing requests because of built-in safeguards. The situation stabilized after OpenCode started using OpenAI's Daybreak cybersecurity model for defensive work, which it had been approved to use that same day.

OpenCode's email to affected users shows the company is working with Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic to resolve the incident. The company is also considering reimbursements for users who were hit with charges. Raad has been quoted in the coverage describing the attack and the investigation, and the company itself has been the source of the notices sent to users. The articles do not say who the attackers were or whether any of them have been identified.

The incident follows a pattern in which AI tools and the accounts linked to them become targets for misuse, though the articles frame this specific case as a single breach rather than a trend. Published reports from TechGig on October 21, 2026, put the coverage in the days after the announcement. The articles do not say whether further disclosures, legal action, or changes to how keys are stored are planned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: persistent systems q2 fy27 revenue up 30 3 year on year

Persistent Systems reported that its revenue for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 rose 30.3 per cent year on year to ₹4,663.9 crore, up from ₹3,580.72 crore a year earlier. The figures were published by TechGig on October 15, 2026. Over the same period, sales and marketing expenses rose 20.3 per cent to ₹345.21 crore, compared with ₹286.87 crore in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. As a share of revenue, that expense fell to 7.4 per cent from 8 per cent a year earlier. Sequentially, revenue grew 8.4 per cent from ₹4,303.23 crore in the first quarter.

The company is also moving ahead with a proposed combination with Nagarro, a German digital engineering firm. Persistent has secured roughly 94.04 per cent of Nagarro's share capital and voting rights, excluding treasury shares. Shareholders approved an equity raise of up to $450 million, with combined equity and borrowings capped at $1.25 billion. The deal is intended to strengthen engineering capabilities, widen geographic reach and expand global delivery capacity, and it remains subject to regulatory approvals. Persistent's earnings before interest and tax reached ₹697.72 crore, up 19.5 per cent, although its margin narrowed to 15 per cent from 16.3 per cent.

Persistent is positioning its business around AI-led digital engineering, enterprise modernisation and agentic AI solutions. Its quarterly presentation pointed to work involving AI-enabled software engineering, enterprise automation and data platforms across technology, banking and financial services, and healthcare. Total selling, general and administrative expenses rose 17.4 per cent to ₹709.64 crore, and their share of revenue dropped to 15.2 per cent from 16.9 per cent. stories.Headline: Google overhauls software engineer interviews with AI fluency checks
stories.Summary:
Google is changing how it hires software engineers by adding AI-related steps to its interview process, according to internal documents reviewed by Business Insider. The changes, which the company has been rolling out in phases this year, let candidates use AI tools during coding interviews. Interviewers may also use Gemini, Google's AI model, to help draft feedback for candidates. The documents indicate that many engineers are now expected to show a degree of AI fluency as a minimum requirement for the job.

The company has also been piloting a new "code comprehension" interview format that assesses candidates on AI fluency and prompt engineering. In that format, candidates can use Google's Gemini as an assistant while they work. Brian Ong, Google's Vice President of Recruiting, said the updates are meant to reflect how the company's teams currently operate. He did not present the changes as a reversal of existing hiring standards, but as an alignment with daily practice. The articles do not give a specific date for when each phase took effect beyond saying it occurred during this year.

The reasoning behind the changes ties to how work at Google is already done. The company previously reported that three-quarters of new code created there is generated by AI and then reviewed by humans. Because of that, the hiring process now tests the skills engineers use on the job, including directing AI tools and reviewing their output. The coverage reports these shifts as internal policy and does not describe any outside response or further announced steps. The articles do not say how candidates have reacted or how the new format will be scored.

stories.Headline: The Pentagon’s guidelines for “responsible AI” aren’t always followed, report shows
stories.Summary:
The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog, published a report on October 14, 2026, finding that the Pentagon is building AI-enabled weapons and projects that officials say don't always closely follow the agency's own guidelines for responsible AI. The GAO surveyed 10 officials working on 10 tools that use AI to identify battlefield targets, process surveillance and aid tactical decisions, out of more than 300 such projects at the Pentagon. Six of those officials said their teams had identified risks in using the projects in an operational environment. The report was published in October and drew on that survey, offering a rare look inside how these projects are developed.

The guidelines, set out in a 2021 memo, are six tenets stressing Pentagon-wide oversight, verification, real-time monitoring of the technology, and cooperation with allies to advance shared global norms. Alissa Czyz, who directed the review, said the tenets are not formal rules but are understood by people building AI tools at the Pentagon as important to follow. Most of the officials said their teams had taken at least initial steps to follow them, though some projects were at early stages. Four officials told the GAO that the requirements for their projects were not aligned with the tenets, and three said they did not know whether their projects would be continuously monitored after deployment.

The GAO also found that the group that manages education on the guidelines, the Department of the Responsible AI Division, is understaffed. Although it was authorized to hire 10 people in 2023, only three positions were filled as of February, and the report states the Pentagon is unlikely to fill the vacancies or add staff. The GAO issued two recommendations: that the Pentagon more clearly define the responsibilities and meeting schedules of the office overseeing AI regulation, and that it address the understaffing. The Pentagon agreed with both, but as of October 22 had not put the changes in place, a GAO representative confirmed. NPR asked the Pentagon when it planned to act and did not receive a response.

The report comes as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has pushed for faster AI development and dismissed earlier caution. In a January speech at SpaceX, he said the Pentagon's staffing and committee cycles were unacceptable and that the risks of moving too slowly outweigh the impacts of imperfect alignment. A January memo declared the department an "AI-first" warfighting force, and last month Hegseth announced a new warfare command focused on autonomous weapon development, including drones. AI researchers and international organizations have long called for strict regulation of AI in weapons that could become unpredictable or operate with little human control.

Articles.Title: The Pentagon’s guidelines for “responsible AI” aren’t always followed, report shows

stories.Headline: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity leaders are warning that artificial intelligence could expose far more security weaknesses in global internet infrastructure after researchers found a severe flaw in PHP, a programming language used across millions of websites. The discovery was announced on 21 October 2026, and researchers said they used AI tools to help identify the bugs. Some experts estimated that as many as 70% of websites on the internet could have been at risk of hacking. The flaws may have gone unpatched for years, and the problem has been dubbed "Black October."

Executives say AI will speed up both the discovery and the exploitation of security holes. Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, said the coming months would bring a "vulnerability tsunami" and that there would not be enough time to patch critical infrastructure. Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff called the situation a "code red." Sam Altman said on Thursday that he no longer believed all bugs could be patched.

Matthew Prince, chief executive of Cloudflare, said AI can find flaws at a pace the security community cannot match, so the situation will feel catastrophic. He wrote that the next two years would be extremely difficult as tools with endless patience search the internet for weaknesses. Prince also said Cloudflare had seen thousands of attempts to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before the announcement, a number that rose to millions shortly afterward. Researchers at the AI security platform Wiz called the flaws among the most severe vulnerabilities ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history.

Government and private websites in the US and UK temporarily went offline to apply patches after the announcement. The US National Security Agency urged every site running PHP to install the patches immediately, warning that attackers could use the flaws to steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into networks. The underlying flaws had existed for decades, and the researchers said exploiting them required an unusually complex chain of steps. Tech leaders worry that malicious actors will use the same AI tools to exploit such bugs just as quickly as defenders can find them.

Articles.Title: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking

stories.Headline: Light-Field-to-Bits Computing via an Online-Trainable Cascaded Optoelectronic Neural Network
stories.Summary:
A team has posted a preprint on Research Square describing a proof-of-concept optical computing architecture they call light-field-to-bits (LFB) computing, dated October 24, 2026. The work is described as an online-trainable, cascaded optoelectronic neural network that maps information-bearing light fields onto predefined 4-bit codewords. The authors state that the paper has not yet been peer reviewed by a journal. The article carries the abstract and subject classification, and the authors are not named in the material provided.

The architecture uses two cascaded diffractive layers that route optical energy at the output plane into eight predefined regions of interest, arranged as four differential pairs, with each pair encoding one bit through relative-intensity comparison. The authors physically implemented the first diffractive layer and computationally emulated the second, using a CMOS sensor to capture the intermediate intensity distribution. They also developed a differentiable, physics-assisted surrogate model within a camera-in-the-loop framework. The reported accuracies are 95.31% for geometrically perturbed hexadecimal inputs and 93.36% for traffic-sign inputs subjected to combined viewpoint distortion and noise. The abstract describes the optical front end as performing operations equivalent to about 51.2 giga-operations of multiply-accumulate work within an optical time of flight of about 1.16 nanoseconds, while the electronic stage handles lightweight spatial aggregation on the order of tens of mega-FLOPs.

The authors frame the work as a possible interface between continuous optical information processing and discrete digital decision-making, aimed at latency-sensitive machine vision and edge sensing. They present it as establishing feasibility rather than a finished system. The articles do not describe any independent verification, commercial deployment, or planned follow-on steps beyond the preprint itself. Whether the work will appear in a peer-reviewed journal, and how it compares with existing optical neural network approaches, is not stated in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Light-Field-to-Bits Computing via an Online-Trainable Cascaded Optoelectronic Neural Network

stories.Headline: SafeEvo: Deciphering the Safety Alignment Mechanism and Evolution in Language Models
stories.Summary:
A group of six researchers led by Miao Yu posted a paper titled "SafeEvo" to arXiv, an online repository for scientific preprints, with a listing dated October 24, 2026. The paper introduces an interpretability framework that examines the internal circuits of large language models, the sparse subgraphs responsible for behaviors such as refusing harmful requests. According to the abstract, the authors used an optimization-based method to find weak refusal circuits in pretrained base models, and removing those circuits completely eliminated the base model's refusal of harmful inputs. They also traced how these circuits changed across successive alignment checkpoints.

The authors say those structural changes suggest that the so-called alignment tax, a loss in general usefulness after safety training, may come from refusal-circuit updates affecting parameters tied to utility. To test this, they introduced Safety Circuit Alignment, which limits safety updates to the refusal circuits. Across three language models and two alignment algorithms, the authors report that this method on average lowered a harmfulness score by 63.21 percent and cut refusal rates for benign queries by 58.44 percent. It also retained 99.58 percent of the original models' capabilities.

The paper is authored by Miao Yu, Hao Huang, Lu Yuan, Yunpeng Li, Kun Wang and Zuming Jiang, and the abstract presents the results as the authors' own findings. The article does not describe any independent review, adoption by developers, or external reaction to the work. The arXiv listing offers a PDF and HTML version of the full paper for readers who want the complete experimental details. Because the work is a preprint, its findings have not been confirmed through the formal peer review that typically precedes publication in a scientific journal.

Articles.Title: SafeEvo: Deciphering the Safety Alignment Mechanism and Evolution in Language Models

stories.Headline: The AI-Discovered Bug That Could Have Become a Cybersecurity Disaster
stories.Summary:
In early August, Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz, asked an AI agent to test whether a flaw it had found in WordPress could also be used against Drupal. After about eight hours, the agent reported that it had failed, but it also said it had found a flaw in PHP, the programming language that both systems rely on. The weakness had gone undetected for more than a decade, and the exploit worked. Tzadik first assumed the AI had made a mistake, but he later confirmed the flaw was real.

Researchers at the cybersecurity firm Calif, working with OpenAI, had separately used AI to find a related flaw. The discoveries show a new phase in which AI helps defenders find vulnerabilities but leaves them less time to fix them. Word of the bugs began circulating online two days before the patch's scheduled release, so PHP's maintainers moved the release up by a day. Hours later, Calif mistakenly posted a video showing its exploit, and copycat attempts multiplied. Cloudflare counted millions of attempts, and many webpages, including those of government agencies, were taken down as a precaution while teams installed the update.

Tzadik and Tomer Schwartz, Wiz's CTO of exposure management and appsec, described the response as a loosely organized effort. After Calif and Wiz reported the bugs to PHP, the groups joined forces with researchers from competing companies. They worked together for weeks, speaking almost daily with roughly 15 people, with no contracts governing the arrangement. Schwartz said the process was "just based on trust" and that a leak a month earlier, before a patch existed, would have produced a very different outcome. OpenAI said the PHP bugs were among several significant vulnerabilities it had found and predicted that similar discoveries would increase sharply in the coming months.

The articles also note that AI does not remove the labor involved. Testing ideas that once took weeks can now happen in hours or days, but Tzadik and his colleagues still spent days working out the cause of the bug after the agent could not explain it. Joshua Saxe, a former AI security tech lead at Meta, said an organization had spent roughly $1 million using Anthropic's Mythos to identify bugs, and that more remain. Adam Meyers of CrowdStrike said that even a successful exploit gives defenders chances to intervene. Schwartz added that defenders must cover every vulnerability while attackers need to succeed only once.

Articles.Title: The AI-Discovered Bug That Could Have Become a Cybersecurity Disaster

stories.Headline: Did AI Funding Delays Just Shift Coherent's (COHR) Investment Narrative?

It also cites an alternative view focused on the risk of AI optics overinvestment, with the most cautious analysts modeling earnings near $3.8 billion by 2029 before the news and a price-to-earnings ratio of 24.9 times. stories.Headline: Traders, Is It Time to Buy the AI Dip? Goldman Sachs Says Yes, but Pick Your Spots

stories.Headline: Flying Cars, Smart Homes, and Cracks in the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is a podcast transcript rather than reporting on a discrete event, so the usual breaking-story fallback does not fit. The transcript, recorded October 16, 2026 and published October 24, 2026, centers on three product areas: Apple's HomeView home device, Tesla's Roadster, and AI wearables and devices. The hosts Travis Hoium, Lou Whiteman and Jason Moser debate whether these products answer real needs or are merely new for their own sake. They also discuss a sharp sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks and the financial pressures on the AI industry.

On Apple's HomeView, the hosts see it as a refined version of existing home products, not a new category. Lou Whiteman calls it "Apple 101," an incremental product that reinforces Apple's advantages without redefining anything. Jason Moser argues the smart-home market already has entrenched players, including ADT, SimpliSafe and smart speaker makers, so Apple is late. The hosts also criticize Apple's three-minute advertisement for the device and question whether it would serve younger users. Travis Hoium suggests the device could be useful as a family video-calling tool but not one worth its price.

The hosts also discuss a broader pattern in which companies release AI devices and services without clear everyday uses. Jason Moser says Meta's Muse assistant asks for access to emails, texts and bank accounts before it serves any purpose, which he finds unappealing. Amazon's rollout of a line of AI devices, including a smartwatch and a card that attaches to a phone, drew similar skepticism. Lou Whiteman argues that the stronger opportunity would be a unifying platform, the way Windows works across many products, rather than a closed ecosystem like the one Apple used with HomeKit.

On Tesla's Roadster, Travis Hoium says the demonstration, which showed the car flying, was impressive. Lou Whiteman, however, says the car is a concept meant to show engineering capability and build hype, and he doubts non-road-legal cars will be on the roads by 2028. The transcript does not include details about the sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks or the financial pressures on the industry beyond the episode's stated topics. The article's text is cut off before the hosts finish their discussion, so further points may exist in the full transcript.

stories.Headline: Constellation, Vistra, and GE Vernova Ranked From Worst to First for the AI Power Boom
stories.Summary:
Constellation Energy and Vistra are both benefiting from demand for electricity to power artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis published October 24, 2026. The article ranks the two independent power producers alongside GE Vernova, which makes the turbines utilities use to generate power. The author, Reuben Gregg Brewer, compares the three companies from an investor's standpoint. He describes Constellation as the more conservative choice and GE Vernova as the most growth-oriented option. Electricity demand is the central driver in the piece.

Demand grew 10% between 2005 and 2025 and is expected to grow 60% between 2025 and 2045, a shift the article attributes to new technologies such as artificial intelligence. The International Energy Agency expects AI power demand to grow four times faster than all other power demand over the next decade. Because Constellation and Vistra sell power at market rates outside the regulatory framework, they can benefit if demand pushes prices higher. Both trade at price-to-earnings ratios of around 24x and yield about 0.6%.

The author favors Constellation for investors who want less risk, pointing to its size, which is nearly twice Vistra's, and its status as the largest nuclear power plant operator in the United States. He also notes its faster dividend growth and lower debt-to-equity ratio of 0.8x, compared with Vistra's 3.6x. Vistra may appeal more to growth investors, the article says, though its higher leverage makes its risk and reward less attractive. For GE Vernova, the article cites a backlog of $176 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026 and a price-to-earnings ratio of about 24x.

It describes the company as a supplier that can sell to any power producer, not just one. The article concludes that Constellation suits conservative investors, GE Vernova suits growth investors, and Vistra sits in the middle. It was republished on Yahoo Finance with several other Motley Fool and Insider Monkey pieces on the same AI power theme. The piece also carries a promotion for a Motley Fool stock-picking service that did not list Vistra among its top picks.
