stories.Headline: See it, Say it, Sorted: Mechanistic Diagnosis and Parameter-Space Mitigation of Emergent Misalignment in LLMs
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an arXiv preprint, posted on September 28, 2026 by Weiqiao Que, Ruizhe Li, Chengyu Wang, Dakan Wang, Emine Yilmaz and Xiaofeng He, titled "See it, Say it, Sorted." It studies emergent misalignment, a failure in which safety-aligned large language models, after narrow domain adaptation, unexpectedly produce catastrophic safety failures in unrelated domains. The authors say earlier static analyses did not map training dynamics, and existing defenses rely on heuristics that reduce a model's usefulness. The paper was made public on arXiv under the subject areas of machine learning and computation and language, with a DOI assigned through DataCite.

The authors describe a dynamic, second-order geometric study of the problem, tracking training trajectories over time. They report that directional Hessian curvature concentrates sharply on semantic pivot tokens, and that Grassmannian projections show that, in most settings, the gap between harmful and safe behavior widens mainly because the overlap of safe gradients declines. Building on this, they introduce a parameter-level Geometric Mitigation Framework that orthogonally projects the empirical harmful gradient subspace out of parameter updates. On the Qwen2.5-14B-IT model, the authors say their defense suppresses free-generation emergent misalignment by up to 80.0 percent. Across three other open-weight instruction-based model families ranging from 3B to 20B parameters, they report that teacher-forced evaluation shows the same harmful subspace controls the conditional support of frozen misaligned responses, even where single-layer behavioral misalignment is already near zero.

The paper's authors are responsible for the work and the accompanying code, which the abstract links to. In their abstract, they argue that these diagnostics reveal an illusion of behavioral safety, because the same subspace remains measurable and steerable in models where behavioral misalignment appears absent. The record shows the preprint is labeled as a preprint and has a single version, v1, with a file size of about 2.7 megabytes. The articles do not say whether the work has undergone peer review or been accepted at a venue, nor do they report any response from other researchers or from the developers of the models studied. The articles do not say what follow-up work the authors plan.

Articles.Title: See it, Say it, Sorted: Mechanistic Diagnosis and Parameter-Space Mitigation of Emergent Misalignment in LLMs

stories.Headline: Has XRP Bottomed? We Asked Claude AI Where the Selling Stops
stories.Summary:
Claude AI, Anthropic's model, was asked to estimate where XRP's selling might stop, and the 24/7 Wall St. article published on October 23, 2026 reports its output. According to the piece, XRP has fallen more than 60% from its all-time high of $3.65 in July 2025 and was trading at $1.31 after a 12.1% drop that month. Claude put a 40% chance on the October 18, 2026 low of $1.25 marking the cycle's bottom and suggested selling could slow near $1.12 if that level fails. The article notes that recent lows have been trending upward, with a higher low of $1.28 during the week of October 19.

The article describes a supply issue that it says investors often overlook. About 63.13 billion of XRP's 100 billion total tokens were in circulation, which puts its market capitalization at $83.2 billion and its fully diluted valuation near $131.8 billion. Ripple holds much of the uncirculated supply in escrow and releases it gradually, so each price level requires more buying as supply grows. The author states that holding a $1.25 floor in October 2026 therefore demands more capital than in earlier cycles. Over the past year XRP fell 44.9%, compared with declines of 25.2% for Bitcoin and 37.8% for Ethereum.

The article reports that spot XRP exchange-traded funds recorded net inflows of $708,500 on October 21 and $3.55 million on October 22, citing SoSoValue, with total net inflows of $1.80 billion and net assets of $1.49 billion by October 22. It argues these inflows have had limited effect, noting a $2.47 million outflow on October 16 and a September peak inflow that briefly lifted the price to $1.63. Santiment data cited in the piece shows a record 8.24 million non-empty XRP Ledger wallets, which the author says has not prevented a 28.8% price decline this year. The article also mentions a cross-border stablecoin initiative in Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand involving Ripple, Visa, and Mastercard, but says Ripple's role and any direct use of XRP remain unclear.

The article's conclusions come from Claude's projections, which the author presents as scenarios rather than facts. Claude calls $1.25 the key support, sees a 55% chance XRP trades below it before the end of 2026, and estimates a 20% chance of a drop below $1.00. Its year-end 2026 scenarios range from $0.95 in the bear case to $1.45 in the base case and $2.10 in the bull case. A confirmed bottom would require XRP to reclaim its 20-day average of $1.37, close above its 50-day average of $1.41, and finish a week above $1.45, while a daily close below $1.25 would bring the $1.12 area back into focus.

Articles.Title: Has XRP Bottomed? We Asked Claude AI Where the Selling Stops

stories.Headline: SOAR AI Details Expansion Roadmap and Phased Financing Plans
stories.Summary:
SOAR AI, Inc. has laid out its plan to expand its artificial intelligence infrastructure, including upcoming deployment dates and a phased approach to financing. The company said its Ohio campus will serve as the base for future growth. The plan follows its merger with Alignment Engine Inc. on September 11, 2026, and a rebranding on October 19, 2026. The announcement was reported on October 23, 2026, by Zacks Equity Research.

The company has secured a master services agreement and two four-year, take-or-pay orders from a major AI customer, with an aggregate contract value of $1.2 billion. These agreements are expected to bring in about $133 million in customer prepayments. SOAR AI expects revenue of $175 to $200 million in 2027 from the signed orders, and annual revenue of roughly $294 million once both deployments are fully running. A first deployment of 4,096 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs is backed by a three-year revenue commitment of about $215 million. The company is targeting internal power-on at its Ohio campus for November 30, 2026, with the first GPU deployment ready for service by December 31, 2026.

SOAR AI said each deployment phase will move forward only after the required commercial commitments and funding are in place. It plans to pay for expansion through customer prepayments, equipment financing, senior debt, and equity. A second contracted deployment of 4,032 AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs could become operational as early as April 2027, ahead of its June 30, 2027 contractual start date. Two more deployments of 4,032 MI455X GPUs each are planned for 2027, which could raise the campus total to 16,192 GPUs. The facility currently has access to 154 megawatts of power, with a longer-term roadmap targeting 480 megawatts.

The company's leadership framed these steps as a way to build a scalable AI infrastructure platform and meet growing demand for AI computing. Beyond Ohio, SOAR AI is exploring other sites across the United States and in international markets, including repurposed industrial facilities and new developments with access to behind-the-meter power. The article suggests these moves could improve revenue visibility, help the company fulfill existing contracts, and open the door to additional customers. It also notes that the power expansion could let the company grow without immediately building new facilities. Further progress will depend on whether the planned deployments and financing arrangements are completed on schedule.

Articles.Title: SOAR AI Details Expansion Roadmap and Phased Financing Plans

stories.Headline: AI Chips Today - Boosting AI Compute Efficiency Without Extra Power Consumption
stories.Summary:
Karman, formerly known as Utilidata, has helped NexGen Cloud, a European AI cloud provider, raise its AI compute capacity by 60 percent without drawing additional power at its Montreal data center. The gain comes from Karman's power orchestration platform, which lets 16 NVIDIA B300 servers run within a power budget designed for 10 servers without hurting performance. The deployment was announced in a press release dated October 22, 2026, and reported by Simply Wall St on October 23, 2026. The companies have since expanded their partnership to bring the same technology to NexGen Cloud's European operations. The article presents this as a way to use existing power capacity more efficiently as demand for AI compute keeps rising.

The article names Karman as the party behind the technology and NexGen Cloud as the customer that deployed it. Karman's own announcement, as cited in the piece, described the result as turning stranded power into added compute. The article does not give figures for the cost of the deployment or the size of the expanded European rollout. It also does not say how many data centers beyond Montreal will adopt the platform.

The same article is a market roundup that lists several chip-related stocks and their daily moves. NVIDIA closed at $212.21, down 4.4 percent, while MACOM Technology Solutions fell 15.9 percent to $229.73 and Broadcom ended at $323.24, down 4.3 percent. Advanced Micro Devices fell 8.1 percent to $507.93, and Micron dropped 6.3 percent to $856.49. The roundup also cites an unrelated Vultr expansion of AMD-powered infrastructure in Chennai, India. Much of the rest of the piece is promotional material and general disclaimers from Simply Wall St.

Articles.Title: AI Chips Today - Boosting AI Compute Efficiency Without Extra Power Consumption

stories.Headline: SpaceX may not follow Meta's bold plan to raise money for AI
stories.Summary:
JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth said on Friday, October 23, 2026, that SpaceX is not expected to follow Meta's recent move to issue a new class of nonvoting stock to fund its AI build-out. In a post-earnings note, Anmuth wrote that SpaceX told him it is not considering raising equity. The company instead indicated it has several pools of capital available on the debt side. The report was published by Yahoo Finance writer Brian Sozzi.

SpaceX's earnings report showed capital expenditures guidance of $35 billion to $40 billion for the fourth quarter. That compares with $19.6 billion in the third quarter, $18.4 billion in the second quarter and $10.1 billion in the first quarter. The company ended the quarter with $36.1 billion in debt. Other reports cited in the article say SpaceX is reportedly seeking a $40 billion capital raise with Goldman Sachs and Apollo.

Chief financial officer Bret Johnson, according to the article, did not appear concerned about recent strains in debt markets tied to neocloud companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius. Moffettnathanson analyst Julie Zhu said the earnings call highlighted large capital needs over the next few years, especially in the AI segment. She pointed to a rapid run of recent deals and launches, including the Cursor acquisition, a new Starbase in Louisiana, a large IaaS contract, Starship flight 14 and the purchase of Grain's 800 MHz spectrum. She said each of these carries heavy spending ahead.

The article also notes that SpaceX's stock was listed at 147.30, up 1.76 percent, in the quote data shown on the page. Several other outlets in the related coverage described the reported $40 billion chip-financing plan as a major move, though the article itself does not give those outlets' conclusions about its long-term effect. The article does not say when a debt raise would close or what terms it would carry. It also does not say whether SpaceX would rule out equity permanently.

Articles.Title: SpaceX may not follow Meta's bold plan to raise money for AI

stories.Headline: Explaining Hyperbolic Neural Networks via Geometry-Aware Relevance Propagation
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, by Ping Xiong, Shanglin Li, Yi Ding, Thomas Schnake and Shinichi Nakajima presents a new method for explaining hyperbolic neural networks, which are models that use non-Euclidean geometry to represent data. The paper is listed under machine learning and was first submitted that day. The authors say that the geometric operations in these networks need special handling when relevance, meaning how much each input contributes to an output, is traced backward through the model. They note that equivalent geometric ways of building the same network can yield different feature attributions, even when relevance is conserved locally.

To address this, the authors study two criteria: Geometric Representation Invariance, a specialized form of implementation invariance, and zero-curvature consistency, which requires that relevance pass through unchanged when a geometric module approaches the identity. They propose a propagation rule called LRP-radial-all for modules centered at the origin, which treats geometric scaling as modulation and assigns all relevance to the signal branch. According to the paper, this rule conserves relevance, stays the same across equivalent radial factorizations, and satisfies zero-curvature consistency for a specified Poincaré-Lorentz logarithmic-map construction. A conservative baseline, LRP-half, can violate both criteria.

The authors evaluated the approach on hyperbolic classifiers trained on MNIST, sEEG and CIFAR-10 data, measuring attribution fidelity, qualitative explanations and runtime. They report that LRP-radial-all achieves competitive attribution fidelity across the datasets, with runtime comparable to Gradient×Input and substantially lower than Integrated Gradients. The authors conclude that these findings motivate geometry-aware propagation rules that separate relevance conservation from consistency across equivalent computations. The articles describe a single version of the preprint and do not report peer review, publication in a journal, or any further follow-up.

Articles.Title: Explaining Hyperbolic Neural Networks via Geometry-Aware Relevance Propagation

stories.Headline: General-purpose LLMs as constrained crystal composition generators
stories.Summary:
General-purpose large language models can systematically cover a targeted region of a materials design space, according to a new paper in npj Computational Materials published on 24 October 2026. The authors, led by researchers including Maximilian L. Ach, Konstantin S. Jakob, Christian Carbogno and Karsten Reuter, tested whether an off-the-shelf LLM, GPT-5.4, could propose Elpasolite compositions with low formation energy without task-specific fine-tuning. Elpasolites are quaternary double-perovskites with the general formula ABC2D6, and the target was formation energy below −2.26 eV/atom, a threshold met by under 0.2% of the composition space. The model was run in an iterative prompt-and-response loop in which each candidate was checked for format, scored against a pre-computed formation energy database, and fed back to the model before the next proposal.

The study used a well-defined benchmark from earlier work by Faber et al., which substituted 39 main-group elements into the four crystallographic sites of the Elpasolite prototype, yielding close to two million possible compositions. Those formation energies were predicted with kernel ridge regression trained on roughly 10,000 density functional theory calculations, so the full space was known in advance and performance could be measured exactly. The authors report that the iterative framework recovered on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. They attribute this performance mainly to iterative in-context learning, meaning the feedback between rounds, rather than solely to chemical knowledge stored in the model's parameters.

The result is set against earlier task-specific models studied by Türk et al., which had been trained on this system. Those models, a generative adversarial network, a variational autoencoder and a reinforcement learning model, recovered 40 to 46% of the 3,740 target compositions within 5,000 attempts, rising to 75 to 94% within 250,000 attempts. The authors argue that their findings establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows. The paper is concerned with choosing compositions for a fixed structural prototype; generating space groups, lattice parameters or full crystal structures is treated as a separate problem that the authors say has been addressed elsewhere.

Articles.Title: General-purpose LLMs as constrained crystal composition generators

stories.Headline: Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Building trust in the agentic AI era
stories.Summary:
Microsoft held its Frontier Tour in London on 21 October 2026, attended by 6,500 people, where leaders argued that the next stage of artificial intelligence depends on trust, human control, security and skills rather than technical capability alone. The same day, KPMG and Microsoft announced the opening of the KPMG and Microsoft Frontier Innovation Hub, a co-innovation environment for building trusted agentic AI, which is designed to help organisations design, test, govern and scale AI solutions. The Hub sits near Microsoft's Redmond, Washington headquarters and is described as a seven-year strategic co-investment. Its stated aim is to help clients become what Microsoft calls Frontier Firms, meaning organisations that are human-led and agent-operated.

The London event focused on how AI agents, which carry out specific or multi-step tasks under human oversight, should be given access to information and actions. Satya Nadella said organisations should treat AI models as new forms of insiders and build a zero-trust architecture around them, and Microsoft described its Project Perception as using specialised AI agents to test safeguards and help mitigate problems. Microsoft IQ is meant to give AI access to organisational context such as documents, databases and messages while respecting existing controls. The Hub announcement adds that KPMG and Microsoft intend to develop real-time agentic assurance and runtime enforcement, so that autonomous agents operate within defined boundaries of trust, compliance and accountability.

Darren Hardman, Microsoft's UK and Ireland chief executive, said Microsoft research ranks the UK eighth among 147 economies for generative AI adoption, and that four in five business leaders think the UK can become a world-leading AI economy within five years, compared with only two in five employees. He cited examples including a trial of Copilot across 90 NHS organisations, where users reported average savings of 43 minutes a day on administrative tasks, and NHS England's plan to roll it out to more than 500,000 clinicians and support staff. He also pointed to Network Rail, the AA, UK Power Networks and BT, where BT reported time savings of up to two hours a day for employees. Hardman said 71% of employees using AI report a positive impact on their work and career, and that nine in ten business leaders report having a clear AI strategy.

Nadella and Hardman, along with Todd Lohr of KPMG and Cherie Gartner of Microsoft, presented these efforts as a response to a gap between ambition and confidence, with Hardman saying the UK must close that gap through clear controls, human oversight and useful skills. Gartner, quoted in the Hub announcement, said the next challenge in AI is not just innovation but trust. Lohr said organisations are moving quickly from experimenting with AI to using it to execute work. The articles do not give a timetable for the Hub's first outputs, so what follows from these commitments remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Building trust in the agentic AI era

stories.Headline: Emerald AI, Nvidia share results of latest pilot at Nscale data center in Iceland
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI has released the results of its latest pilot, conducted with Nvidia at Nscale's data center in Iceland, according to an article published on October 23, 2026. During the test, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform worked with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology to cut the power used by the AI server racks at the site by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the racks returned to normal operations. The companies shared the results during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin that week, and the test marked the first time the Emerald Conductor system was fully integrated with Nvidia's DSX technology.

The pilot shows that AI computing can cut its power use on request, which is what utilities need to see before they can connect AI factories faster, according to Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI. Sivaram said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out, and making AI factories flexible enough to use existing grid capacity could both relieve that limit and keep energy affordable for local communities. The Emerald Conductor program acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so facilities can adjust their energy consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. The approach is aimed at supporting grid stability.

The Iceland test is the seventh pilot Emerald AI has undertaken. Earlier tests include three in the United States, in Santa Clara, Phoenix, and Chicago, and one in the United Kingdom in partnership with the National Grid. The company also announced in October that its orchestration software is set to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia, its first commercial project. Emerald AI has raised funding across several rounds, including a further $150 million in Series A funding announced in August.

Articles.Title: Emerald AI, Nvidia share results of latest pilot at Nscale data center in Iceland

stories.Headline: How to Tame a Multi-Headed Hydra? Adaptive Multi-Category Safety Steering for Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Chenxi Wang, with co-authors Ruiyang Huang, Li Huang and Yifan Wu, has posted a paper on arXiv describing a new method for making large language models safer. The paper was first submitted on September 28, 2026, and a revised version followed on September 29, 2026. The work is categorized under Cryptography and Security, with related listings in Computation and Language and Machine Learning. The researchers present the method as a response to a specific weakness in existing safety techniques.

The method is called CAM-Steer, short for Category-Adaptive Multi-category Safety Steering. Activation steering changes a model's internal activations during inference, without updating its parameters. The authors point out that one prompt can involve several kinds of harm at once, and steering toward safety in one category may leave harmful content in another unaddressed. CAM-Steer estimates the risk for each harm category by comparing the model's current hidden state with safe and unsafe prototypes.

It then combines the safety directions into one steering direction, sets the strength of the intervention, and rotates the hidden state while keeping its norm unchanged. According to the abstract, the authors evaluated CAM-Steer across three LLM backbones and seven harm categories. They report that it outperforms the baselines they tested in average defense success rate, including when categories co-occur within a single prompt. The paper also states that further analyses support its component designs and the usefulness of its risk scores, and that the added inference overhead is negligible.

The abstract does not name the baseline methods or give the specific success-rate figures, so those details would have to come from the full text. The articles do not describe any deployment of CAM-Steer by a company or agency, nor any reaction from outside the research team. They also do not say whether the code or data is publicly released, though the arXiv page lists a link for associated code and data platforms. Because the paper is a preprint posted on arXiv, its findings have not been described as peer-reviewed in the material provided.

Articles.Title: How to Tame a Multi-Headed Hydra? Adaptive Multi-Category Safety Steering for Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Microsoft Strengthens Digital Sovereignty Push with New Cloud and AI Protections
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced new sovereign cloud and AI protections this week, expanding tools that give organizations more control over where their data sits, who can reach it, and how critical systems run. The announcement, reported by Redmondmag.com on October 23, 2026, came from Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, who outlined updates across public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes are aimed at governments, regulated industries, and other organizations that need firmer control over sensitive workloads while still using cloud-based AI. Phillips said digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on while continuing to innovate. The article frames these moves as a response to AI becoming a larger part of enterprise infrastructure.

Among the additions is the Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite and is available through the Azure portal. IT administrators can use it to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify risks that could disrupt operations. Microsoft is also tightening access to sensitive systems through Data Guardian, which requires oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. A companion tool, Production Touch Ledger, keeps tamper-resistant records of that access.

On encryption, external key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud. The company is further expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings with GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and more data services on Azure Local. Microsoft's Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, separately addressed the risks of autonomous AI systems in an announcement made on Monday. The related Project Perception initiative targets what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents that can reach sensitive information and act without constant human supervision.

Under that effort, Microsoft plans Guardian Agents, specialized security agents that monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior, and step in when actions become risky. Gallot said monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. The article distinguishes the two efforts: Project Perception limits what AI agents can do, while the sovereign cloud work addresses where those systems run, who administers them, and how data stays protected. Taken together, the two initiatives suggest Microsoft is placing more weight on oversight in its enterprise AI strategy, not just on automation.

Phillips said AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations deploy intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure. The article does not say when the Sovereign Control Panel will become generally available beyond its public preview, nor does it report customer adoption figures. It also does not detail pricing or availability outside the regions named. Readers should check Microsoft's own documentation for timing and regional details.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Strengthens Digital Sovereignty Push with New Cloud and AI Protections

stories.Headline: uGAP: A Unified Geospatial AI Platform for African Geographic Data
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Research has introduced uGAP, a unified geospatial AI platform for African geographic data, as described in a research page dated October 23, 2026. The page presents uGAP as a way to bring together more than 100 African datasets, which it says are currently fragmented and hard to access. It is listed as part of the MSR Africa Seminar Series, with a talk dated October 6, 2026. The page identifies the speakers as Ian Ocholla, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Cape Town, Gilles Quentin Hacheme, a senior applied research scientist, and Stephanie Nyairo, a senior product designer. According to the page, uGAP combines data discovery, processing, and model training into one workflow through a Python SDK.

The platform is intended to remove technical bottlenecks that slow down local researchers. The authors say this would let them turn raw data into community-relevant resilience policies. The page also notes that reliance on external models often overlooks local vulnerabilities, which the platform is meant to address. The authors credited on the page are Ian Ocholla of the University of Cape Town, and Gilles Quentin Hacheme and Stephanie Nyairo of Microsoft. Their description of the platform is taken from the seminar abstract on the Microsoft Research page.

The page is tagged under artificial intelligence, data platforms and analytics, ecology and environment, and technology for emerging markets, and it is linked to Microsoft Research Africa in Nairobi and the AI for Good Lab. The article does not give further details on release timing, availability, or funding. The page does not say what comes next for uGAP, such as public release dates, licensing, or planned partnerships. Beyond the seminar listing, it offers no independent evaluation of the platform's performance. More to follow.

Articles.Title: uGAP: A Unified Geospatial AI Platform for African Geographic Data

stories.Headline: Nvidia's Latest AI Power Play Could Shake Up Video Industry
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and the investment firm TCV have backed Higgsfield, an AI video startup, in a new funding extension announced on October 23, 2026. According to the article, the company's user base has passed 40 million and its annual revenue is approaching $1 billion. The extension builds on Higgsfield's August Series B round, which raised $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation and was led by DST Global. The company has added roughly 10 million users since that summer round.

Higgsfield was founded in 2023 by Alex Mashrabov, a former Snap executive, and Yerzat Dulat, an AI engineer from Kazakhstan. The platform combines its own AI engine with about 35 external AI video models and offers tools for storyboarding, character creation, audio and final video editing, aimed at brands and creators. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang highlighted the company during a visit to Astana, Kazakhstan, where much of its engineering team is based. Huang said AI video systems have improved greatly, especially in producing longer videos with consistent characters and scenes, and he credited advances in agentic reasoning systems for much of that gain.

The article attributes the praise and the investment to Huang and to the investors named above, and it presents Nvidia's stake as part of a broader push to back companies that may drive future demand for AI compute. The article also notes the competitive landscape: China's Kling AI reportedly raised $2.8 billion at a $15 billion valuation this summer, and the U.S. company Runway AI raised $315 million at a $5.3 billion valuation earlier this year in a round that included Nvidia. The commentary in the piece says the most important takeaway is that AI video is moving from experimentation toward a real commercial market, while cautioning that video generation remains compute-intensive. Investors are advised to watch Higgsfield's revenue growth, monetization, compute costs, competitive differentiation and whether usage expands from creators into enterprise workflows.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's Latest AI Power Play Could Shake Up Video Industry

stories.Headline: Where Do LLMs Decide to Break the Rules? Mechanistic Localization of Prompt Injection Compliance
stories.Summary:
Researchers Rui Wen, Jiayang Liu, Zeyu Yang, Jun Sakuma and Lu Sun posted a preprint to arXiv on September 29, 2026, asking where inside a large language model the decision to follow an injected adversarial instruction, rather than its assigned system role, actually takes place. Earlier work had mostly measured how often such prompt injection attacks succeed, but this study looked at the internal network itself. The authors ran layer-by-layer causal activation patching on five models ranging from 4 billion to 32 billion parameters. The paper was also listed through doi.org on October 24, 2026.

The team found that attack information can be linearly decoded from the first layer of the network, yet it has little causal influence on behavior until a late-layer bottleneck in the final third of the model. Patching that bottleneck reversed compliance in 77 to 92 percent of cases. According to the abstract, the compliance mechanism occupies a compact linear subspace of rank 8 in the 4B and 14B models, rising to rank 64 in the 32B model, and the pattern held across different model families. The authors also report that the same peak layer is the best place to detect attacks, outperforming early-layer classifiers that degrade under obfuscation such as leetspeak substitution.

The paper is a single-version preprint, and its authors are the only parties described as responsible for the work, with the abstract presenting their findings in their own words. The article does not name any organization or funder beyond the arXiv listing's general funding acknowledgment. The authors frame their results as converging evidence that the late-layer bottleneck captures decision-relevant computation rather than an artifact of the intervention method. The articles provide no information on peer review, follow-up work, or planned changes to deployed models.

Articles.Title: Where Do LLMs Decide to Break the Rules? Mechanistic Localization of Prompt Injection Compliance

stories.Headline: SpaceX won't follow Meta's playbook to fund its AI build-out, JPMorgan says
stories.Summary:
SpaceX has told JPMorgan that it is not considering raising equity to fund its artificial intelligence build-out, which sets it apart from Meta, which this week said it would issue a new class of nonvoting stock for the same purpose. The comments came from a discussion with management after SpaceX's earnings report, and JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth described them in a post-earnings note on Friday, October 23, 2026. According to Anmuth, the company indicated it has a number of available pools of capital on the debt side. The note said capital requirements are front and center across the market.

The earnings report gave investors a sense of how much the company expects to borrow and spend. SpaceX guided to capital expenditures of $35 billion to $40 billion for the fourth quarter, up from $19.6 billion in the third quarter, $18.4 billion in the second quarter and $10.1 billion in the first quarter. The company ended the quarter with $36.1 billion in debt. Chief financial officer Bret Johnson did not appear concerned on the earnings call about recent tremors in the debt markets tied to neocloud companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius.

Reports have said SpaceX is weighing a capital raise of about $40 billion with Goldman Sachs and Apollo, though the articles do not confirm the terms or timing of any such deal. The articles note that Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management. Analyst Julie Zhu of MoffettNathanson said the earnings call underscored the large capital needs ahead, particularly in the AI segment. She pointed to a string of recent moves, including the Cursor acquisition, a new Starbase in Louisiana, another large infrastructure contract, the launch of Starship flight 14 and the purchase of Grain's 800 MHz spectrum. Zhu said each of these signals a significant amount of spending ahead.

Articles.Title: SpaceX won't follow Meta's playbook to fund its AI build-out, JPMorgan says

stories.Headline: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack to Contain AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has introduced new capabilities to Project Perception that treat AI agents as a kind of insider threat, according to a Dark Reading report published on October 23, 2026. The update lets Project Perception discover agents running inside an organization, give each one an identity and permissions, and continuously score each organization's risk. When it finds an anomalous agent, which Microsoft calls the "agentic insider," it can cut that agent's access off. The first version of the system, released in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was aimed at AI-driven attacks and used red, blue and green agents to find attacker paths, identify the greatest risks and mitigate threats. The new release adds what Microsoft calls Guardian Agents, which watch the AI agents running across an organization and can contain them when they behave unexpectedly.

Microsoft says each agent will get a distinct identity separate from the user's and will start with no permissions, gaining only what it needs for the task. The update extends detection to 60 types of agents, 35 more than before, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot. Other features include Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score drawn from several Microsoft security products, and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes, restrict network paths, revoke access or stop an agent as its risk rises. Microsoft also describes an execution container that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach. Microsoft says it can interrupt a live agent session without disrupting the user's own work, though the report notes these are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Nadim Abdo, Microsoft's corporate vice president for identity and network access, described an expense-approval agent that could be tricked by a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report, and said the system would raise the agent's risk score if it began trying to make wire transfers. Satya Nadella acknowledged at a CISO conference last week that Perception and Agent 365 "need to be battle tested," and that Microsoft's behavioral monitoring must improve. Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, said the underlying models have proven unpredictable. Competing vendors including Okta, Teleport, CrowdStrike and a group called the Blueprint Alliance are pursuing similar approaches, and Abdo argued that Microsoft's advantage is that its identity, endpoint and network products are already widely deployed together. Skeptics question the approach.

Andras Cser, a Forrester analyst, said Microsoft's third-party integrations have not been first rate and that the company is interested in pushing its own products. Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of Suzu Labs, argued that the worst outcomes can occur inside authorized permissions and that Guardian Agents could themselves be manipulated or compromised. Cser added that one unpredictable agent watching another compounds the uncertainty, and that most organizations remain cautious about adopting guardian agents. The report describes the market as still fluid, with no settled open standard for securing agents across vendors.

Articles.Title: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack to Contain AI Agents

stories.Headline: Meta’s capital-raising plans expose a major weakness in the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook and Instagram, has moved to issue a new class of non-voting stock, a decision that weighed on its shares. In a filing, a special committee of the company's board said the Class C shares would help it raise capital while keeping its chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, in control. The shares are expected to be available as early as the end of 2026 and would be used for equity offerings from time to time, depending on market conditions. The Investing.com report says Meta's stock fell 7% on Thursday, despite strong earnings.

The new shares would be created alongside existing stock through what the report describes as a two-for-one distribution. Meta could then use them for equity offerings, employee compensation and acquisitions without diluting the voting power of current shareholders. Zuckerberg holds a majority of the company's voting power despite owning a much smaller share of its economic value, so issuing additional voting shares could weaken that control. Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, while capital expenditures reached $34.91 billion, and the company raised its projected 2026 capital spending to between $135 billion and $145 billion. Free cash flow turned negative as spending outpaced cash generated.

The special committee's filing cited "an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital," and pointed to recent large capital raises and anticipated raises by Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI to fund similar AI growth. The committee said that while Meta currently has sufficient capital for its needs, it would be prudent to act before other companies absorb more of the available capital in the market. The report notes that Meta is not in immediate financial distress and that its advertising business remains a significant source of cash. It argues that the filing points to a broader question about whether companies racing to build AI may compete for the financing itself, not only for computing power.

The article describes the concern as one of cost and availability rather than an imminent funding crisis. Capital raised by one company does not automatically block another from raising money, and companies can fund themselves through cash flow, bonds, equity, private investors or partnerships. Still, the report says those options carry different costs, since debt adds obligations and equity dilutes shareholders. It adds that the sustainability of the AI spending will depend on whether the technology produces revenue and returns high enough to justify the infrastructure being built. The filing, the article concludes, shows Meta wants financing flexibility before competitors absorb more of the available capital.

Articles.Title: Meta’s capital-raising plans expose a major weakness in the AI boom

stories.Headline: I’m a comedian whose joke was stolen by an AI creator. I blame Meta and feel powerless.
stories.Summary:
A comedian named George Brett Olson says an AI-generated account on Instagram copied one of his jokes, a bit about AI stealing jobs and people still blaming immigrants that he had performed live for about a year. He first learned of it when a friend sent him a video of the account delivering the joke, which he says looked like him in his own clothes but with an exaggerated, 42-inch rear end. When he asked the account whether it was real, the account said yes, but it did not answer whether someone had helped create it. The account then left a comment saying it would not happen again and removed a number of its videos.

Olson's account describes a broader problem he says other comedians have also raised, in which AI accounts copy jokes from live performers and sometimes draw more followers than the people they copy. He said that some followers tried to report the account, and that Instagram head Adam Mosseri responded publicly. Mosseri said it was not practical to ban AI content from the platform because it is becoming harder to identify and is not all bad, but that Instagram is invested in driving traffic to original creators. He said the company would look into what it could do about wholesale copying, though he was not sure what that would be and said he would talk to his team.

Olson places the main blame on Meta, not on the person or tool behind the copying, because he says the people running such accounts are trying to make money with what they have. He said he feels more demoralized by Meta's response, which he describes as suggesting that creators are powerless and that the problem is inevitable. He argues that this is not true and that institutions like Meta can be held accountable in ways individuals often cannot. Olson also says comedians rely on social media mainly to sell tickets and draw people to live shows, and he worries that a flood of AI agents could make it hard to tell what is real online. The articles do not say what, if anything, Meta will change, and they report no further action beyond Mosseri's statement.

Articles.Title: I’m a comedian whose joke was stolen by an AI creator. I blame Meta and feel powerless.

stories.Headline: Anthropic unveils Claude Duet AI agent app
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced Claude Duet on October 21, 2026, a new AI agent aimed at professionals and small business owners. It is built around Claude Opus 5.5 and is launching as a research preview. The agent is available as a standalone app on iOS and Android and also through Claude on the web. It is positioned as a competitor to Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots.

According to Anthropic, each morning Duet sends a short brief on the most important items across a user's connected apps. During the day it keeps watch on those apps and sends a message only when something needs attention. Users can also hand it tasks, from simple jobs like scheduling meetings to harder ones such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps. It draws memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude, and it has a virtual machine with a browser for completing work. Before any big step, such as sending a payment or deleting something, it messages the user for approval.

Anthropic says it added a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt, designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, such as credit card numbers. The company describes Duet as an early version that might still misread a thread or miscalibrate what is urgent. It also says the agent is not as strong at personal errands like booking tickets. To try it, people can join a waitlist, though they must be Pro or Max subscribers in the US. Anthropic has not said whether Duet will be bundled with existing Claude subscriptions or priced separately.

Coverage describes the launch as part of a crowded race to build agents that work inside people's tools rather than just chat. Duet's focus on solo practitioners and small teams is a different target from Meta's consumer-oriented Muse and OpenAI's developer-oriented Dots, and Google has its own agent plans tied to Workspace. Some major sites, including Yelp and Delta, are blocking autonomous agents from other companies over scraping and terms of service worries, which could shape how useful Duet proves to be. The research preview label suggests Anthropic is testing the product before a wider release. What comes next will depend on how well Duet performs once real users hand it their apps and tasks.

Articles.Title: Anthropic joins Meta and OpenAI’s personal AI assistant race with Duet

stories.Headline: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation
stories.Summary:
The workflow for teaching Microduck, a small robot, to walk an obstacle course in simulation was described in an NVIDIA Technical Blog post published on October 23, 2026, by Gabriele Leone, Seun Doherty, Asier Arranz, Johnny Núñez and Asawaree Bhide. The process starts on an NVIDIA RTX Spark machine, where the Hermes agent and the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt model turn a written prompt into a step-by-step project plan. From there, a separate agent called Astra builds the 3D assets the course needs. The post presents this as a walkthrough of a method that others can adapt to their own robots and tasks.

The plan covers far more than asset creation, including environment construction, robot preparation, simulation, training, validation and deployment. Astra creates clearer reference images with cloud image editing, models the geometry in FreeCAD, applies materials in Blender, and exports editable models and USD files. The assets are then assembled in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, where Newton models Microduck's movement and balance. Training runs in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 4,096 parallel environments on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU, using head-camera depth and robot-state observations. The trained policy is then checked locally on RTX Spark for obstacle detection, movement adjustment and course completion.

The authors describe the work as a foundation for physical deployment rather than a finished product. They note that differences between simulation and the real world still require further refinement, and they point to techniques such as Better Actuator Models and domain randomization for the transfer step. The post also points readers to the free SimReady Central Library, which offers more than 2,000 ungated simulation-ready OpenUSD assets, to the Isaac Lab documentation for reinforcement and imitation learning, and to a Microduck sim-to-real tutorial on Hugging Face. The source article was cut off before its final validation and deployment details, so the remaining steps are not described here.

Articles.Title: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation | NVIDIA Technical Blog

stories.Headline: ReCAP: Retrieval-Guided Capability Reuse for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
stories.Summary:
On September 29, 2026, researchers Tao Hu, Zhinuo Zhou, Xialiang Tong, De-Chuan Zhan and Da-Wei Zhou posted a paper on arXiv, an open preprint server, introducing a method called ReCAP. The paper addresses multimodal continual instruction tuning, in which multimodal large language models learn new abilities from a series of tasks without losing what they already know. The article was listed in the computer vision category and was later indexed with a DOI dated October 24, 2026. The authors report that the work is still a preprint and has not been described as peer reviewed in the material provided.

The authors explain that most earlier methods reduce forgetting by limiting how model parameters change or by keeping task-specific adaptations separate. ReCAP instead draws on external knowledge, and at each stage it uses external search and a large language model to build a knowledge base of domain, reasoning and format information from the current training data. For each instruction, retrieved domain knowledge guides generation, while retrieved reasoning knowledge selects and orders capability modules into an instance-specific path. To keep these reused modules stable across stages, the paper introduces adaptive subspace recycling, which uses shared bases and stage-specific cores to protect important past directions while reusing leftover capacity. The authors state that extensive experiments on MCIT benchmarks show that ReCAP achieves state-of-the-art performance, and the article gives no further figures in the text provided.

The paper's authors are responsible for the work, and their stated claim is that leveraging external knowledge can support continual adaptation, a direction they describe as largely unexplored in existing MCIT methods. They illustrate the idea with a question about counting red cubes to the left of a sphere, arguing that domain knowledge supplies concepts about objects and spatial relations while reasoning knowledge specifies ordered steps such as recognition, filtering and counting. The articles provided do not describe any independent evaluation, competing responses, or planned releases of code or models beyond the paper's own links. Readers should treat the reported results as the authors' claims until they are verified by others.

Articles.Title: ReCAP: Retrieval-Guided Capability Reuse for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning

stories.Headline: Machine learning-enabled prediction and interpretation of spectroscopic properties in Nd and Y co-doped fluorite platform via local coordination engineering
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Liang-Bi Su and Feng-Kai Ma at the Shanghai Institute of Ceramics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has published a study in the journal npj Computational Materials on predicting the optical behavior of neodymium and yttrium co-doped fluorite materials. The paper was published online on 29 September 2026, with an earlier online version dated 24 October 2026 according to the publisher's listing. The authors used machine learning to link the local atomic coordination of these crystals to their spectroscopic properties, which govern how they absorb and emit light. The work targets laser materials, where the arrangement of atoms around rare-earth ions strongly shapes performance.

The researchers combined experimental spectroscopy with structural data and trained four models: Linear Regression, Support Vector Regression, a Back Propagation Neural Network, and Extreme Gradient Boosting. These models predict key spectroscopic parameters, including absorption, emission and lifetime, from the relative fractions of three dominant polyhedral structural motifs in the material. Using Shapley value analysis, the team identified how much each structural unit contributes to each property. The article argues that this data-driven approach avoids limits of conventional Density Functional Theory when describing the localized 4f electron states of rare-earth ions. It also presents the framework as a scalable route to designing broadband, high-repetition-rate laser materials.

The article reports funding from the National Key Technologies R&D Program (2023YFB3507402), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grants W2412088, 62475104 and 61905289), the Open Fund of the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Rare Earth Development and Application (XTKY-202402), and the CAS Project for Young Scientists in Basic Research (YSBR-024). The authors state they have no competing interests. The paper is published under a Creative Commons licence permitting non-commercial use. The article does not describe any demonstrated laser device or next steps beyond the authors' stated aim of guiding future material design.

Articles.Title: Machine learning-enabled prediction and interpretation of spectroscopic properties in Nd and Y co-doped fluorite platform via local coordination engineering

stories.Headline: CARAT: Do Materials LLMs Reason or Recite?
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 29, 2026, under the title "CARAT: Do Materials LLMs Reason or Recite?" asks whether large language models built for materials science answer questions about crystal structure by reasoning from the structure or by copying an answer already present in their input. The authors are Jiajun Wu, Jian Yang, Zixiang Ni, Zhenzhu Li and Bin Chong. Their argument is that plain accuracy cannot settle the question, because a structural description often includes the very field the model is scored on. The paper's version history shows a single version, submitted that day and listed under Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI).

To test this, the authors built a framework called CARAT that holds each question and its gold answer fixed while varying the input across eight matched views. It names each structural relation separately in a representation called GraphSpace and adds matched fine-tuning, answer masking, evidence injection, paired inference, and a rule that can withhold claims. On the benchmark's hardest families, the grounded view scored 17.3 points higher than formula-only inputs. GraphSpace beat a plain periodic graph by 19.3 points, but the authors say that margin reflects two effects: about 1.96 points where the plain rendering already carried the needed fields, and 46.7 points where it omitted them entirely. Their conclusion is that the headline gain mostly measures what the baseline lacked rather than how evidence is presented.

The authors also test their own benchmark and report that a shortcut rule reading the list directly answered four of seven hardened families, so they rebuilt the benchmark until eleven such shortcuts sat near chance. They found that the frozen model repeats the relation it is given but answers the same way when that link is redirected, in 95.6 percent of paired cases. After matched supervision it reached 99.8 percent, and with the link deleted it dropped to 23.4 percent, below the 27.0 percent the best shortcut achieved. The paper is 42 pages with 19 figures, including an appendix, and the articles give no outside reaction, funding details beyond the arXiv notice, or information on next steps.

Articles.Title: CARAT: Do Materials LLMs Reason or Recite?

stories.Headline: TabFM-Auto: Self-Evolving Pipelines for Tabular Foundation Models
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Deqing Fu and six co-authors posted a preprint to arXiv on September 29, 2026, introducing TabFM-Auto, a system that pairs a tabular foundation model called TabFM with a language model agent. The paper's authors describe the problem they address: tabular foundation models reach strong zero-shot accuracy by pretraining on synthetic tables, yet they ignore column names, task descriptions, and auxiliary files that carry the meaning of a dataset. Separately, self-evolving machine learning engineering agents train models from scratch on each dataset, but jointly searching features, architectures, and hyperparameters is described as noisy and prone to overfitting. The article indicates the system was posted on arXiv under the subject area of machine learning and carries a listed DOI.

The agent uses dataset metadata and validation feedback to iteratively refine the data pipeline surrounding TabFM, covering data cleaning, feature engineering, context selection, and post-processing, in order to reduce TabFM's error. The authors report that across all 51 datasets of the TabArena benchmark, five TabFM-Auto configurations, each with different agents and language models, take the top five overall positions. The best configuration raises TabFM's score from 1785 to 2013 Elo. According to the paper, the discovered pipelines also transfer to other frozen tabular foundation models, gaining between 69 and 143 Elo without further search. On the 8 tabular competitions of MLE-Bench, the authors say TabFM-Auto ranks first overall among MLE agents.

The paper lists Deqing Fu, Huangyuan Su, Rajat Sen, Taman Narayan, Sujay Sanghavi, Abhimanyu Das, and Weihao Kong as authors, and Deqing Fu submitted the version. The article does not state the authors' institutional affiliations, funding sources, or any claims beyond the benchmark results summarized in the abstract. The arXiv listing presents the work as a preprint, meaning it has not been described as peer-reviewed in the material provided. The article does not say whether the code or models will be released or what follow-up work is planned.

Articles.Title: TabFM-Auto: Self-Evolving Pipelines for Tabular Foundation Models

stories.Headline: HKAW spotlights AI, costs and tribunal standards
stories.Summary:
Technology and the cost efficiency of arbitration emerged as key themes at Hong Kong Arbitration Week (HKAW), according to Domitille Baizeau, co-chair of the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre (HKIAC). Baizeau and fellow co-chair Victor Dawes SC spoke to Asia Business Law Journal on the sidelines of the "ADR in Asia Conference 2026" held at the Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong. Baizeau singled out artificial intelligence as a particularly prominent technology issue, saying its rapid development is raising hard questions. She asked whether there should be limits on its use by arbitrators and counsel, given how quickly the technology changes. HKAW is organised by the HKIAC and runs from 19 to 23 October, and more than 1,200 participants from 53 jurisdictions attended.

Time and cost efficiency were another recurring focus across the conference and side events. Baizeau said the debate over how to manage cases more efficiently, the role of arbitrators and the responsibility of counsel is becoming more pressing. She said the HKIAC is watching user satisfaction closely and is considering how to train arbitrators to be more efficient without interfering too much. For her, this is central to the institution and to international arbitration generally. She also noted that more delegates came from Africa and the Middle East this year.

For Dawes, a major development was the attention paid to the quality of the tribunal. He welcomed the community's willingness to examine whether the system delivers the services it claims to provide. He asked whether arbitration is efficient and how neutrality, impartiality and the quality of awards can be ensured. He described the discussion of how to do better as the most valuable outcome of the week.

Baizeau said open dialogue about improvement is extremely important and that the profession cannot be complacent. Baizeau linked the growing African and Middle Eastern attendance to Hong Kong's need to build stronger ties with those markets, given inbound investment in Africa. Law.asia is an official media partner of the event. The articles do not say what specific measures the HKIAC will adopt on AI rules or arbitrator training.

Articles.Title: HKAW spotlights AI, costs and tribunal standards

stories.Headline: Meta Creates New Share Class to Bankroll AI Arms Race
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on October 21, 2026, that it will create a new class of non-voting shares to raise money for its AI push. The company disclosed the plan in its third-quarter 2026 earnings release, and the shares are expected to begin trading in 2027. The proceeds are meant to fund AI infrastructure, possible acquisitions, and employee compensation. Meta's press release called the required investment "significant," and the move follows a structure Alphabet has used since its 2004 public offering. The new shares carry economic exposure to Meta's performance but no voting power, which allows Mark Zuckerberg to keep his control of the company while raising capital without taking on debt.

CFO Susan Li said on the earnings call that the shares would "expand our funding tools." Investors would receive returns without any say in how the company is run. Details such as the number of shares and their valuation have not yet been disclosed, and Meta expects to file more information with the SEC in the coming months. Meta's leadership has framed the financing as necessary to compete in an industry-wide AI transformation. The company has spent heavily on AI features for its apps, its Llama language models, and the data centers needed to train them.

Analysts and investors have already questioned whether those returns justify the spending, and the company's Reality Labs division has continued to lose money on metaverse projects. Zuckerberg's supervoting control means the new class adds flexibility without changing who decides strategy. The next key milestone is the 2027 start of trading, when the market will judge whether the dilution is justified. Investors will be watching for the detailed disclosures Meta files with the SEC and for evidence that its AI spending produces products that generate revenue. Until then, the plan leaves shareholders exposed to the company's AI bets without any voice in how that money is spent.

Articles.Title: The AI Litigation Arms Race: Why Corporate Defendants Should Be Worried

stories.Headline: OmniRoute: Mapping Temporal Semantic Evidence to Audio-Visual Token Budgets for Efficient Omnimodal Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 29, 2026, under the identifier 2609.37052, introduces OmniRoute, a training-free framework for shrinking the audio and visual input that omnimodal large language models must process. The authors are Yuchen Deng, Zidang Cai, Feidiao Yang, Yufei Wang, Jie Wang, Hai-Tao Zheng and Yuxing Han, and the paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. The work addresses a practical problem: these models turn audio and video streams into long, interleaved token sequences, and processing them up front carries a heavy computational cost. The paper was first submitted on September 29, 2026, as a 1,676 KB file.

The framework works in two stages, and it needs no additional training of the model. The first stage, called Temporal Evidence-Guided Budgeting, decides for each chunk of the input which modality leads and how many tokens that leading modality should receive, based on semantic relevance and local content variation. The second stage, Budget-Constrained Semantic Compression, compresses the leading modality first, then adjusts the retention target for the other modality using the fraction actually kept. For video, the method groups spatiotemporal content and selects tokens guided by the query, while for audio it selects tokens by encoder attention and query relevance and merges the remaining tokens into context anchors guided by visual content.

The authors report experiments on four representative benchmarks, which they say show a better balance between inference efficiency and performance than competing baselines. They also state that the code and interface will be released to support further research, though the articles do not give a release date. The paper is an arXiv preprint and the articles do not say whether it has been peer reviewed or accepted at a venue. The work sits within efforts to make multimodal models cheaper to run on long audio-visual inputs, and the articles do not describe any further steps beyond the code release.

Articles.Title: OmniRoute: Mapping Temporal Semantic Evidence to Audio-Visual Token Budgets for Efficient Omnimodal Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Deep Learning GW Quasiparticle Hamiltonians for Many-Body Excited-State Electronic Structure at Scale
stories.Summary:
The researchers Xiaoxun Gong, Zechen Tang, Woochang Kim, Yang Li, Wenhui Duan, Yong Xu and Steven G. Louie introduced DeepH-GW, a deep-learning framework that predicts an effective GW quasiparticle Hamiltonian directly from atomic structure. The work was submitted to arXiv on 29 September 2026 and listed under condensed matter physics. The authors say that accurate quasiparticle electronic structures underpin the understanding of excited-state properties of materials. They also note that conventional first-principles GW calculations remain computationally intensive for large or configurationally complex systems.

The framework builds on the local, equivariant message-passing architecture of an earlier method called DeepH and is trained on high-fidelity plane-wave GW calculations. A real-space Hamiltonian-reconstruction interface links the training data to the model. According to the paper, this combines the systematic accuracy and broad chemical applicability of plane-wave methods with linear-scaling neural-network inference. Across the systems the authors examined, DeepH-GW reproduces quasiparticle band structures with errors on the order of a few meV.

The authors report that, although many-body interactions are intrinsically nonlocal, the model transfers well from relatively small training structures to substantially larger supercells. They state that it can capture GW-level electron-phonon band-gap renormalization in supercells with thermal displacements. The paper presents this as evidence of the approach's power and as a practical route toward large-scale many-body simulations. The authors also suggest it could support foundation models for excited-state electronic structure. The article does not describe any further publication steps or follow-up work beyond this preprint.

Articles.Title: Deep Learning GW Quasiparticle Hamiltonians for Many-Body Excited-State Electronic Structure at Scale

stories.Headline: DScale: Scaling Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Verification
stories.Summary:
The article is an arXiv preprint, posted on October 24, 2026, that introduces DScale, a method for speeding up large language model inference. The paper was submitted on September 29, 2026, by Rongjian Chen, Minxian Xu, Zhengxin Fang, Kejiang Ye and Chengzhong Xu. It addresses block-diffusion speculative decoding, a technique that struggles at high concurrency because of verification padding, rejected candidates, and mismatches between variable-length prefixes and fixed-shape computation graphs. The authors say uniform truncation discards tokens that could have been accepted.

DScale keeps the drafter's architecture, weights and full draft length intact, and adds a separate predictor of 112K parameters that the paper says needs no confidence calibration or hardware speed-curve preparation. The method uses path-aware tiles to reduce padding and a dynamic verify-length allocation that packs scored prefixes into half the native verification capacity. Fixed-address workspaces let changing boundaries pass through verification and acceptance while reusing captured graphs. The paper reports tests on an A100-40GB GPU with tensor parallelism set to 1, using Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B across four datasets and concurrency levels from 8 to 32.

Against the baselines, the authors report geometric-mean throughput gains for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B of 43.9% and 48.8% over DFlash, 22.2% and 37.7% over DSpark, and 24.4% and 32.0% over Domino, along with lower request latency. Their ablations show each of the three mechanisms successively increases throughput, and budget adjustment improves retention of accepted tokens. GPU profiling indicates that full decode-step time on GSM8K falls by 30.8% to 52.5% relative to DFlash. The paper is 12 pages and is listed under distributed, parallel and cluster computing and artificial intelligence, with a PDF and HTML version available. The article does not describe any peer review outcome or planned release of code beyond what the listing shows.

Articles.Title: DScale: Scaling Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Verification

stories.Headline: ReLMem: Learning Recurrent Memory for Longitudinal EHR Modeling
stories.Summary:
A team of six researchers led by Zijie Meng posted a machine learning paper on arXiv on September 29, 2026, describing a method called ReLMem, short for Recurrent Longitudinal Memory. The work addresses a problem in modeling electronic health records over time: as a patient's history grows with each new visit, large language models face rising computational and memory costs when they must reread every earlier record. The authors describe a fixed-capacity memory that is updated visit by visit, so the model never needs to reprocess the full history. The paper was listed under Computer Science, in the Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence categories.

The core idea is to keep a compact, continually updated patient memory within a fixed budget while a frozen LLM does the prediction. ReLMem attaches lightweight compression adapters to the model, which update the memory from its previous state and each incoming visit without rereading earlier records. Training uses two kinds of supervision: an intermediate step that aligns attention outputs from the compressed memory with those from the full history under identical queries, and a final step that minimizes cross-entropy against ground truth answers based on the final memory. The authors say these steps are meant to keep task-relevant information from being progressively lost as updates accumulate. The paper's stated focus is the case of a fixed memory budget, which is where that loss would otherwise occur.

On medication prediction using EHR data, the authors report that ReLMem approaches the F1 scores of a full-history baseline while reducing average retained historical storage by 97.1 percent. Under the same memory budget, it improved macro-F1 and micro-F1 over the strongest compressed-memory baseline by 4.66 and 4.75 percentage points, respectively. The authors conclude that learning recurrent patient memory is a useful route to efficient longitudinal EHR modeling. The paper is a preprint, and the listed version is v1, submitted on September 29, 2026, with a DOI assigned through DataCite. The articles do not report peer review, an publication venue, or any clinical deployment of the method.

Articles.Title: ReLMem: Learning Recurrent Memory for Longitudinal EHR Modeling

stories.Headline: Cardinal Radcliffe: In age of AI, encourage young people to ask questions
stories.Summary:
Cardinal Timothy Radcliffe told the International Congress for Pastoral Care in Schools and Universities, held at the Vatican on October 22-23 and organized by the Dicastery for Culture and Education, that young people can be inspired in the age of artificial intelligence by being invited to ask questions, be adventurous, and pay attention to life and to others. He made the remarks on Friday, October 23, during a session titled "Human Digital." His talk focused on how to engage the imagination of young people in the digital age. He began by saying that tension is a basic part of life, and that it sits at the heart of Christianity and can be lived fruitfully and joyfully. He observed that young people, though anxious after coming of age in the digital era, long for both security and adventure.

He linked this tension to a passage from The Hobbit, in which Bilbo Baggins leaves his safe home for an adventure. Drawing on St. Paul's letter to the Romans, which says nothing can separate us from God's love, he argued that young people will be inspired if they are offered both a safe home and an invitation to risk their lives. He described this paradoxical love as founded on close attention to others, and he contrasted it with a digital world full of distraction. In that setting, he said, attention becomes precious.

Citing Simone Weil, he described the rarest form of generosity as seeing others as they relate to themselves rather than to oneself. He also said people should be willing to be the object of attention, and he pointed to two Dominican sisters whose recent viral video of laughing together drew wide interest. Cardinal Radcliffe said the same tension appears in Church teaching. He observed that many young people are drawn to Catholicism because they see the Church as faithful to the Gospels and tradition, and that they long for certainty.

He stressed, however, that faith is also an intellectual adventure, since understanding the Church's teachings is always a beginning. He warned that certainty without inquiry becomes fundamentalism, while questioning without fidelity to tradition risks relativism. Citing Pope Leo's Magnifica Humanitas, St. Thomas Aquinas and others, he argued that asking questions, wondering and thinking are essential to human life and cannot be replaced by AI. He noted that God's conversations with humanity in the Bible often take the form of questions that invite people into a deeper life.

Finally, he addressed the effect of AI on work and employment, saying the world urgently needs a new vision of work that is about being human rather than only about survival. He held that presence cannot be imitated by AI, citing social workers, a teacher who stays after class with a child, and a chaplain at a bedside. He concluded by calling for young people to be freed from the abstractions of the digital world and drawn out of self-absorption into wonder at creation and its Creator. The article does not report any further steps or follow-up plans from the congress.

Articles.Title: Cardinal Radcliffe: In age of AI, encourage young people to ask questions

stories.Headline: Is AI going to kill us? Does AI have a soul? A cybermissionary weighs in
stories.Summary:
Wes Woodell, a Tennessee-based ministry technology strategist who founded Connect My Church, spoke with the Christian Chronicle's Bobby Ross Jr. by Zoom in an interview published October 23, 2026, about artificial intelligence. Woodell is developing AI tools, in cooperation with the Renew.org Network, that would let people ask questions of an enclosed set of resources and receive answers, rather than just playing recordings. He is also pursuing a Ph.D. in intercultural studies at Talbot School of Theology at Biola University, and he works through a website called Ask Bible Questions. The interview grew out of a question Ross asked about whether AI could kill people, a concern Woodell said was not unfounded in areas like security. Ross also asked about the soul.

Woodell described the risks of networked machines, such as humanoid robots that a hostile government might hack and control at once. He said that the same advanced tools can be used defensively, and that national security makes it important to stay at the front of the field. He called this more important than the space race. On the spiritual question, he said he does not believe AI can have a soul, because it processes data rather than thinking. He argued that the phrase "supreme intelligence" is a misnomer, since AI is a complex mathematical equation and a computer program.

Woodell acknowledged that others disagree, noting that some people in Silicon Valley believe they can create God and pursue transhumanism, the idea of merging human consciousness with machines to achieve immortality. He offered practical advice for churches, suggesting AI can handle routine work such as scheduling, social media posts, bulletins, and letter drafting. He is building a tool that helps churches put sermons online in search-friendly form. He warned against preachers using AI to write their sermons, saying it is unhealthy and bad for a preacher's heart, though AI may offer some helpful feedback. The article notes that Barna Group recently asked whether AI should hand off to a human in a crisis, a question the piece suggests will remain timely.

Articles.Title: Is AI going to kill us? Does AI have a soul? A cybermissionary weighs in

stories.Headline: Mouser Highlights Industrial AI and Machine Learning in Automation Resource Center
stories.Summary:
Mouser Electronics, Inc., the global distributor of electronic components and industrial automation products, has launched an automation AI and machine learning resource center, as reported by AZoM on October 23, 2026. The hub gives engineers a central place to find content and insights on how artificial intelligence and machine learning are making industrial automation more autonomous, efficient and adaptable. According to the article, AI can reduce the manual effort needed to configure robot cells for changing production needs while keeping controls reliable, and frameworks such as OpenUSD can support system design and validation before deployment. The center offers practical guides and expert commentary on AI-assisted configuration and physical AI, which is AI embedded directly into machines so they can sense conditions and make decisions in real time.

The article describes several ways these technologies are being applied. Machine learning can help existing automation systems interpret and respond to real-world conditions, and AI can support reconfiguring systems while engineers keep control of critical decisions.
