stories.Headline: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation
stories.Summary:
Researchers Liuzhenghao Lv, Yuyang Liu, Yuyang Gao, Li Yuan and Yonghong Tian posted a preprint on arXiv describing RipplePLM, a system for generating natural-language descriptions of how a single point mutation in a protein affects its function. The paper was first submitted on October 1, 2026, and a revised version followed on October 3, 2026. The authors say the work is slated for NeurIPS 2026. The arXiv listing is dated October 24, 2026.

The authors argue that existing protein-to-text systems mix mutation information into a single undifferentiated representation, which ignores how the evidence is organized across structure and biochemistry. RipplePLM addresses this with a component called Direct-Distal Cross-Attention, which builds a residue-level map from pre-trained protein language models and splits mutation information into two pathways: the mutation site's immediate contact neighborhood and its multi-hop distal context. A second component, the Property Latent Chain, feeds expert-guided signals about biochemical changes, such as thermostability and optimal pH, into the language model through latent property tokens. The authors report that on the MutaDescribe benchmark, average ROUGE-L on the structural split rose from 22.23 to 35.65 under a matched-backbone comparison, and that expert reviewers judged a higher share of its descriptions biologically accurate or relevant than the mutation-specific baseline.

The authors state that ablations, representation diagnostics and low-data fitness regression experiments further support the learned mutation-aware representations. The paper's abstract and listing do not identify any external reviewer, institution-level endorsement or independent replication of these results. The code is linked from the abstract page. The articles do not say what follows next, such as peer review outcomes or adoption by other groups.

Articles.Title: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation

stories.Headline: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on October 1, 2026, by Fengpeng Li and five co-authors describes a new training method called TRACE, short for Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure, aimed at multi-turn safety in large language models. The authors note that safety-aligned models often refuse a harmful request made in a single prompt but comply once the same goal is spread across several turns. They argue that existing preference objectives, which score whole responses to single prompts, cannot control this risk on unseen conversation histories. The paper was listed under the Artificial Intelligence category, and its DOI was given as 10.48550/arXiv.2610.01323.

The paper presents analysis giving sufficient conditions under which suppressing harmful behavior at supervised single-turn contexts yields a bound on multi-turn trajectory risk. That bound is described as accounting for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and as measuring contraction relative to a base-policy risk budget. TRACE turns this principle into a token-level objective, weighting each token of a safe response by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. The advantage compares a frozen reference model with a copy whose refusal behavior has been ablated, so earlier response tokens can receive credit from later refusal-related evidence. A gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set in the method.

The authors report testing across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, and they say TRACE produced the lowest attack success rate in all 35 model and attack pairs. They also report that model utility, measured on the MMLU and HellaSwag benchmarks, dropped by at most 1.23 points. The paper states that source code is included in the supplemental material. The article itself does not describe any reaction from outside researchers, companies, or regulators, and it does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed or accepted at a conference. The submission is a single version, v1, dated October 1, 2026.

Articles.Title: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety

stories.Headline: Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on October 2, 2026, by Reiho Li, Razmik Arman Khosrovian, Takaharu Yaguchi, Hiroaki Yoshimura and Takashi Matsubara introduces a neural network model called Dirac-interconnected neural elements, or DINEs. The paper, which runs 29 pages with 3 figures and 8 tables, is listed under machine learning and was indexed by doi.org on October 24, 2026. The authors describe it as a way to model physical systems built from interconnected components. The article's own figures give no evidence of any wider release or institutional announcement beyond the paper itself.

The authors say existing methods either need the connections between components to be known in advance or reduce a system to an ordinary differential equation, which discards the algebraic constraints that the interconnections impose. DINEs instead represent a physical system as a differential-algebraic equation, with those constraints given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. From data, the model identifies both the interconnection among components, as a Dirac structure, and the behavior of each component, as a neural network. The learned subsystems stay in unreduced form, so they can be isolated or combined into a new system without retraining, and the model can also handle partially observable systems. The paper reports experimental results on physical systems that the authors say existing methods cannot reach.

The article names the five authors and their paper but does not describe any affiliations, funding details beyond a partial acknowledgment, or public statements from them beyond the abstract. It also does not say whether code or the trained models have been released. The paper is an unreviewed preprint, and the excerpt does not indicate any peer review or follow-up work. The provided text does not say what the next steps for the research will be.

Articles.Title: Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric Unveils Modular Power Systems for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric announced on October 23 that it has unveiled new Prefabricated Power Modules and Power Skids meant to let operators build power infrastructure for artificial intelligence data centers in as little as six months. Both products rest on a reference design for AI data centers that the company developed together with Nvidia. The aim is to manufacture power equipment in advance, rather than assembling individual pieces at the data center site, so that construction timelines shrink and electricity delivery stays stable. Power demand is rising fast as dense, high-performance graphics processing units are deployed, and the denser the GPUs, the more electricity and cooling they require.

The reference design targets Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 system and supports power density of up to 142 kilowatts per rack, while combining power management with liquid cooling controls. The power modules use Schneider Electric's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities: 2 megawatts, 2.25 megawatts and 2.5 megawatts. The 2.5-megawatt version has the largest capacity of any single-container prefabricated power solution the company has released so far. Capacity can also be expanded by adding modules, so operators can build for initial demand and scale up in stages as more GPU servers arrive.

An official at Schneider Electric said that securing the necessary power infrastructure quickly and reliably is critical to scaling AI data centers. The official added that by applying the design co-developed with Nvidia, the company hopes to help customers handle high-density AI environments and expand their equipment as power demand shifts. The company plans to sell the products not only to large hyperscale data centers but also to neoclouds, which provide AI-dedicated cloud services, and to colocation data centers that host servers for multiple companies. It expects the approach to suit facilities with large power needs, such as clusters used to train AI models and large GPU server deployments.

The products will be designed, manufactured and tested at the company's production facility in Sant Boi de Llobregat, near Barcelona, Spain, before shipping. Schneider Electric recently expanded that site to keep up with rising demand for modular data center infrastructure. Sales will begin in Europe, with supply widening to North America during 2026 and then reaching other regions, including Asia-Pacific. Separately, the company announced a collaboration with Nvidia and HPE on October 22 to bring industrial AI agents to process industries at the edge, though that effort is distinct from the power modules.

Articles.Title: Schneider Electric Unveils Modular Power Systems for AI Data Centers - Seoul Economic Daily
